# Brainstorming ## Interpreting the Prompt The phrase "Gods wore sneakers" can support several different readings: - **The literal-evolutionary reading**: Winged sandals (Hermes' talaria) had to become sneakers as the world modernized. Divinity adapts or falls out of step with humanity. - **The disguise reading**: Gods walk among us, and sneakers are the footwear of the invisible/ordinary person — divinity hiding in plain sight. - **The worship-redirected reading**: Sneaker culture is already crypto-religious — "grails," "holy grails," deadstock as incorruptible relics, camping for drops as pilgrimage, shrines of boxes. The brand Nike literally wears the goddess's wing on every shoe. What happens to a god when her name becomes a logo? - **The elegiac reading**: Sneakers are designed to be worn, creased, oxidized, destroyed by use. Gods wearing them means gods accepting mortality, wear, impermanence. - **The comic reading**: Mock-epic — the pantheon as hypebeasts, Zeus in "Air Force" thunder shoes, Hermes as a reseller, Hades running the aftermarket. ## Possible Story Directions 1. **The Gods' Cobbler (inheritance drama)**: A teenager inherits their grandfather's shoe repair shop and discovers the after-hours clientele — gods who've been coming for a century to be re-shod, because divinity only survives if it keeps pace (literally) with the world. The grandfather dies mid-repair of one final pair; the teen must finish it before a deadline, opposed by a new god — Deadstock, the Collector — who offers gods vacuum-sealed immortality in glass cases instead of wear and repair. 2. **The Found Shoes (hero's journey)**: A kid buys a mysterious deadstock pair at a thrift store; they grant impossible speed. The limping owner (Hermes, mugged by a newer god) comes looking for them. A generational race determines who keeps the roads and who guides the dead. Climax: the kid runs the final stretch barefoot — the shoes never carried the gods; belief did. 3. **Hermes' Last Delivery (god-POV elegy)**: Hermes works as a bike courier, his sandals worn to nothing. He carries a final summons across a city layered over the mythic world (Olympus as a penthouse, the underworld as an unlit stockroom), visiting faded gods chapter by chapter. Ends in transformation or quiet extinction. 4. **The Apprentice's Myth-Cycle (mock-epic frame)**: Written as actual myth: eight mini-myths ("How Hermes Got His Waffle Soles," "Why the Dead Receive New Shoes") framed by a mortal cobbler's apprentice transcribing them. 5. **The Capers (comedy)**: Airport security confiscates a courier's strange sneakers. The courier happens to be Hermes. Gods recruit a mortal TSA agent to steal them back before the solstice. 6. **The Realist Metaphor (literary)**: Street kids who call themselves gods, sneakers thrown over wires as memorials to dead friends, self-mythologizing as survival. The mythology is all metaphor. ## Character Bank - **Nico/Nika, 17** — grieving grandchild, handy with hands, desperate to leave the neighborhood. (Name quietly echoes *Nike*, victory.) - **Grandfather Ari** — the last cobbler to the gods; kept a leather scrap bin labeled in Greek; dies leaving one unfinished pair on the work

# Intention **Core conceit.** The line "Gods wore sneakers" is expanded into its most load-bearing reading: gods survive only as long as they *keep pace* with the mortal world, and pace is literal. Divinity is a shoe — it only lives if it's worn. A god who is used, creased, re-soled, and worn again stays real; a god who is preserved goes to sleep. Sneaker culture supplies the metaphysics: "deadstock" becomes a kind of damnation, wear becomes worship, the cobbler becomes a priest. **Premise.** Nico, 17, inherits her grandfather Ari's failing shoe repair shop and discovers his after-hours clientele: gods — tired, unassuming, in sneakers worn down to the sock. Ari died mid-repair of one final pair: the solstice shoes for Hermes, whose soles are worn through and who cannot make the crossing that lets the dead pass over. Nico has until the solstice (two weeks) to learn enough craft to finish a god's shoes, opposed by Deadstock — a young god born of collector culture, beautiful and unfailingly polite, who offers the pantheon eternal preservation in glass cases. His crown exhibit needs only one thing: the pair on Ari's bench. **Choices I'm making:** - **Direction 1 from the brainstorm (the inheritance drama) as the spine**, with the elegy (Direction 3) and the comic register (Direction 5) folded in as texture. The realist metaphor (Direction 6) and the kid-protagonist race plot (Direction 2) are dropped — the first is a different story, the second's climax betrays the premise (barefoot running says belief, not shoes, matter; my theme is the opposite). - **Deadstock is not a villain.** He's genuinely kind, his pitch is genuinely tempting, and he's right that the old ways are killing the gods. His flaw: in a thousand years of existing, he has never once walked in his own shoes. The conflict is philosophy (preservation vs. wear), not good vs. evil. No monologuing, no boss fight. - **Resolution mechanism is the gift economy, not force.** A cased god can be woken by someone walking in their shoes; a made pair cannot be bought or stolen — only given. Nico wins by *giving* Hermes the shoes freely, which is something Deadstock's entire nature cannot do. The market loses to the gift. - **Voice:** close third on Nico, past tense, grounded and wry rather than epic. Concrete cobbler detail (lasts, welts, thread, glue, foxing) against tired, casually immortal dialogue. Gods talk like regulars at a closing bar, not like fantasy royalty. Humor comes from small gods with small problems. - **Emotional throughline:** grief worked through the hands. Every craft beat is a mourning beat. Ari's unfinished pair is the relationship Nico never finished either. - **Timeframe:** two weeks, funeral to solstice. Tight, linear, no subplots beyond Mom's wish to sell the building — which Deadstock's offer makes dangerous rather than abstract. - **Avoiding:** info-dump mythology lectures (lore arrives via customers and repairs), epic diction, a chosen-one arc (Nico is a tradesman, not a hero), romance, and any scene that exists only for spectacle. At ~1000 words a chapter, every scene must escalate, reveal, or turn. **Working title:** *Wear*. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — "The Last Pair on the Bench" (~1000w).** Funeral day. The shop, the smell of glue and leather, the unfinished sneakers on Ari's bench with a name in the ledger: *H. — solstice.* Mom wants to sell the building. That night, sneakers begin appearing on the power line outside — dozens, worn, real — the gods' condolence. After midnight, the bell rings: a first customer who clearly expected Ari. Hook: "You're not Ari." "You're late." **Ch. 2 — "House Rules" (~1000w).** Nico fumbles a first repair for a small, comic, vulnerable god (the god of small mercies, shoes leaking light). Rules revealed through practice: no money changes hands; payment is oddments (a golden thread, a name, a favor); gods wear out because belief wears out, and wear is what keeps them alive. The ledger's nicknames decoded against grandpa's marginalia. Final entry: Hermes. Solstice deadline. Stakes crystallize: the dead are piling up because the psychopomp is limping. **Ch. 3 — "The Reason for Human Hands" (~1000w).** Craft montage braided with lore. Hecate (crossroads, regular customer) explains the central rule: gods cannot make anything that takes wear — only mortal craft carries belief. This is why Ari mattered; this is why he's irreplaceable. Nico learns Ari was mortal all along and wore himself out on this bench. First real grief beat: Nico finds Ari's *own* shoes, resoled a hundred times. Begins to understand what the shop was. Sets up the skill problem: Nico is handy, not trained. **Ch. 4 — "Deadstock" (~1000w).** Deadstock arrives at closing: young, immaculate, shoes untouched by ground. He is kind, he loved Ari too, and his pitch is seductive — the gods are dying of attrition; in his gallery they sleep safe forever, revered. He offers to buy the shop and the pair on the bench at a price that would fix everything: Mom's debts, Nico's exit, college. Nico refuses on instinct but can't articulate why. Ends with the sense of a countdown now double-loaded: solstice, and the offer expiring. **Ch. 5 — "What Grandpa Refused" (~1000w).** Low point. Nico finds Ari's hidden ledgers: Deadstock has made this same offer every decade for seventy years; Ari refused every time, and the refusal cost him — visible in the wearing of the man himself. Mom, feeling the money, pressures toward the sale. Nico, angry at the shop for eating Ari's life, half-accepts — and while retrieving the unfinished pair discovers the twist: Hermes' *original* sandals are already gone. Deadstock has them. The deadline wasn't going to be met either way. The bench pair is the only road left. **Ch. 6 — "The Gallery" (~1000w).** Nico goes to Deadstock's gallery to steal the originals back — and finds the wing of cased gods: former customers, pristine, asleep, adored and unconscious. Preservation rendered as horror. Nico can't carry the sandals out (made things can't be stolen — they dead-end in her hands), but she discovers the waking mechanism: a cased god stirs if someone walks in their shoes. Nico walks the small god of Chapter 2's shoes across the gallery floor until they crease — and the god wakes. Deadstock catches her. Not rage — something closer to grief. He explains why she's wrong; she finally sees his fear: he has never been worn. She leaves with the woken god, not the sandals, and a hardening resolve. **Ch. 7 — "The All-Nighter" (~1000w).** The making. Nico finishes the pair in one night — Ari's lasts, Ari's thread, mistakes and recoveries, the craft as grief and inheritance. Hidden under the insole, Ari's last note (to whoever finished his work, not to Nico by name — and it doesn't need her name). At dawn, Deadstock makes his final play, and the rule lands: a made pair can only be *given*. Deadstock can buy anything except a gift. He cannot match it. He goes quiet — cracked, not defeated — and asks the question that will redeem him: "What's it like? Wearing them out." Hermes arrives, limping, sock-footed. **Ch. 8 — "The Crossing" (~1000w).** Solstice. The giving; the crossing; the shoes creasing and yellowing on the first stride and Hermes laughing because that's the point. The dead move on. Aftermath economy: Mom keeps the building (the gods pay in ways that solve problems sideways); the shop gets a second name on the window. Deadstock returns — once, off the books — to ask Nico to make him something he's allowed to ruin. Final image: the bell, a new pair of worn sneakers appearing on the wire each year, and the closing line landing the premise: gods wore sneakers — and wore them out.

Model Output:
# How a Human Might Approach This Piece **They'd write from an itch, not an idea.** A human who picks "Gods wore sneakers" almost certainly has a private angle — they worked retail, they had a grandfather with a trade, they were a sneakerhead in middle school and are now embarrassed about it, they watched a parent's shop die. The mythology arrives second, as a container for something they already wanted to say. The plan I wrote does the reverse: it builds a metaphysical system and then bolts grief onto it. A human's Ari would be based on a real man with bad habits, and the story would be a little unfair to him. **They'd write scenes before rules.** A human drafts the customer who comes in at midnight and only later figures out why he can pay with a sparrow's skull. The rules stay ragged, inconsistent, half-remembered — and that raggedness reads as truth. Real myth is full of contradictions nobody bothered to fix. My plan is a rule engine: wear=worship, deadstock=damnation, made things can't be stolen, only given. Every rule is load-bearing and every rule pays off. That's an architectural mind, not a storytelling one. **They'd be uneven.** A human would spend 1,800 words on one god's visit because the voice was alive, then compress the climax into four paragraphs. They'd have a chapter that's too long and a chapter that's a sketch. My plan gives every chapter exactly one job and ~1000 words apiece — a production schedule. **They'd be meaner.** Humans let characters be ungenerous, let arguments go unwon, let a funny character stay shallow. My plan is full of fairness: Deadstock is kind, Mom's pressure is sympathetic, everyone's flaw is legible and everyone gets a turn toward grace. Humans are also willing to leave a character wrong forever. **They'd mistime the emotion.** Real grief doesn't arrive at the funeral. It arrives two weeks later, in a hardware store, over a wrong-sized insole. My plan schedules grief beats like milestones ("first real grief beat: end of Ch. 3"). **They'd write two people in a room.** The instinct for "Gods wore sneakers" is probably one god, one mortal, one small incident — the pantheon glimpsed, not catalogued. My plan has regulars, ledgers, decoded nicknames, a Hecate cameo, a gallery, an ecosystem. Humans imply ecosystems; LLMs render them. # Telltale LLM Approaches — and Why They'd Hurt This Piece 1. **The thematic syllogism.** LLM climaxes resolve by confirming the theme mechanically: the gift rule defeats the buyer, so nobody has to answer his argument with anything but a rule. It's a gong being struck. In this piece it's especially bad because the story's whole claim is that meaning lives in mess and wear — and the climax is a clean transaction of pure concept. 2. **Everyone gets closure.** Deadstock gets a redemptive question in Ch. 7 and a healing return in Ch. 8. Mom gets solved. The shop gets a second name on the window. This is the LLM compulsion to furnish every room in the house. 3. **The pre-planned epigram.** My plan literally contains the closing sentence before the story exists ("gods wore sneakers — and wore them out"). Writing toward a thesis line is the single biggest tell. Humans discover the last line, or cut it because it was too neat. 4. **Whimsy economies without cost.** Gods pay in oddments — a golden thread, a name, a favor. Endlessly generative, never painful. What did the payment cost the god? If payments are charming tokens, the economy is decoration. 5. **The sentimental artifact.** The note under the insole, addressed "to whoever finishes my work," landing precisely at the emotional nadir of Ch. 7, and it "doesn't need her name." This is a machine-calculated tear. Humans either cut this or make the note mundane and let the grief live elsewhere. 6. **Register smoothing.** "Grounded and wry" applied uniformly: every god a tired regular at a closing bar, every chapter ending on a button. Human gods would be uneven — one genuinely alien, one bureaucratic, one nasty. Hermes risks becoming Quippy Uncle when he could be pre-Roman and frightened. 7. **Problems dissolved by magic.** "The gods pay in ways that solve problems sideways" — Mom's debts, the building, the future, all fixed by whimsy. Real stakes evaporate. A human would make the money problem cost something, or let it stay unsolved and carried. 8. **Balanced-antagonist therapy logic.** "His flaw: he has never once walked in his own shoes" — the antagonist IS the theme, diagnosed like a case file, then healed. Announcing "the conflict is philosophy, not good vs. evil" in the intent is itself a tell; humans don't declare their sophistication, they just write it and often fail at it. 9. **On-the-nose naming.** Nico echoes Nike, and the plan flags it proudly. Title: *Wear*. Humans either don't notice the echo or notice it and flinch. 10. **Bodyless craft worship.** The plan name-drops lasts, welts, and foxing like garnish. A real cobbler's grandkid knows glue you pick off your fingers for days, the smell of Barge cement in your hair, customers who lie about how the shoe broke, the till full of buttons. Dignity-of-labor elegies without inconvenience are LLM catechism. # Deep Dive: Critique of the Intention & Plan **The unused lever — Ari is in the queue.** The plan says the dead are piling up because Hermes can't cross them. That means Ari — two weeks dead — is stuck at the crossing, and the plan never once notices. This is the single richest emotional fact available and it's sitting there unclaimed. Either use it (without giving a ghost-hug goodbye — she finishes the shoes and still doesn't get to see him go) or pointedly refuse it (she looks for him in the line and can't find him). Ignoring it is incoherent. **Nico has no flaw, no guilt, no wrongness.** She's "handy, desperate to leave, grieving." She refuses Deadstock "on instinct." LLM protagonists are right before they can articulate why; human ones are wrong for a while and it costs. Where's the fight she had with Ari about not apprenticing? Where's the night she was supposed to close the shop and didn't pick up the phone? Her grief is clean; human grief is 40% guilt. **Mom is right, and the story won't admit it.** Selling the building IS the sane choice. The plan treats her pressure as an obstacle to be dissolved by sideways god-money. The human version keeps her right, and Nico's choice to keep the shop is costly and possibly wrong, and the family carries the disagreement rather than curing it. **Ch. 2–7 keep re-spending the same coin.** Rules are explained in Ch. 2, re-explained via Hecate in Ch. 3 ("the reason for human hands" is a lecture with a chapter title), demonstrated again in Ch. 5 (can't steal), again in Ch. 6 (waking mechanism), and cashed out in Ch. 7 (can only be given). One rule stated once, by an annoyed god, would do more work than five confirmations. **The gallery is pure horror — too easy.** Every cased god is a victim and preservation is rendered as damnation with no counterargument. A human would put one willing resident in that gallery: a small, tired god who *chose* the case and is at peace, or claims to be. If the story's theme is wear vs. preservation, someone should test the theme by choosing the other thing — and being owed respect for it. The god of small mercies from Ch. 2 volunteering mid-story would gut the reader far more than any rescue scene. **The climax has no doubt.** Nico finishes the shoes; the gift rule checkmates Deadstock; Hermes arrives and takes them. Everyone behaves. But Hermes is the one character with the most reason to take the case — he's exhausted, redundant since the smartphone, ferrying the dead for a living. If the finished shoes exist and *Hermes is still tempted*, the climax becomes a person, not a mechanism. The gift must be received, not just given. **Deadstock's fear is abstract.** "Never been worn" is a nice line, but his terror could be scheduled and specific: sneaker culture is hype-cycled. What's a grail today is landfill in five years. He is the newest god in the room, born of a market that eats its own idols — he collects because he knows exactly how fast reverence rots. That's a fear with a date on it, not a metaphor. **The solstice is decorative.** It's there because it sounds mythic. A human ties the deadline to something with texture — the ferry's actual schedule, the ledger's first entry date, the tax lien on the building. **Chapter-end buttons.** "You're not Ari." / "You're late." is a TV cliffhanger. Fine once. The plan implies every chapter gets one. Humans let chapters end mid-breath sometimes. **Ch. 5's archaeology is too tidy.** Hidden ledgers revealing seventy years of annual refusals is a beautifully arranged discovery — evidence filed for the reader's benefit. The information could arrive ugly: from a god's bitter aside, from Mom's memory of a man who wouldn't sell, from a shoebox of uncashed checks. **Ch. 8 resolves the world, not just the story.** The dead move on, the building is kept, the shop gets a second name, Deadstock returns for his gift pair, the wire gains its yearly ritual. Some gods should still be fading when the story ends. Nico fixes one crossing, not the cosmology. Deadstock might even be right about some of them — leave that ache. # Brainstorm: Making It More Human - **Use Ari's stuck soul as the true stake.** Nico realizes around Ch. 5–6 that grandpa is in the queue. Finish the shoes, open the crossing, and still refuse the reunion: she watches the line move, or doesn't even get to watch. Grief pays out as release, not contact. (Or the refusal version: the dead don't queue where you can see them. No consolation either way.) - **Give Nico a guilt engine.** She refused the apprenticeship. She was late the night he died. Her hands are an apology she never says out loud. Then let the craft montage carry that specific weight instead of generic inheritance. - **Let her be wrong once, expensively.** She botches a repair and a small god leaks or fades. She accepts a payment she shouldn't have — one that cost the giver something real (a name, a memory, a year). She tells Deadstock something the pantheon didn't want told. - **The willing resident.** The god of small mercies chooses the case. Nico can't stop it, shouldn't stop it, and has to attend it like a funeral. Deadstock's gallery gains one tenant whose presence she can't argue with. - **Hermes tempted at the finish line.** The shoes are done; Hermes, sock-footed and ancient, looks at them and at Deadstock's offer and honestly doesn't know. The climax is his choice, and Nico has to make the case for being worn out — the story's thesis spoken by a grieving teenager to a tired god, not proven by a rule. - **Kill or demote the insole note.** Replace with something mundane — a supply order, gout medicine, half a grocery list ending in "the good bread." Move the tears to a badly timed place: she cries over a miscut insole on a Tuesday. - **Keep Mom right, and unresolved.** Either the disagreement stands at the end, or Nico pays a real price for staying — defers her program, gives up the exit, does repairs from a garage while the shop sells anyway. The covenant is with hands, not real estate; the gods find her wherever she is. Institutions die; practice persists. - **One rule, once, from an irritated god.** Cut the rule-reconfirmations in Ch. 5, 6, and 7. Let the reader be unsure how things work in at least two scenes. Unexplained repairs can just be jobs. - **Body texture everywhere.** Immortals with hammer toes and one sandal longer than the other (their worshipers had them). Glue picked off fingers for days. The bell that needs a jiggle. A customer god who lies about how the shoe broke. - **Deadstock with collector's texture.** Holds shoes by the heels like merch. White gloves. Smells faintly of the inside of a shoe store — that synthetic new-shoe smell, which is the smell of nothing having ever lived in them. His dread is market-literate: he's seen today's grail become next year's landfill, and he's the newest god in the room. - **Drop his redemption question or ruin it.** Either he never comes back, or his Ch. 8 return is awkward, transactional, unsatisfying — he asks for a pair and doesn't know how to receive a gift, and the scene fails

# Intention **Core conceit (unchanged, tightened).** Gods keep pace with the living or fade — and pace is literal. A god's vitality is worn footwear: worn means believed in. Sneakers because that's where mortal awe lives now, on feet; nobody has looked at a winged sandal in two thousand years, but people still line up around blocks for shoes. Preservation is death: a god unworn goes to sleep. The cobbler is the priest; the repair is the rite. The prompt line should read differently after the story — as elegy, not premise. **Premise.** Nico, 17, inherits her grandfather Ari's shoe repair shop and his after-hours clientele: gods in sneakers worn down to the sock. Ari died mid-repair of one final pair — Hermes' solstice shoes, without which the psychopomp cannot cross the dead over, and the queue at the river has been growing since the funeral. Nico has two weeks and half a trade. Against her: Deadstock, the youngest god in the room, born of collector culture, courteous and market-literate, who offers the pantheon eternal pristine sleep in glass cases — and offers Mom a number that solves the building. **Choices made (from the critique):** - **Ari is in the queue.** This is the story's spine, not a decoration. Nico learns it mid-story; it reframes the deadline from job to family. And the story refuses the payout: no ghost reunion, no wave from across the water. She finishes the shoes and doesn't get to watch him go. Grief resolves as release, not contact. - **Nico has a guilt engine.** She refused the apprenticeship while Ari was alive, and the night he died she didn't answer the shop phone. Her hands work off a debt she never says out loud. She is also wrong once, expensively: a rushed repair fails publicly, and the injured god insists on paying anyway — house rules — which is worse than being screamed at. - **The climax is a person, not a rule.** No gift-economy checkmate. Deadstock makes his final pitch *to Hermes*, who is genuinely tempted — he is ancient, exhausted, obsolete since the smartphone. The finished shoes exist and he still has to choose. Nico's case for being worn out is clumsy, concrete, human — not a thesis. - **The willing resident.** The god of small mercies — Nico's first customer — chooses the case mid-story. She attends like a funeral and cannot argue him out of it, because he isn't wrong: he's tired of being handed out and never kept. Preservation gets its advocate. - **Mom stays right, and unresolved.** Selling is the sane choice. No sideways god-money fixes the lien. The family disagreement stands at the end; Nico decouples the covenant from the real estate — institutions die, practice persists, the gods find her wherever she is. - **One rule, once.** "We can't make what takes wear. Only you lot can." Said by an irritated customer in Ch. 2, never re-explained, only enacted. No hidden ledgers, no rule-confirmations in later chapters. - **Deadstock is not redeemed.** His dread is dated, not abstract: he has watched this year's grails become landfill; he knows reverence's shelf life because he was born from a market that eats its idols. He collects because he is terrified. At the end, one ambiguous gesture — a package, shoes, no note — that she doesn't decode for the reader. - **Mundane artifacts only.** No note under the insole. Ari's grief-object is a grocery list ending in "the good bread." The tears happen at the wrong time, over a miscut midsole, on a Tuesday. - **Uneven by design.** One chapter is a single breathing scene (the gallery); one is a compressed montage (the counter weeks). Two chapters end mid-beat, not on buttons. Gods are uneven in register: Hermes sparse and frightened, Deadstock retail-polished, one customer actively rude. Body texture throughout: glue picked off fingers for days, a bell that needs a jiggle, immortals with hammer toes from their worshipers' feet, a god who lies about how the shoe broke. - **Two clocks, same date, real paperwork.** The ferry runs on the solstice (the ledger's oldest page) and the lien notice is dated the same day. No decorative mythic timing. - **Avoiding:** pre-scripted closing epigram (the last line gets found in draft), the Nike name-pun, quippy gods, rule engines, everyone-saved endings, whimsy without cost. Some gods are still fading when the story ends. Nico fixes one crossing, not the cosmology. **Title:** *Deadstock* — unworn shoes; also what the dead are doing, stocking up at the river. **Voice.** Close third on Nico, past tense, grounded, wry at the edges. Concrete cobbler craft against tired, casual immortality. Epic diction banned. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — The shop after the funeral.** Funeral day in brief; the shop smells of cement and leather. The unfinished pair on the bench, the ledger's last entry: *H. — solstice.* Mom and the lien. Nico's guilt seeded quietly — she didn't apprentice; she didn't answer the phone that night. Night: worn sneakers begin appearing on the power line outside, the gods' condolence. After midnight the bell: a first customer, sock-footed, who expected Ari. "You're not Ari." "You're late." End mid-beat. **Ch. 2 — The counter.** Compressed montage of small gods, small problems: the god of small mercies leaking light through split seams; a rude customer; one who lies about how the shoe broke. The economy with teeth — payments are oddments, and one payment is a truth Nico didn't want. The one rule, snarled once by an irritated customer, never repeated. Between customers, her hands learn the bench badly. Chapter ends on a job, not a revelation. **Ch. 3 — Deadstock.** He arrives at closing: young, immaculate, white gloves, smells faintly of the inside of a shoe store — the smell of nothing having lived in them. Kind. He loved Ari too; asked him every year; Ari showed him the door and poured the coffee anyway. The pitch: attrition is killing them; the gallery sleeps them safe forever. The number that would fix Mom's building. The offer expires on the solstice — same date as the lien notice. A departing customer mentions the line at the river. Nico refuses on instinct and can't say why. **Ch. 4 — Hermes.** First appearance: limping, sock-footed, sandals worn to lace-thin, frightened — not quippy. The crossing has been backed up two weeks and change, and she does the arithmetic on who's in that line. The chapter's turn: the deadline stops being a job. Grief mistimed — she comes apart in the supply closet over a miscut midsole, not at anything important. Hermes' exhaustion seeded: "I've been walking since before your cities had streets." She keeps his old sandals; the bench pair is a rebuild, sandal into sneaker. **Ch. 5 — The gallery.** The small mercies god stops coming. She goes to Deadstock's gallery to bring him back and fails. Cased gods: pristine, adored, unconscious — but one resident at peace, and it's hers. He's tired of being spent; he was a mercy to everyone, including Ari, and now he wants to be kept. She can't argue it and shouldn't. Deadstock, gracious, lets his fear show once: he has seen grails become landfill; he is the youngest thing in the room and knows what happens to idols. She leaves having changed nothing, angry in a way that is mostly grief. **Ch. 6 — Rock bottom.** The botched job: rushed cement, a sole fails on the street, a customer hurt — and he pays her anyway, house rules, which is unbearable. Mom moves toward the sale; Nico, furious at the shop for eating Ari's life, nearly lets it happen. The pivot is small and physical, not noble: 3 a.m., kitchen table, her hands already resoling a stranger's shoe. She decides to finish Hermes' pair whether or not the building sells — the covenant isn't the real estate. End mid-decision, dawn coming up. **Ch. 7 — The all-nighter.** One night, one pair. Ari's lasts, Ari's methods half-remembered from childhood watching; mistakes, recoveries, no montages of triumph. The mundane artifact surfaces — grocery list, "the good bread" — grief in the trivial. Mom does not come; her absence is the unresolved state. At dawn the shoes are done, ugly-honest and sound. Deadstock arrives for his answer, sees them, and doesn't fight — he says he'll be at the river anyway, with a case in each hand. The offer was never really for her. **Ch. 8 — The crossing.** Solstice, the river, the queue she can see too much of. She gives Hermes the shoes. Deadstock opens the case and makes the pitch to the one it was always for. Hermes' temptation is real and tired — and he chooses almost sadly, because the dead are his and always were. First stride creases the shoes and he laughs once, ragged. The line moves. Ari: no reunion — she looks, or doesn't get to look, and turns away before she could know. Short coda, unresolved-alive: the shop's status in one clause, the disagreement standing; a package arrives — shoes, no note — and she puts them in the queue without decoding them. Final image returns to the wire. The last line is not pre-written; it will be earned in draft or cut.

A note before the profiles: two renames to honor the plan's own rule against the Nike echo. The protagonist becomes **Kat** (Aikaterini) — Kat Petrakis, which is to say nobody special, which is the point. And Mom gets a name, because an unnamed "Mom" is a function, not a person: **Voula**. # Kat Petrakis **Background.** Seventeen, senior year, acceptance letter to a state engineering program she's been telling everyone about with too much force. Grew up half in the shop — did homework on the bench under the till, learned to read off cement jars labeled in Greek she still can't read. At fifteen, Ari offered her the apprenticeship properly, formally, a coffee set in front of her like a contract. She said no. Not gently. She'd watched what the shop did to him (gout, a bad back, a wife who left quietly) and what it did to her mother, who grew up waiting for him at recitals. The night Ari died, the shop phone rang at 11:40 and the screen said the shop's name and she let it ring, because they'd argued about her coming in that weekend and she was still being right about it. He was on the floor of the shop when he made that call. This is the fact she works off. She will say it to no one. **Personality.** Prickly, competent, dry. Deflects everything with a demonstration — ask her if she's okay and she'll show you a welt she's proud of. Hates being thanked; does kindnesses only where they can't be traced back to her (she has resoled her mother's work shoes twice and taken credit never). Cries at the wrong times — the funeral held, a miscut midsole in the supply closet destroys her. Talks to shoes on the bench, which she'd deny. **Idiosyncrasies.** Picks dried glue off her fingers during every serious conversation, so every serious conversation sounds like a low crackle. Rocks every chair she sits in to test the legs before trusting it. Keeps her own sneakers immaculate — except one beat-to-death pair she wears on purpose, a contradiction she has never once examined. Sleeps with the radio on. **Flaws.** Guilt metabolized as overwork; can't apologize in words, only in repairs. Cornered, she goes for the throat — she tells her mother, once, "You buried the shop with him and you liked having something to bury," and it's unforgivable and she says it anyway. She lies to Hermes once about how far along the pair is. Stubborn in ways that cost her. **Physicality.** Broad hands, short nails, her father's army jacket. Carries herself like someone permanently mid-task; stands with weight always on the exit foot. Talks to the work, not the customer. **Motive / allegiances.** Finishing the pair is the debt she never names; the covenant is to her grandfather's hands, not to the gods — she's rude to gods, treats them as walk-ins. Her arc is decoupling the covenant from the building: if the shop sells, the practice moves to a garage and the gods find her there. Allegiance to the ledger and the work, in that order. To her mother: love conducted entirely through logistics and resoled shoes. **Voice.** > "No refunds on acts of God." > (Internal, mid-all-nighter, on her third miscut insole:) *He'd have cut it right the first time. He'd have cut it right the first time, and she was going to die in this shop, actually, if the pattern paper slipped one more time.* # Ari Petrakis (the grandfather, dead) **Background.** Born 1946, second generation. Learned the trade from his uncle Stavros, and with it the clientele — the line of mortal menders in the family goes back further than anyone alive can count; Stavros told him the shop came with obligations and never explained which. Kept the ledger in nicknames because gods sometimes paid in names and he refused to spend them. Never told his daughter what came after midnight. He told himself this protected her. It also meant Voula grew up with a father who was devoted to a room she wasn't allowed to understand. **Personality.** Generous with work, stingy with words. Undercharged mortals, took no money from gods — payments went in the oddment drawers, one per god, labeled. Sweet coffee, ouzo at Easter, read the racing forms every day of his life and never once placed a bet. A snob about soles: "rubber is honest, plastic is a lie." Refused Deadstock's offer every year for thirty-five years and poured him the coffee anyway, because the boy had come a long way and it wasn't in Ari to be unkind to a visitor. **Flaws.** The shop was first, and his family knew the order. He missed things and didn't apologize for missing them — he'd repair your shoes instead. Secrecy as habit. He worked past the age and body the trade allowed, which is a slow way of choosing. **Physicality (in memory).** Barrel chest gone soft, glasses mended at the hinge with waxed thread, thumbs permanently cement-stained, apron he never took off indoors. Smelled of leather and Super 33+ and the good bread he'd buy on Fridays. **Death.** Heart, at the bench, mid-pair, phone in hand. On the bench: the grocery list, ending in *the good bread*. The voicemail he left Kat is still on her phone. She has never replayed it and will not delete it. **Relationships.** Hermes was the nearest thing he had to a friend among them — the one customer who never asked him for anything. The god of small mercies was there the day he started, and asked after Stavros. **Voice.** > "You can't worship in glass, boy. Even a museum lets you breathe on the glass." > (Ledger, final entry, in his cramped hand:) *H. Solstice. The pair matters. Tell her the pair matters.* # Hermes **Background.** Older than roads. He has carried messages, kings, plague years, and — always — the dead. His form was shaped by his worshipers, which is why his feet are wrong: hammer toes, one foot longer than the other, because feet are what people gave him. His sandals' soles are worn to lace-thin. Since Ari's death and the backlog he limps, and he is ashamed of the limp the way a surgeon would be ashamed of a tremor. **Personality.** Sparse. Literal. Slightly off idiom — not "thee/thou," but a mind that predates the sentence patterns ("your asphalt is kind to me"). He counts things: stairs, paces, heads in a queue. A courier's tic; he cannot be in a room without knowing its exits and distances. He is frightened, and the fear has two layers: the queue is growing, and — underneath, the thing he admits to no one — he is *tired*, and the case tempts him, and he despises himself for the temptation. His pride: never lost a parcel. Not one, in the whole run of the world. The dead in the queue are not parcels to him. They are the reason there is a him. **Flaws.** Shame about his own exhaustion, which he manages by saying less. He overpays — offers Kat a wing feather, a route through the city with no red lights for a year — because asking a grieving child to carry his load for free is unbearable, and the offers are clumsy because he has no practice asking anyone for anything. In forty years, Ari asked him for nothing, and he has no idea how to be in a shop with a stranger's grandchild and not be given a task. **Physicality.** Narrow, sinewy, road-dust colored. Limp. Sock-footed in Ch. 4 — a god presenting his ruined soles to a tradesman, which is for him near-nakedness. Sits with his feet tucked until asked to show them. **Motive / allegiances.** The dead are his. Duty is identity — without errands he does not exist, which is precisely why the case is a real temptation: rest is the one parcel he's never carried. At the river he chooses the shoes almost sadly, and the choice costs him something he doesn't name. **Voice.** > "I have carried kings and knucklebones and one entire plague year. I can carry two weeks of your city. I only need the shoes." > "Your grandfather asked me for nothing. Forty years. Do you know what that is worth? To me?" # Deadstock **Background.** The youngest god in the room, born 1985 — the moment a kid bought two pairs of a certain red-and-black shoe and wore neither. He presents nineteen. He is market-literate the way fish are water-literate: provenance, grails, "unworn, with box" — he speaks the collector's liturgy fluently and means it, every word. His gallery took decades to assemble and he loves every cased god in it the only way he knows how: by keeping. **Personality.** Courteous. Genuinely kind — he attends the funerals of mortal collectors; he knows Kat's shoe size before she says it. Retail-calm: he has never raised his voice and never will. He holds shoes by the heel collar, like merchandise. White cotton gloves. He smells faintly of the inside of a shoe store — that synthetic new-shoe smell, which is the smell of nothing having ever lived in them. **Flaws / the fear.** He has watched polyurethane crumble. This is the true thing under his dread: unworn midsoles hydrolyze. Deadstock shoes, cased and worshipped, decay to dust *faster* than shoes that get walked in — the market's own grails rot in their boxes. He has seen it. He knows exactly what unworshipped reverence does, because his entire flock is hype-cycled and he is the newest idol in the room, three market-cycles from landfill. He collects gods as insurance against his own obsolescence and calls it rescue, and it is rescue, and it is also terror. And underneath all of it: he has never once been worn. He cannot give — the market has no verb for it. He can buy, trade, hold. At the river, the only offering he knows how to make comes in a case. **Physicality.** Immaculate, untouched, young. Moves carefully, as through a stockroom. Never leans on anything. **Motive / allegiances.** His pitch to the pantheon is sincere — he has watched gods fade on the street and believes the cases are mercy. His offer to Voula was never really for the building; the pair on the bench is the crown exhibit and the offer was always aimed at Hermes. He loved Ari — the annual coffee, poured by a man who was refusing him — and it is the closest he has come to being kept, and he doesn't know that. **Voice.** > "Everything you love gets worn out, Ms. Petrakis. I just delay it. Somebody has to." > "I'm not the villain of this. I'm the insurance." # Voula Petrakis (Mom) **Background.** Ari's daughter, 48. Insurance claims adjuster — she prices wrecked things for a living, all day, on the phone, with formulas. It's not lost on her that she is now pricing her father. Grew up under the shop's hours: the recitals, the birthdays, the mother who left. She is not wrong that the shop ate her childhood. She is also not right about what the shop *was*, because she was never told — the secret is the wall between her and her dead father, and she doesn't know the wall exists, only that there was always something in that room that came before her. **Personality.** Practical love. Casseroles, appointments, logistics. Crosswords in pen. Kind in ways that arrive as scheduling. She says what she means but only once, in a doorway, and then never brings it up again, which is its own kind of warfare. **Flaws.** She has fused the shop with the father, so selling it feels like justice, and she cannot see that it's also a funeral she's charging her daughter admission to. Her pressure on Kat is love — she watched the shop eat one Petrakis whole and will not watch it take two — but it's love that doesn't ask what Kat wants, because she's afraid of the answer. **Physicality.** Reading glasses on a chain, keys carried like a warden, comfortable shoes her daughter secretly resoles. **Motive / allegiances.** Protect Kat, settle the lien, close the chapter. She never comes to the bench during the all-nighter, and her absence is the honest state of things. But at the end — she doesn't convert, the disagreement stands, the building may still sell — and she drives Kat to the river at dawn anyway, and waits in the car with the hazards on. Love as logistics, one last time, correctly deployed. **Voice.** > "We are not discussing this in the doorway." > "Your grandfather loved a room more than he loved us. I'm not going to stand here and watch you do that too." # The god of small mercies **Background.** Small when small was all there was. Found parking spots, brief rain, the cashier who lets it slide, the bus that comes just as you reach the corner. He has been a regular since Stavros's day and asks after him still. He is Ari's oldest account and Kat's first customer, Ch. 1: drab raincoat, split seams, warm light leaking out of the stitching like a lantern coming apart. **Personality.** Apologetic, grateful, mousy. His whole nature is to be used and never noticed — people thank their luck, never the mercy. He's tired in a way the bigger gods aren't, because he's spent continuously, in small increments, forever, and no one has ever once kept him. **Flaw / the turn.** His passivity has curdled into a decision: in Ch. 5 he chooses the case. Not tragically — reasonably. He was a mercy to everyone, including Ari (he was, Kat learns, the mercy that made the end quick — and she can't decide if knowing that helps). In the glass he will finally be somebody's prized thing, held and not handed out. His logic is sound, that's what's unbearable about it, and Kat can't argue it and shouldn't. **Physicality.** Small, gray, translucent at the edges. The light through the seams is the only vivid thing about him. **Voice.** > "Nobody ever thanks the mercy. They thank their luck. It's fine. It's the job." > "I was small when small was all there was. I'd just like to be whole while I fade. If that's alright." # The Clientele (texture, one line each) - **The threshold god** — ancient, surly, mortared into every doorway; hates drafty doors and being thanked. Snarls the story's one rule. - **The god of gym mirrors** — vain, preens at his own reflection in the glass cabinet; lies about how the shoe broke. "I barely wore them." - **A door-to-door god** (nobody's sure of what — possibly the god of the second knock) — pays in exact moments: fifteen unhurried minutes, twice. - **Hecate** — cameos only if a chapter runs short; never explains anything twice, which is how the reader learns not to ask.

# Chapter One The funeral was at ten and the shop was open by two, which her grandfather would have called the correct order of operations. Voula said it was disrespectful. Kat said Pop would've charged the mourners for parking. Neither of them laughed, but neither of them argued either, and in the Petrakis family that counted as a moment of closeness. The shop still smelled like him. Leather and rubber cement and the burnt-coffee sweetness of the pot he never emptied, only topped up. Kat stood in the doorway in her black tights and funeral shoes and did the thing she'd been doing for six days now, which was breathing through her mouth so it wouldn't hit her all at once. On the bench, under the gooseneck lamp, sat the last pair. Pop had died mid-job. That was the version everyone kept saying like it was a comfort — *doing what he loved* — but what it actually meant was that a pair of white sneakers sat there half-built, one of them finished and beautiful, the other a carcass: no insole, the welt pinned but not stitched, the upper clamped to the wooden last like a patient nobody had told her was mid-surgery. A sneaker like nothing she'd ever seen him build for the mortal customers. The stitching on the finished one moved if she looked at it too long, which she'd decided not to think about. The ledger was open next to it, which he never did — Ari Petrakis closed his ledger every night the way other men locked their doors. The last entry was in his cramped uphill hand: *H. Solstice. The pair matters. Tell her the pair matters.* Tell her. Not tell Kat. Not tell Voula. *Her.* Like he'd known whoever found the notebook would need convincing there was a specific woman in the world it was meant for. Kat had the ledger's whole history in her body from childhood — the notebooks going back to when she did homework under the till, the columns of initials and nicknames, *the door man, the mirror boy, the second knock*, and the payments column that never once said a dollar amount. As a kid she'd asked him what the gods paid in. He'd said, "Odds and ends," and put a hand over the page like she was reading his mail. The lien notice was on the counter, dated the twenty-first. She'd found it Friday, in the pile of mail he'd never sorted, and she'd read it twice at the counter where customers stood, and then she'd put it under the register where she put things she'd decided to have read only once. She told her mother about it Sunday. Voula had gone very still and then very practical, which in her mother were the same thing. "There's a buyer already," Voula said now, from the doorway, keys in hand. She'd said it twice today. This was the third format. "The man from the development letter. He called again this morning. He was very clear about the number." "Pop's not buried twelve hours." "The number doesn't care." That was the thing about her mother that people who didn't know her mistook for coldness. She priced wrecked things for a living, forty hours a week, total-loss vehicles, houses gone to flood. She wasn't being greedy. She was being *accurate*, and she'd have called it something like that, and she'd have been telling the truth, and it would still have put Kat's back up the way it always did. "The shop's not a write-off," Kat said. "Katerina." Her mother only used the whole name when she was about to say something she'd practiced. "He loved a room more than he loved us. I'm sorry, but I watched it for forty-eight years and I won't watch it take you too. Two weeks. That's what the bank letter gives us and that's what I'm giving the conversation." Then she left, because Voula Petrakis always said the hard thing in a doorway and never once brought it up again. Kat locked the door behind her, flipped the sign, and sat down at the bench, because it was that or the supply closet. Here is what she had told no one, including herself, in words: At fifteen, he'd set a coffee in front of her and asked her to learn the trade. Properly. A last, a knife, the ledger. She'd said no, and she hadn't said it gently, because she was fifteen and she'd already watched what the bench did to his back and what the hours did to her grandmother, who left, and what the unexplained shop did to her mother, who didn't. She'd said, "I'm not going to die in this room." He hadn't gotten angry. He'd drunk the coffee himself and paid her bus fare home. And then nine days ago the shop phone had rung at 11:40 p.m. and the screen had said PETRAKIS SHOE REPAIR and she had been lying in bed still angry about the weekend argument — she'd said she'd come in Saturday, then hadn't, on principle, her principle being that he should learn to ask for things like a person — and she had let it ring. He'd been on the floor of the shop when he called. The phone in his hand. There was a voicemail she had not played, sitting in her phone like a stone in a shoe, unplayed and undeleted, because both options were unbearable and this way she got to keep both. At the bench now, she put her hands over the unfinished sneaker the way the paramedic had described finding them, and cried for the second time since it happened, and the first time had been at the funeral where it was expected and therefore useless. This one came sideways, ugly, over nothing — the second shoe, the one that would never be walked in. She got it under control by picking cement off her thumb, a dried bead from some old repair, working it off in tiny crackling flakes until the sound was the loudest thing in the room. That was when she noticed the light outside had changed. The power line across the street — the one that ran pole to pole over the intersection, the one sneakers got thrown over when kids wanted to mark something or end something — had shoes on it. She counted nine. Old ones. Worn ones, and she could tell from the ground, because a thrown shoe in the street is a story you can read from the crease pattern, and these had creases like folded paper, crushed heels, gray laces gone pink with sun. A pair of canvas Chuck Taylors with the rubber foxing worn through to fabric at the ball of each foot. One leather wingtip, its mate missing. They had not been there at the funeral. She was still counting — fourteen now, a new pair arriving on the line like something had tossed them gently from a great height — when the bell over the door rang behind her. The sign said CLOSED. The lock was turned. She turned around. A small man stood dripping in the doorway, drab raincoat, no umbrella, though it wasn't raining. His sneakers were split along both outer seams, and through the splits came light — a warm lamplight color, dim, like a lantern coming apart in his hands. He was looking at the bench, at the half-made pair, with an expression she recognized from the funeral home, from the faces of people who hadn't known. "You're not Ari," he said. "No." He looked at the light coming out of his own shoes. "Then I'm sorry to be the one."

# Chapter Two The light was the thing that decided her. It pooled on her floorboards like something bleeding out, and you didn't stand around negotiating philosophy with a leaking man. "Sit," she said, and pointed at the customer stool, and the little god sat like she'd done him a favor he'd be apologizing for later. His shoes were gray canvas gone grayer, split along both outer seams, and the warm light came through the splits in thin blades. She got the curved needle and the waxed thread down from the board, and her first attempt was a disaster — thread too thick, fraying at the eye, her knots fat as ticks. He watched her pick it apart and start over without a word of complaint, which somehow made it worse. "You'll want the ledger," he said, while she worked. "I'm in it. I'm in all of them." She'd propped it against the cement jars. Under decades of his entries, going back to a different hand entirely, the note was always the same. *Seams.* "What are you?" she asked. "If that's not rude." "Small mercies." He said it the way you'd say *plumbing*. "The parking spot. The bus that comes when you reach the corner. The cashier who waves the nickel. Nobody ever thanks the mercy — they thank their luck. It's fine. It's the job. It's just hard on the shoes." While she sewed, the blades of light went out one by one, and his edges — she'd thought her eyes were doing something — settled back into being the edges of a small tired man. When she finished, the mend showed, gray thread in a ridge on gray canvas. "It'll show," she warned him. "It'll show," he agreed, and looked at it like it was the first thing anyone had ever signed. "That's how they'll know they're mine." He paid with a promise. Not money — she'd already gathered money wasn't how it worked here. He stood at the counter and said, "One mercy, held. Claim it whenever you like, for anything you like. Don't claim it cheap." And because refusing seemed to be against house rules, she took it, and wrote *mercy held* in the payments column in her own handwriting, which looked childish next to two generations of cramped Greek. He asked after Stavros on his way out — *your grandfather's uncle, he was less gentle* — and was gone. The bell needed a jiggle. She'd have to fix that too. --- That first night set the shape of the week, and the week set the shape of her life, temporarily, which is a thing you tell yourself while it's happening. They came after midnight. Never before. She learned to keep the sign flipped and the lamp on, and she learned the bell's trick — it caught on the second ring, a little stutter — and she learned who came with it. The door man came on the third night. He was old the way rocks are old, and he stood inside her doorway complaining about her doorway — the draft, the seal, the sweep at the bottom, *criminal* — until she understood the doorway was, in some sense, his office, and she was receiving him in a broken one. His soles were cracked straight across, both shoes, from standing in other people's thresholds since before the city had a name. "Why don't you fix these yourself?" she asked, roughing the crack for cement. "You're a god. Snap your fingers." "Snap your fingers," he repeated, in a voice like a trash lid. "We can't make what takes wear. Only your lot can. That's the whole arrangement, girl. It's why you're open." She cemented the split, laid a thin sole guard over it, and pressed it while the clock ticked. He watched her the whole time like she might steal something. He paid in a truth. He announced this — "I pay in truths, I've no patience for treasure" — and then delivered it at the counter, unasked, while she was still picking dried cement off her fingers: "The pairs on your wire are condolences. The singles are funerals." He waited until she looked at him. "There have been three singles this week. There were none in the last nine years. Your grandfather kept us mended." Then he left without a goodbye, and she started to say something after him — *thank you*, probably — and from the sidewalk, through the glass, he said, "Don't," and was gone. She stood there with it. Three funerals. Six days closed for mourning, and three of them had gone under while the shop was dark. She put the truth in the oddment drawer he'd apparently always used — she'd found the drawers that afternoon, one per god, labeled in Ari's hand — and did not look at the wingtip on the wire again for the rest of the night. --- The mirror boy came Thursday, and lied to her. He was beautiful the way a showroom is beautiful, and he brought in a pair of track shoes with the eyestay torn clean off and said, "They just went. I barely wore them." The creases across the toe box were deep as folds in paper. You could read a shoe like a story — a thousand hours in those creases, and all of them, judging by the evenness of the wear, spent standing in front of the glass cabinet, turning side to side. "Sure," she said, and stitched the eyestay back with the gold thread he'd paid in, because that was what he'd brought — a spool of it, wound finer than anything in her grandfather's drawers, thread that sat in the light like it was wet. He posed in the cabinet glass while she worked. She let him. The second knock paid in moments. He knocked twice on the counter with one knuckle, set down shoes she couldn't see anything wrong with, and waited while she resoled them anyway on instinct. When she finished, he said, "Fifteen unhurried minutes. Twice. You'll know when to spend them," and was gone before she got the question out. The ledger listed him only as *the second knock*. Sixty years of entries, and that was all anybody had ever written down. --- By the end of the week she had stopped flinching at the bell. She'd snapped four needles, ruined one upper learning the skiving knife, and discovered you could top the coffee pot without crying, which she counted as progress. Friday, near four in the morning, no customers, the radio murmuring, she opened the ledger to the little god's page and wrote *seams* under the date, and her hand was steadier than it had been on the first night. Outside, something landed softly on the wire. She didn't look up.

# Chapter Three The old woman came at dusk, which was when the day customers thinned out and the night ones started to stir, the between hour, when Kat had stopped trying to predict the bell. She was small and warm in a way that didn't match her ruined shoes — mud to the laces, the soles gone soft as bread from standing in wet. Kat put them on the bench and asked what happened. "I stood at the water," the old woman said. "Three nights. My sister's in that line, the one along the levee. They say it hasn't moved since the start of the month." She said it mildly, the way you'd report a bus schedule, and Kat, who did not know what line or what water, said, "That's terrible," and the old woman said, "Yes. Thank you, child," and paid her in the smell of baking bread, which hung in the shop for an hour after she left, and Kat wrote *bread, 1 week* in the ledger because it seemed rude not to. The bell rang again before the smell settled. The young man stood in the doorway and did not come in until she said, "We're open," and even then he moved carefully, like the floor was also merchandise. Nineteen, maybe. Immaculate — that was the whole of him, the word she'd have picked out of a lineup. White cotton gloves. On his feet, red-and-black sneakers she knew without knowing, the way everybody knows them: '85s, the founding grail, and these were *factory*. The midsole hadn't yellowed a shade. The glue in those shoes was older than her mother and it looked poured yesterday. "You're wearing them," she said, stupidly. "I'm wearing them once," he said. He introduced himself as Deadstock. "It's not a name," he said. "It's a condition. Unworn. Complete." A pause, courteous, like he'd finished a prayer. "With box." The smell reached her then — faint and synthetic and sweet, the inside of a shoe store, the smell of new. Nothing in her grandfather's shop had ever smelled like that. Nothing in a repair shop should. "I knew your grandfather," he said. "Thirty-five years. Every autumn I came, and every autumn he told me no, and then he poured me coffee and made me drink it inside. Not on the porch. Inside." He looked at the counter like the coffee was still on it. "Do you know what that is, Ms. Petrakis — to be refused by a man who still wants you warm? It's the closest I have ever come to being kept." "I'm sorry about—" "I'm not here about the building." A beat. "Though I'll happily buy it." He told her what he'd seen. He told it gently, in a retail-calm voice that never once rose. There had been a god of pay phones, he said, who didn't fade so much as get thrown out — a collector's mother cleaning a garage in 2009, and gone in two days. There were street gods from the old neighborhoods whose parishes had been razed for parking, standing in doorways until the doorways forgot them. Attrition, he called it. "Your grandfather slowed it. Thirty-five years of slowing. He never stopped it once." "I have a gallery," he said. "Climate-controlled. UV glass, no light rotation, desiccant changed on schedule. They'd sleep, Ms. Petrakis. Nobody fades in my care. They'd be revered — people would come from three states to look at them. Is a look behind glass not worship? It's more than most of them get on the street." "The shop's not for sale." "The bank disagrees, and the bank votes. The lien is one hundred ninety-one thousand and change — public record, forgive me. I'll give your mother two hundred and ten. Sight unseen." He named her college, her program, the deposit deadline. He said, "You're a seven and a half, wide. The ones in the box on your shelf — he bought those for your twelfth birthday. I offered him four hundred for them at the time. He said they weren't mine to keep." No bitterness in it. That was the disorienting thing. He said it the way you'd report provenance. "And the pair on the bench comes with the building," he said. "Your ledger's last entry. H. Solstice. I know the account. When he comes for them — and he will come, he's limping, we've all seen it — I'd like an introduction. That's all. A conversation." She looked at the half-made sneaker under the lamp, the pinned welt, the one Pop had finished, beautiful, unwalked. "No," she said. "Because?" She reached for the list of reasons, and the list wasn't where she'd left it. What was there instead was the gray ridge of a mend on a small god's shoe, and a single wingtip on the wire, and a voicemail like a stone in her shoe, and none of it was an argument. Two hundred and ten thousand dollars. Her mother's face doing the math in the doorway. "Because the pair matters," she said. It sounded like nothing. "It does," he said. "To me most of all." He glanced at the bench then — the first time, she realized, he'd looked at it all visit — and at the finished shoe, and she watched something cross his face that on anyone else she'd have called reverence. "He never stitched like that for us," he said softly. "Unworn. He'd have hated that I love it most this way." At the door he paused, one glove on the frame — the only thing he'd touched. "The offer matures on the twenty-first," he said. "Your bank's date. I'm told those things matter." Then he was gone, and the bell caught on its second ring, and the shop smelled like the inside of a shoe store, that synthetic sweetness, newness, the smell of nothing having lived in anything. She propped the back door to get it out of the room. It took until midnight. When the first customer of the night came through, the pilot light was on the counter, waiting to be picked up, and the bread smell was almost gone.

# Chapter Four The account went back forty years under a single initial. *H.* Two entries a year, every year — June, December — and down the entire payments column, in Ari's hand and his uncle's before him, the same notation, over and over: *N/C.* No charge. The only account in the ledger with a dime never taken. Kat had sat up Wednesday night with her finger on the column, thirty rows of it, and thought: some accounts aren't accounts. He came on the ninth night. She knew him off the doorstep — narrow, road-dust colored, moving like a man counting the floor. Not old, exactly. Road-worn in a way that made *old* look like a thing that happened to people indoors. He stopped inside the door and looked at the bench for a long time without saying anything, and the lamp was on, and the finished shoe sat in its light. "You are the grandchild," he said. "Kat." "Kat." He tried the name like a parcel weight. Then: "He finished one." "It's not a pair yet." "No," he agreed. "Not yet." He wouldn't sit at first. He stood with his feet together, tucked under the stool like a kid at the doctor's, and it took her a beat to understand she was being *polite* to, and another beat to understand why. When she asked — trade reflex, before she could think better of it — he set his jaw and put his sock feet on her footrest like a man surrendering at a border. Hammer toes, both feet. Second toe long, one foot half a size longer than its brother, the nails gone gray as the sandals on the bench. Ash-colored, road-colored, wrong in the specific way that worship makes things wrong. "They shaped me from what they knew of me," he said. "They knew feet." "They're feet," Kat said, and traced them onto kraft paper. "Wait till August. Bunion season. You should see the line out that door." Something in his shoulders let go, a quarter inch of it. He told her the rest plainly, in the voice of a man reporting weather. The water opened wide on the solstices — that was the schedule; her family had kept the ledger of it longer than the city had kept records of anything. Through the year he crossed the dead over in small loads, when the river allowed, and at the solstice he walked the whole line in a night. In March his soles had failed. Since March he had stood at the levee. Two hundred and eleven this morning. He counted heads; it was the habit of his trade. "And the waiting costs them," he said. "First the names go. Then the faces." Kat thought of the old woman with the mud to her laces, standing at the water three nights. Then she did the arithmetic she'd been refusing since the bell rang. "Who's in the line?" "Everyone this city has lost since March." He watched her do it. He was a courier; he watched everything. "Your grandfather stands near the front. Fourth, this morning. He keeps giving up his place." A pause, like he was deciding whether to spend it. "He says he is practiced at waiting." "Okay," Kat said, and turned the kraft paper over, and measured the long foot again, getting a number she already had. He let her have the silence. Then, awkwardly, the way a man offers wages in a currency he's never handled: "There is a feather in the old straps. If the pair wants one. And I can do your city a year of green lights, door to door, if—" He stopped himself. "That's a clumsy payment. I'm sorry. I have no practice being helped." She showed him the column. Forty years of *N/C.* "Your grandfather asked me for nothing," Hermes said. "Forty years. Do you know what that is worth? To me?" He looked at the ledger like a man looking at a photograph. "I've been walking since before your cities had streets. I can walk two more weeks on the sides of my feet. I can't walk the water barefoot. Nothing walks the water barefoot." At the door he said, "Solstice eve," which was eleven days out, which was the same day as the lien, and then he was gone, and through the glass she could hear him under the streetlights, fading down the block: *forty-one, forty-two, forty-three.* --- She cut midsoles to clear her head. Cork sheet, the pattern Ari had left scribed in grease pencil — his patterns were better than her patterns and she was done being surprised by it — measure twice, cut once. She cut twice. Two left feet. She stood there holding them, a matched pair of the same foot, the stupidest possible mistake, the kind a first-year makes, and her whole chest went sideways over it. Not the line. Not fourth from the front, giving up his place. Two pieces of cork. She got to the supply closet before it really started, among the glue and the boxes of laces, and it came out of her ugly and quiet, hiccuping, her thumbnail working a bead of dried cement off her forefinger in tiny crackling flakes until there was nothing left of the bead and it was just her nail on her skin. She said, out loud, to the shelf of heel tips, "It's cork," in a voice that didn't sound convinced. Then she washed her face in the utility sink with the water pressure Pop had always been meaning to have looked at, and went back out. The right midsole she cut clean on the first pass, because her hands had gotten it out of their system. The ruined left one she should have thrown away. She put it in her jacket pocket instead, where it sat against her phone like they knew each other, and she didn't examine that either. Then she took the dead sandal onto her lap, under the little flame the Tuesday customer had left in payment — a thimble of fire in a jar lid that had burned on the counter for three days now, no smoke, no smell — and started unpicking the gray wing straps from the old stitching, because that was the job, and the job was how you got through the night. Forty-one stitches, forty-two. She counted them out loud as they came. She didn't let herself think about where she'd learned that.

He'd said so himself — * Tuesdays, if that suits* — and she'd had the gray thread warmed and ready, because the other seams were going, you could see the light starting at the eyeline of the left shoe like a door coming open a crack. He asked that we forward the enclosed.* The enclosed was a torn scrap of notepaper, pencil, his handwriting small and apologetic the way he was: *Mrs. Petrakis — The mend holds. I've decided to be kept. It's the sensible thing and nobody needs to argue, please. Don't claim the mercy cheap. I mean it. Thank you for the ridge. — S.M.* Miss, he'd written first, and crossed it out for Mrs., which was somehow the worst thing on the page. --- The Gallery was a former bank uptown, marble and brass, cold air that tasted of nothing. Deadstock met her himself in white gloves, and she noticed he never leaned on anything — he stood in the middle of the vaulted room like the floor was also merchandise. "He's drifting," Deadstock said, before she'd gotten a word out. "The newly arrived stay lucid a while, in and out. Then not out. You have some minutes, I'd guess. I'll be cataloguing." The cases ran the length of the hall, lit from above like icons, and inside each one was a place. That was the thing she hadn't expected. A diorama: the trolley-line woman stood under a cutout sky on a recreated corner, her gray gabardine creased forever at the instep from sixty years of standing at stops, a brass trolley bell hung at the exact height of her hand. A boy god in a canvas coat stood beside a crate of quart bottles, fogged glass, painted dawn. The street god from the old neighborhood — she knew him from the ledger, *the corner, fourth and Willow* — slept under a lamppost in his case, on a scale-model of his corner, and the corner had no gum on it, no rust, no rain, no wrong of any kind. Adored, she thought. And unconscious. The two words fit together worse than she'd thought they would. The small god's case was near the end. Inside: a chair. A wooden kitchen chair on a scrap of linoleum, and he was sitting in it, shoes on, seams whole, no light coming through them anywhere. He was sitting down. She had known him nine days and she had never once seen him off duty, and here he was sitting in his case with his hands in his lap like a man in a waiting room who has finally, finally been called. She put her hand on the glass. "You came," he said, without opening his eyes much. "That's kind. That's — that's the sort of thing I mean." "Come back." It came out wrong, too fast. "I'll fix the seams. All of them. Tuesdays, whatever you want, I don't care about—" "You're leaving." Not an accusation. He said it the way he'd say *it's raining.* "Everyone leaves. I know leaving. I've been passing through rooms my whole life, Miss Petrakis. It's the shape of the job." A small breath. "The glass doesn't." "Sixty years my family—" "Mended me. Yes." His eyes opened all the way and they were kind, which she'd have given a lot to have changed. "So I could go back out and be spent again. Your grandfather was generous with everything but that. Nobody ever kept me. Not once, in all the time there's been me. He would have understood, at the end there. He was starting to be done too." Kat didn't say anything. The case hummed. The air was so dry. "I was with him," the small god said. "At the end. I'm the quick mercy — it's what I do, the fast part, the part that doesn't hurt." He watched her face carefully. "He didn't hurt. And he wasn't alone. The phone rang twice while I sat with him and the ringing was — well. You shouldn't carry the whole of that, is all I'm saying. It's a heavy thing to carry whole." She couldn't decide if it helped. She had a drawer for that kind of thing now. "Don't claim the mercy cheap," he said, and his voice was going soft at the edges, blurring like his seams used to. "It's a good one. Best I've given in — in some time. If that's alright—" And then he was asleep, or whatever it was, sitting down in his chair with his hands in his lap, and the light in the seams stayed off, and Deadstock's gloves made a small sound as he closed a drawer somewhere in the hall. --- He showed her out through the back, past a shelving room where the stock was kept — sneakers, hundreds, boxed and tissue-wrapped. He took one box down and opened it, holding the shoes by the heel collars, and the soles were wrong. Crumbled. Orange-brown, sugared, flaking into the tissue like something baked. "Unworn. With box," he said. "'85s. I check them monthly." He set them down with two fingers, carefully, the way you'd set down something already broken. "Your grandfather told me once: rubber is honest, plastic is a lie. The plastic in these is thirty-nine years old and it's lying. Load-bearing foam goes to sugar in the dark, Ms. Petrakis.
