# Chapter Six The pair on the bench was a lie, and she'd been keeping it. Not a big one, at first. Hermes had asked, on his second visit — she'd told him tracing went well — "How much of it is done?" — and she'd said *most of it* — and he'd said, "Good," and tucked his feet under the stool, and she'd let the word *most* do all the work of the word *some*. Then it stopped being small. Because the fact was that the shoe Pop had finished was beyond her. She'd known it since the night she traced Hermes' feet — the stitching was a weave she couldn't reverse-engineer, a pattern that moved when she looked too long, and she'd unpicked three attempts at replicating it before she understood the attempts were the problem. The mend wasn't a technique. It was forty years of *N/C*, stitched into a shoe. The second shoe wasn't missing its maker's skill. It was missing its maker. So she'd been faking the parts she couldn't make — surface rows, show-stitching along the eyestay, careful work, real work, but not the working part — and telling herself the story she'd told everyone: almost done. Mostly done. Enough done. She cemented the practice shoes at 9 p.m. with the window fan going, because June. She'd made the cement batch wrong. She knew it at the mixing cup — too thin, the smell wrong, off, not right, the release sheets sticking where they should sheet off — and she decided to run it, because the night was hot and the customer was waiting and *almost done* was the story of her whole month. Too thin meant too slow, and too slow meant the green between cement and bond had a hole in it, and she pressed the sole on, held it ninety seconds like her grandfather had taught her, and let go. It held. It held beautifully. It held for eleven days and then it failed on Fourth Avenue at two in the afternoon in front of God and the crosstown bus and a wet man's whole dignity, because the sole of a shoe is the only part of a repair that is also a safety feature, and she had known the batch was off, and she had run it anyway. --- He came in at dusk with the shoe in his hands like a bird with a broken wing. He was wet — always slightly wet, a rain that didn't fall anywhere else, the god of the second knock, or possibly something to do with downpours, the ledger wasn't clear — and he set it on her counter and said, "It came off in the street." "I know. I'm sorry. The batch—" Her throat closed. "I'll redo it tonight. Better than new. I'm so—" "Nobody was hurt." He said it gently, which was so much worse than the alternative. "You'll redo it. That's the trade." Then, at the door, because house rules are house rules even in June, he turned and paid her. He always paid in moments. This time he gave her one unhurried minute. He said, "Spend it on your mother." And then he stood there and waited, dripping faintly, while she understood he was going to watch her spend it, and there was no wriggling out of it, and house rules are house rules. The minute she chose — her own, to spend — was in the kitchen, 10 p.m., her mother at the table with the lien papers and a pen and her reading glasses on their chain, going down the columns of the number that didn't care. Two hundred and ten thousand dollars of don't-care, against a room that had taken a whole Petrakis and was going for the rest. She spent the minute unhurried. She made tea. She sat down across from her mother without opening the ledger of grievances she carried everywhere, sat with the steam and the ticking of the good clock, and said nothing, and let the minute be a minute. Voula looked up once over her glasses, wary, like the kindness was a bill. "What," her mother said. "Nothing. Tea." Her mother drank the tea. Nothing was solved. The lien papers stayed exactly where they were. But Voula said, at the end of it — without looking up, in her doorway-voice, the practiced thing you get one shot at: "The developer's buyer wants an answer Friday. Deadstock's people sent the contract yesterday." A pause. "It's his number, you know. Two-ten. The developer's is one-sixty. He's covering the gap." Kat didn't say anything. The clock ticked out the rest of the minute. "Your grandfather loved a room more than he loved us," her mother said, to the tea. "I'm not going to stand in a doorway and watch it take you too." That was the practiced thing, said a second time, and her mother never said things twice, and Kat understood she had been saving it. Friday was the twenty-first. The lien. The solstice. The one date, three names. And Kat, seventeen, handy, half a trade, no plan, nearly said *yes*. She got as close as the counter. She had the contract out of her mother's folder — she knew which drawer, she'd watched which drawer — and the pen from the cup by the register, the one Pop kept for customers who paid mortal money, and she stood at her grandfather's counter in her grandfather's shop with her grandfather's pen and read the number at the bottom, two hundred and ten thousand, and understood, standing there, that she was going to sign it, that she had been going to sign it since the wet man paid her in a minute and she had chosen her mother over the shop, and that this was the exact shape of the thing she had done at fifteen, run from the room before the room could take her, only this time running meant staying gone forever. The midsole. She'd kept the ruined left midsole in her jacket pocket for two weeks, the two-left-feet cork, the first-week mistake, carried around like a stone, and it was in her hand before she knew she'd reached for it, thumbnail working the cut edge the way it worked dried cement beads and every other thing her mouth wouldn't do. Cork doesn't crackle. It's quiet. It gives. And she put the pen down. Not a decision exactly. More like her hand had a vote and the vote was *no* — the hand that had sewn a ridge of gray thread into gray canvas so a small tired god could be known by his mend, the hand that had cut two left feet and grieved over cork like it was a person, the hand that mended thresholds and eyestays and seams with light coming through them. The hand knew the trade was real and knew she was halfway in it, and halfway wasn't nothing, and nothing wasn't what the pair on the bench deserved. Because the pair mattered. *Tell her the pair matters.* She put the contract back in the drawer. Not torn up. Put back. Because two hundred and ten thousand dollars was her mother's whole life priced accurately, and refusing it wasn't clean, and she was done pretending it was. Then she went to the shop and worked till dawn on the parts she could do — welting, skiving, the ugly honest work — and the work was how you got through the night, and she left the show-stitching, the faked parts, the beyond-her parts, for last. And at four in the morning, out of excuses, alone, she finally unpicked the last of it — every false row, the whole scaffolding of *almost* — until the second shoe stood on the last in its honest skin, unfinished, unrescued by lies. The bell didn't ring all night. On the wire outside, nothing new landed. The line at the river was two hundred and sixty. She let the light on the bench stay on and sat with the shoe and the truth of it and waited for morning, and made herself a promise with a crack in it, which is the only kind of promise a human can make: she'd finish the pair by solstice, or she'd finish it after. And whichever way the building went, the work would get done, and the gods would find her wherever she was. Garage. Kitchen table. Wherever. Institutions die. Practice persists. She was almost believing it when the bell rang. It rang twice, cleanly, no stutter. She'd fixed the bell Tuesday. The stutter had been the bell's whole personality. She knew that ring. The light through the front glass was warm, lamplight-colored, and it did not come from any streetlight. She got up and went to the door, and stopped with her hand on the lock, because the morning was coming up gray over the rooftops, solstice eve, and through the glass she could see him standing under the wire, waiting to be let in, translucent at the edges, holding a box. The box was cream-colored, uptown postmark, and it had been opened and re-closed, and it was addressed in a small apologetic hand that she knew, and it had no return address, because there wouldn't be one, because the Gallery regretted to inform her. He'd walked out of the case. He'd walked out of the case and the shoes had let him, and that was the answer to something, though not, she suspected, to everything.

# Brainstorming ## Reading the Prompt Closely Three loaded elements, each with productive ambiguity: - **"A month ago"** — the story opens *after* arrival and *after* first speech. First contact isn't the climax; it's the backstory. The narrative present is the aftermath: living with them. - **"First, the fish started dying"** — cause and effect implied but unexplained. Did the structures kill the fish? Is the die-off a side effect, a harvest, or — interestingly — a *medium* of communication? - **"Then they spoke"** — who is "they"? The structures? The fish? Something speaking *through* the fish? The ambiguity is the hook. ## The Megastructures — What and Where - **Abyssal towers**: nine (or twelve) spires rising from the abyssal plain, tops lost in cloud. Visible from the coast as a fence of impossible verticals. Ocean-based feels right given the fish. - **Orbital lattice**: a ring or web at geostationary orbit, dripping filament "roots" into the sea. Bigger scale, less intimate. - **Strung along the SOFAR channel** (the real deep-ocean sound channel): the structures as beads on a thread through Earth's natural acoustic waveguide. Hard-SF texture with built-in thematic payoff — *they chose sound as their medium because water carries it*. Whales already use this channel. Humans barely do. - Human nicknames as worldbuilding: "the Needles," "the Fence," "the Quiet," "the Buoys" (bitter irony from fishermen). ## The Die-Off — Mechanisms - **Collateral of speech**: their broadcasts resonate in swim bladders and otoliths. The fish die because the aliens are *shouting into the wrong organ*. Their voice, at full power, is fatal to anything that hears the way fish hear. (A diver dies near a tower mid-broadcast — the stakes become human.) - **The ocean being "read"**: the die-off is a scanning process; every death is a data point in a census. - **Triage**: the die-off is the first stage of a treatment — harsh medicine for a sick ocean (dead zones, acidification, anoxia). The aliens as oncologists; the fish as cells lost to chemo. - **Testimony collection**: they're gathering the dying — as archive, as evidence, as souls. ## Who Speaks, and What They Say - **A single repeated phrase**, translated with increasing accuracy across the story — chapter epigraphs each re-gloss the same message, e.g. "SPEAK SPEAK SPEAK" → "WHO SPEAKS" → "WHO SPEAKS FOR THE WATER" → a final full sentence that recontextualizes everything. - **A litany of names**: they recite the names of extinct species — learned from our sediment and ice cores. They arrived because they heard our silence growing. - **An apology**: they know the die-off hurts us. They keep saying sorry while continuing. - **They're not talking to us at all**: they address the ocean's remaining life. Humanity overhears first contact happening on its own planet, as bystanders. Devastating, humbling twist — with room for a final grace note: at the end, one sentence aimed at us. - **The fish themselves speak** — washed-up bodies arranged on the tideline, one sentence spelled per night in carcasses. Coastal-gothic horror-wonder; the towers never confirm or deny. ## Alien Intent — Menu of Motives 1. **Undertakers/archivists**: they perform funerals for dying biospheres; Earth flagged as terminal; the speech is a eulogy in progress. 2. **Healers**: the ocean was dying anyway; they're stabilizing it — not for us, without asking us. 3. **Midwives**: the structures are a nursery/cradle, seeding something new into the sea. 4. **Refugees**: fleeing something that ate *their* ocean; our sea as lifeboat or seed vault. 5. **Translators**: the structures exist to give a biosphere a voice. First contact is with ourselves. 6. **The reversal**: undertakers who discover mid-job that the patient isn't dead yet — the story pivots on the moment they realize. ## POV & Cast Options - **Marine acoustician** (protagonist): her life's work was recording reef soundscapes; the reefs she recorded are now silent. Grief + expertise + hydrophone access. Strong fit. - **A linguist losing her voice to ALS**: first contact by a woman going mute. Resonant but risks sentimentality. - **A deaf marine geologist** who feels the speech through the hull as vibration — communication across modality; the aliens' language is partly pressure, partly chemistry, partly sound. - **A sonar tech** whose submarine brother died during the first broadcast — personal grief braided with ecological grief. - **A fisherman's kid** who heard the speech first through a hull, in the dark. - **The committee**: political satire, nations fighting over who speaks for Earth. Good as seasoning, not as the whole meal. - **One chapter from a whale's POV** — bold, could be the emotional core or could break the story's spine. High risk, high reward. ## Tone Options - **Elegiac literary** (Chiang's "Story of Your Life" crossed with VanderMeer's *Annihilation*): grief, translation, unknowability. - **Clinical thriller** (*Three-Body* meets *Andromeda Strain*): labs, deadlines, escalation. - **Coastal gothic**: a dying fishing town, mist, fish on the sand, a community unraveling. - **Cosmic horror**: the speech is a countdown; the structures are measuring Earth for burial. - **Wondrous**: *Solaris* with warmth — the payoff is awe, not answers. ## Structure Options for 8 × 1000 Words - **Braided timeline**: open in narrative present (post-speech), flash back through arrival and first words in ch. 2–3, then run forward. Honors "a month ago." - **Day-countdown chapter titles**: "Day 34," "Day 41"… - **Translation epigraphs**: each chapter opens with the current best translation of the alien phrase — the reader watches understanding sharpen alongside the plot. Cheap in words, rich in payoff. - **Found fragments**: news tickers, hydrophone transcripts, committee minutes — global scale without POV sprawl. - **Single POV** (tight, emotional) vs. **rotating 3-POV** (wide, political) vs. **single POV + chorus** (fragments supply scale; protagonist supplies heart). ## Story Beat Skeletons — Variants **A. "The Litany" (single POV, elegiac):** (1) Present: shore of dead fish, towers on horizon, speech ongoing. (2) Flashback: arrival day; die-off begins in hours. (3) Flashback: first speech — names of extinct species. (4) Present: attempts to reply; a diver dies in a broadcast; military strike fizzles. (5) The question is isolated: *who speaks for the water?* (6) Discovery: ocean chemistry is *healing* — they're undertakers who've realized the patient lives. (7) Cracking the question; humanity was never the addressee. (8) The reply: the protagonist broadcasts her old field recordings — the ocean's own lost voice. The die-off stops mid-litany. **B. Political thriller (rotating POV):** linguist, admiral, fisherman's kid. Strike triggers ocean-wide retaliation; translation averts it. Global, fast, colder. **C. Cosmic horror:** the speech is a funeral rite; final chapter reveals the mercy at its heart — bleaker, tighter. **D. "The Tideline Alphabet":** dead fish spell sentences in the sand; small-town horror; towers silent throughout. Most unconventional, most imagery-driven, hardest to sustain over 8 chapters. ## Endings Menu - Towers dissolve/sink into artificial reef; first live shoal returns; final image mirrors the opening corpse-strewn shore. - The aliens restore something — at a price (memory, territory, a promise). - They answer the reply with a single sentence addressed, for the first time, to *us*. - They finish and leave; the ocean changed but alive; grief and hope unresolved — literary, unresolved-but-resonant. - The last epigraph is the completed translation of the phrase — the emotional payload lands in a fragment, not dialogue. ## Motifs, Names, Titles - Motifs: otoliths (ear stones — hearing made bone); the SOFAR channel; bioluminescent blooms; a jar of dead minnows on a windowsill; hydrophone static as lullaby. - Protagonist candidates: Dr. Maren Ostrovsky, Dr. Ana Reyes, Dr. Yara Sendak. Secondary: sonar tech (Petty Officer Ruiz), deaf sister, fisherman's kid (Junie). - Titles: *The Water's Children*, *Fishfall*, *Litany*, *The Quieting*, *What the Water Wants*, *Dead Tongue*, *Salt Psalm*. ## Risks & Traps - Info-dumping acoustics/oceanography. - Too many POVs for 8,000 words. - Aliens too legible (kills wonder) or too opaque (unsatisfying). - The "humans are the virus" moral bludgeon. - Sentimental whale stuff. - Ending too neat (fish all better) or too nihilist (eulogy for Earth). --- # Reflection **On the prompt's shape.** The strongest reading is the one that makes the *aftermath* the story: the arrival and the first words both sit in backstory, and the narrative present is about living alongside something enormous, grieving, and barely understood. That pushes me away from the political-thriller variant (B) and cosmic horror (C), which both want contact as plot engine, and toward the elegiac mode where the engine is *translation and grief*. Variant D (fish spelling sentences in carcasses) is genuinely haunting but I doubt it can fill eight chapters without either repeating itself or abandoning its own device; it feels like a novella's centerpiece wearing a novel's clothes. **On the aliens.** The motive options cluster into two families: *predatory/harvest* stories and *funerary/medical* stories. The predatory family is more conventional — been done, and it flattens the aliens into antagonists, which makes the middle chapters tactical rather than contemplative. The undertaker-who-discovers-the-patient-lives reversal (motive 6 above) is the richest: it gives the fish die-off a terrible double meaning (they began a funeral; the funeral is what's killing the fish), it makes the speech a eulogy that must be interrupted, and it hands the climax to *understanding* rather than to weapons — which suits the word budget, since a military subplot eats chapters. The humbling twist that they weren't addressing humanity at all also feels right for this tone; it's the thematic spine (we assumed first contact would be about us; it wasn't), and it converts the ending from "humans negotiate" to "humans answer anyway" — more moving, less procedural. **On the speech.** The single-repeated-phrase device, retranslated in chapter epigraphs, is almost too good to pass up: it gives the reader a progress bar for understanding, it makes each chapter's turn *legible as a turn*, and it delivers the emotional payload in the final epigraph rather than in expository dialogue. It also disciplines me against over-explaining the aliens — we only ever know as much as the current translation supports. Pairing it with the SOFAR channel gives the hard-SF grounding that keeps the lyricism from floating away. The litany-of-extinct-names idea could either be the *content* of their speech or fold into the phrase device as a discovered layer in the middle chapters. **On POV and cast.** Eight thousand words is roughly one protagonist's worth of depth. The marine acoustician is the strongest anchor: her recordings of dead reefs give her a personal archive that can *become the plot* (her old tapes as humanity's reply — the ocean's voice answering for the ocean). The ALS linguist is thematically potent but doubles the "losing voice" motif; I'd rather keep that resonance embedded in the recordings than in a second major character. A small chorus — a sonar tech, a fisherman's kid, news fragments — can supply scale in a paragraph each without diluting the POV. The whale-POV chapter is tempting but I suspect it would puncture the story's realism membrane; the whales might work better *heard* through hydrophones, mourned from outside. **On structure.** The braided open (present → flashbacks → forward) honors "a month ago" and creates early suspense, but two flashback chapters is the maximum — more than that and the present-day momentum stalls. Day-countdown titles and translation epigraphs could combine cleanly: date as title, current gloss as epigraph. Beat-wise, chapters 1–3 establish and reveal the speech; 4–5 must escalate (human cost — the diver's death, the failed strike, the whale die-off); 6 carries the reversal; 7 the understanding; 8 the reply. That's a workable one-turn-per-chapter rhythm, and each beat has a natural scene rather than needing summary. **On tone calibration.** The risks are sentimentality and moral bludgeoning. The ecological grief could curdle into lecturing if the aliens exist to indict us; better if their motive is *impersonal* — they respond to silence, not to sin, and would have come for a dead ocean regardless of who killed it. That keeps the humans' guilt ambient and self-recognized rather than authorially delivered. For the ending, the full-restore ending is too neat and the departure ending is too cold; the version where the reply changes their behavior mid-rite — the litany stopping, something given back, one sentence finally addressed to us — lands between hope and irresolution, which matches the elegiac register. **Open questions to settle before drafting:** the exact final translation of the phrase (this is the load-bearing line of the whole piece); whether the diver's death or the submarine brother carries the human-grief thread; how legible the aliens' biology/interiority should be (leaning: almost entirely illegible — only their *actions* become legible); and whether chapter 8's reply is the reef recordings alone or recordings plus the protagonist's own voice — the difference between the ocean answering and the ocean-and-us answering, which is ultimately a decision about what the story believes first contact is *for*.

# Intention **Working title:** *Litany* **Premise.** Nine megastructures rise overnight from the abyssal plains — not from the sky; they *emerged*, and later we'll understand they had been drawn toward us for a long time, called by the ocean's growing silence. Their arrival kills fish by the millions: their voice, at full power, is lethal to anything that hears the way water-life hears. Within days they speak — a single enormous utterance carried along the SOFAR channel, and it is a funeral rite: a recitation of the names of every extinct marine species, read out of the seafloor's strata like a ledger, climbing through geologic time toward the present. They are undertakers who came to bury a dying ocean and discovered, mid-rite, that the patient isn't dead yet. The rite cannot conclude unanswered. The eulogy kills the mourners. And the question at the heart of their speech — *who speaks for the water?* — was never addressed to humanity at all. We are eavesdropping on a funeral being held on our own planet. **Plot shape.** The undertaker-reversal from the brainstorm (Variant A): chapters 1–3 establish the aftermath and flash back to arrival and first words; 4–5 escalate the human and ecological cost; 6 carries the reversal (they're healing the water even as the rite kills it); 7 is understanding and preparation; 8 is the reply. The climax is an act of translation and voice, not violence — a military strike appears once, briefly, and fizzles; it is not a subplot. **POV and cast.** Single close-third POV: Dr. Maren Ostrovsky, late 50s, marine bioacoustician stationed on Faial in the Azores (deep water close to shore; a town — Horta — that was once the hub of transatlantic telegraph cables: a town already built for messages from across the water). Her life's work is thirty years of reef soundscapes — an archive of the ocean's voice from before the die-offs, which becomes, in chapter 8, humanity's answer. Supporting cast, kept minimal: **Theo**, her former graduate student, a diver who dies during a broadcast; **Inês**, a chemical oceanographer who brings the reversal; **Junie**, a fisherman's daughter collecting otoliths from the dead fish — hearing made bone, the story's central motif in miniature. The aliens are never seen and never explained. Only their *actions* become legible. No interiority, no anatomy, no motive monologue. **Voice and style.** Elegiac literary SF — Chiang's translation grief crossed with VanderMeer's unknowable presence. Past tense, lyrical but precise; sound described with tactile, synesthetic attention (a healthy reef *crackles*; a dead one *hisses*). Each chapter is titled by day-count ("Day 31") and opens with an epigraph: the current best translation of the aliens' repeated phrase. The epigraphs are the reader's progress bar for understanding, and the final one — correcting a single mis-segmented word, *for* → *with* — is the story's last turn, placed as the final line of chapter 8. Hard-SF texture (SOFAR channel, hydrophones, resonance, soundscapes-as-biodiversity) delivered through Maren's practice, never lectured. Occasional short found fragments (a monitoring log, a news ticker, a committee communique) inside chapters, each under 80 words, to supply global scale without POV sprawl. **The load-bearing machinery.** The phrase evolves: "SPEAK SPEAK SPEAK" → "WHO SPEAKS THE WATER" → "WHO SPEAKS FOR THE WATER?" → "WE HEAR THE WATER DYING. WHO SPEAKS FOR THE WATER?" → "WE CAME FOR THE DYING WATER. THE WATER IS NOT DEAD. WHO SPEAKS FOR THE WATER?" → the fully parsed liturgical call → final correction: **"WHO SPEAKS WITH THE WATER."** The answer, when it comes, has two movements: the water's own recorded voice (Maren's archive — the ocean speaking for itself), and then Maren joining it, taking up the litany where the towers stopped — the living reading the roll call of the dead. The aliens' single sentence ever aimed at air, at us: "We were too late for ours. You were not." — grief for their own dead ocean, delivered once, unexplained. **What I am aiming for.** Wonder braided with grief; the humbling realization that first contact was never about us; an ending between hope and irresolution — the die-off stops, the rite ends, the spires remain, changed and changing; something is given back (ninety seconds of an alien sea — their archive, the funeral they arrived too late for); a first live shoal returns; the silence at the end is not empty. **What I am avoiding.** No whale POV chapter. No villain, no harvested-Earth, no invasion logistics. No "humans are the virus" moralizing — the aliens' motive is impersonal; they respond to silence, not sin, and our guilt stays ambient and self-recognized. No sentimental anthropomorphizing of the structures. No neat restoration (the ocean is scarred; the towers don't leave; the whales don't come back all at once). No committee farce beyond one fragment. No romance. No acoustics info-dumps. --- # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — Day 31: "SPEAK SPEAK SPEAK SPEAK SPEAK"** Epigraph: raw, unparsed repetition. Present-day open. Maren walks the tideline below the town — a month of dead fish, silver drifts decomposing to bone, the water hissing where it used to crackle. On the horizon, ninety kilometers west: *a Agulha*, the Needle, one of nine spires worldwide, its top lost in cloud. Everyone carries the hydrophone feed now, the way they once carried weather. Introduce Junie on the shore, winnowing otoliths from the dead into a jam jar ("when something dies, you can read how long it lived from its stones"). Establish Maren's archive — shelves of tape and drives, a career of recording reefs that no longer exist. End beat: the global translation team publishes a new parse — *WHO SPEAKS FOR THE WATER?* — and a UN reply committee, sixty drafts deep, formally requests "acoustic materials of ecological significance." They want her archive. She isn't sure the question is hers to answer. Hook: the phrase follows her home, playing on every speaker in town. **Chapter 2 — Day 0: the arrival (flashback)** Epigraph: a monitoring log line — "02:14 — signal onset," no translation. The night the sea broke. No ships, no fireball: sonar shadows blooming worldwide, then nine points of emergence as the spires breached the surface at dawn. The fish died first — within hours, swim bladders hemorrhaging, the deep changing before anything visible did. The town wakes to grounded boats and silver water; Junie's father motors out and comes back silent. Maren's long-placed hydrophone array catches the first structured sound rising out of the channel — vast, patient, repeating. End beat: she plays the recording for the harbor crowd off her laptop, and the sound is recognizable even raw: cadence. Rhythm. It has the shape of *speech*. First human shiver of the story. **Chapter 3 — Day 3: first words (flashback)** Epigraph: "WHO SPEAKS THE WATER" — syntax unresolved. The world arrives in Maren's lab — her array is the finest receiver near the Azores Needle. The speech resolves into pattern: recitation. Names. Latin binomials rendered with impossible acoustic fidelity — *Tiktaalik*-era dead, Ordovician dead, climbing upward through the strata. The realization lands in the room: they are reading the seafloor like a ledger of the dead, and the litany is moving through geologic time in one direction. Toward now. Toward us. Inês, met here, delivers the chemistry aside that plants chapter 6's seed: the deep water samples are *wrong* — cleaner than they've been in decades. End beat: the fragment chorus (news ticker — nations claiming ocean rights, cable-history irony of Horta the message-town), and Maren alone at night, listening to a name she herself has said at a funeral: a whale that died in her recordings' era. The litany is approaching living memory. **Chapter 4 — Day 34: the price** Epigraph: "WHO SPEAKS FOR THE WATER?" Return to present. The broadcasts are intensifying; the Needle's voice rises on a cycle. A Navy strike on the South Pacific spire makes one news fragment and nothing else — the tower drinks the explosion; the recitation doesn't pause. Theo, Maren's former student, dives to service the array node near the Needle — against her objection, the mission cleared anyway — and a broadcast begins while he's down: resonance, hemorrhage, dead in the water at forty meters. Maren's grief braided with guilt: her array, her access, her student. His dive recorder survives, holding his last minutes. End beat: she plays the recording once — under

# How a Human Might Approach This Piece A human writer handed this prompt almost certainly doesn't start with architecture. They start with an obsession — and this prompt practically selects for one: *sound*. Someone who's actually listened to a hydrophone feed, who knows the 52-hertz whale, who has heard a reef crackle like frying fat at dusk. The story is an excuse to make the reader *hear* something. Everything else — the towers, the plot, the translation — is scaffolding around that sensory obsession. Humans also draft to discover. A human plan for this story would be a page of scribbles with gaps: "don't know how the fish die yet," "maybe she lost someone?," "end = ????" — with the expectation that the draft will overturn half of it. Even meticulous outliners hold their plans loosely. The plan I wrote is a treaty. Every beat is locked, the final line is pre-scripted, the alien motive is fully narrated in the author's head. That's not a plan a writer makes; it's a specification an executor fulfills. And prose written to specification reads like it. A few other human tendencies this plan lacks: - **Off-axis stakes.** Humans let a story be "about" something adjacent to its theme. Maybe it's really about Theo. Maybe it's about a marriage that ended the same month the towers arrived, and the world-event refracts the private one. My plan keeps everything on-theme, aimed at the thematic bullseye. - **Lumpy weight.** Human chapters are not equal containers. Chapter 4 (Theo's death) would balloon to 1,800 words and something else would shrink to 400. A chapter that's one page long — after a death, say

# Intention **Title:** *Fishfall* (alternate: *Ear Stones* — the title stays provisional, like everything else in the plan that can survive being wrong). **Premise.** Nine spires rose out of the abyssal plains — not from the sky; out of — one month before the story opens. Their arrival killed the fish first. Theirs is a voice at a scale water-life cannot survive: the broadcasts resonate in swim bladders, in otoliths, and the ocean dies by the million whenever the towers speak. And they speak constantly — a recitation. Translation consortia slowly resolve it into names: Latin binomials of extinct marine species, read out of the seafloor's strata like a ledger, climbing through geologic time toward the present. The story's working understanding — held as *hypothesis*, never confirmed on the page — is that they are undertakers who came for a dying ocean and are discovering, mid-rite, that the patient is still breathing. Their repeated question, *who speaks for the water*, was never addressed to humanity. The climax is not a word-trick or a negotiated treaty. It is an act: a small group at Horta's old telegraph cable station transmits thirty years of recorded reef sound — the water's own voice — plus the live noise of the harbor. The recitation stops mid-name. What answers, once, is ninety seconds of a sea that is not Earth's — overheard, unaddressed, undecidable. **What I've cut from the earlier plan, and why.** The for/with mis-segmentation twist — too puzzle-box; the answer here is behavioral, not lexical, and the translation stabilizes mid-story. The pre-scripted closer "We were too late for ours" — cut entirely; if the aliens ever aim anything at us, it stays ambiguous. Theo no longer dies to give Maren grief — a functional sacrificial death is the cheapest beat in the plan. He lives, works consortium liaison, argues for transmitting before she does, and loses the hearing in one ear servicing her array node during a broadcast — cost without ceremony, and the horror is the towers' indifference ("it didn't even pause" is the beat; the phrasing belongs to the draft). The epigraph apparatus is gone — translations arrive in-scene as dispatches Maren reads, so understanding stays experiential. At most two embedded documents in the whole story. **Off-axis stakes.** Maren, 57, has age-related high-frequency loss and a hearing-test appointment card she keeps not using. This is not an allegory engine; it's a mundane fact of her body that the story never resolves and never heals. It pays off only once, at the end, when she takes off the headphones and listens to the real harbor with what hearing she has left. **Cast.** Maren Ostrovsky, marine bioacoustician at the oceanographic institute above Horta, Faial — thirty years of reef soundscapes, some reels degraded, some mislabeled; her archive is flawed and biased toward reefs she loved, and that imperfection is the point of it. Theo, ex-student, consortium liaison, pro-answer. Inês, chemical oceanographer, whose data (shrinking dead zones, pH nudging) lands mid-story as an argument, not a revelation. Junie, fisherman's daughter, winnowing otoliths from the dead on the tideline — she states facts flat, like kids do, and no one poeticizes them for her. The aliens are never seen, explained, or given interiority. Three live readings of their motive stay open through the whole draft. **Place.** Faial earns its keep with facts, not symbolism: deep water close to shore; a town built for messages from across the water (the 1890s telegraph cables); the quay murals painted by every passing yacht crew — a harbor wall already covered in signals; old men who watched Capelinhos rise from the sea in 1957 and are therefore harder to astonish than anyone else on Earth. Portuguese words unitalicized, used sparingly. **Voice and style.** Past tense, close third, plain lyricism. Sound is described concretely — a healthy reef crackles like a pan; a dead one hisses — never with awe-vocabulary ("vast," "ancient," "ineffable" are banned). Dialogue is short, oblique; people talk past each other; no one explains the theme aloud. The military strike is one radio item, no scene. Chapters are all ~1000 words but deliberately unequal in *texture*: one is a single real-time scene, one compresses a week, one is nearly all listening, one is mostly one long paragraph. Endings vary too — only two or three chapters end on a strong turn; the rest end flat and quiet, the way days do. **What stays open for the draft to decide** (the plan is scaffold, not treaty): whether the litany resumes afterward at whisper-register or stops forever; whether the ninety seconds were meant for us; the exact final image and line; whether anyone is ever punished for the unauthorized transmission. **Aims.** Grief braided with awe; the humbling that first contact wasn't about us; an ending between hope and irresolution — die-off stopped, towers remaining, a handful of sardines off the marina that could mean everything or nothing, Maren's hearing unchanged. **Avoids.** Whale POV, villains, harvest plots, committee farce, romance, restoration-bows, aphorisms, acoustics lectures, and any sentence that sounds more like a plan than a person. --- # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — Day 30.** Present. Maren walks the tideline below Horta: a month of fishfall reduced to bone, water hissing where it used to crackle, the Needle on the western horizon with its top in cloud. Junie and the jam jar of otoliths — practical, unadorned. Maren mishears her once; unremarked. The hydrophone feed is ambient everywhere now, like weather. A consortium email requests her archive. She doesn't answer it. Ends quiet, on the sound in her earbuds, not on a hook. **Chapter 2 — Day 0–1 (the one flashback).** The night the sonar shadows bloomed and the spires breached at dawn; the fish dead in hours, bladders hemorrhaging, the deep changing before anything visible did. At the café, old men compare it to Capelinhos — the sea made land here once before. Her array catches the first structured signal; she plays it off her laptop for the harbor crowd. No words yet — just cadence. The shape of speech. **Chapter 3 — Day 33.** Present. Dispatches arrive; the translation stabilizes: *who speaks for the water.* The realization it's a recitation — binomials, climbing out of deep time. Maren recognizes a whale's name she once said at a funeral. Theo introduced properly: he wants to answer, she resists — their friction carries the should-we-speak question. Inês seeds the chemistry thread in one aside. The arithmetic of dread: the litany is approaching living memory. **Chapter 4 — Day 36.** The dive. Theo services the array node near the Needle — his call, over her objection. A broadcast begins while he's down; he surfaces alive, half-deaf, ruined in one ear. The recitation never paused. Their argument afterward resolves nothing — he's not angry at her, he's angry at the indifference. The South Pacific strike is one item on the harbor radio, between football and weather. Her appointment card stays in a drawer. **Chapter 5 — Day 40.** Inês's data: oxygen returning to dead zones, deep water cleaner than her whole career. Argued over, not announced — the institute splits into camps (healing / triage / preparation for something), and the story keeps all three readings alive. Maren forms the undertaker hypothesis out loud and gets a consortium cable back: *anthropomorphic projection, reject.* Meanwhile every official answer so far — state choirs, presidents' speeches, even whale-song compilations — has failed to pause the recitation. The insight begins forming: everything sent was speech *about* the water, addressed to the towers. No one has sent the water. **Chapter 6 — Day 44.** The interior chapter, mostly one long paragraph: Maren alone with thirty years of tapes. Degraded reels, mislabeled boxes, reefs she loved and reefs she recorded out of duty, the grief of a career that is also an inventory of loss. Junie drifts through. Theo, reconciled enough to work, helps rig the transmission from the old cable station — chosen because that's where the infrastructure is, not because it means something. The committee has refused; they'll do it anyway, small and local and unauthorized, the kind of insubordination nobody stops because nobody believes it matters. What to send: the archive, and the live harbor feed — past voice and present, humanity unavoidably inside it. No speech. No speech. **Chapter 7 — Day 45.** Night at the cable station, real-time. The litany climbs into living memory — recent names, hers — while her recordings play out into the channel. The recitation stops mid-binomial. For the first time in a month, the world's hydrophones carry nothing: one paragraph of the whole planet noticing the silence. Then, once, ninety seconds of a sea that is not ours — overheard, maybe a gift, maybe a mirror, maybe not for us at all. Ends before dawn, no interpretation: Theo's good ear against the speaker, Junie asleep on the floor. **Chapter 8 — Day 46 and after.** Consequences stay small: the transmission quietly absorbed, credit claimed elsewhere, no arrest worth the paperwork. The die-off stops. The towers hold a new, lower register — whether the rite has ended or dropped to a whisper is one of the seams the draft decides. A handful of sardines off the marina that could mean everything or weather. The quay gains a new mural. Maren's hearing is what it is. Final movement: she takes off the headphones and listens to the actual harbor — gulls, engines, water on stone, less than she could once hear, and enough. The last line is not written yet; the plan only promises where she'll be standing.

# Maren Ostrovsky **Background.** Born in Gdańsk; her father was a shipyard electrician who got the family out in the eighties when she was nine. She retains exactly three things from this: a permanent accent in every language she speaks, a distrust of large machinery that hums, and one lullaby she doesn't remember learning. PhD in a cold country on cod spawning sound, then a two-year postdoc on Faial in 1994 that never ended. Her career-defining paper — the one everyone cites — she considers a minor work, a fluke of timing. The work she cares about is the long dull gold: Station 9, a patch reef off Pico, recorded every June for thirty-one consecutive years. Nobody funded it after 2003. She kept doing it with borrowed gear and her own money. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Reserved to the point of being misread. Comfortable with silence — professionally comfortable — and she lets pauses run long enough that visitors think they've offended her. She responds to emails three weeks late or never, not out of rudeness but because a request left unanswered long enough answers itself, and saying no requires a confrontation she'd rather not have. The consortium email in chapter 1 dies exactly this way. Her work life is ruthlessly ordered; everything else is soft chaos — a bike with a flat she's walked past for two years, a kitchen drawer of orphaned screws and keys to nothing. Chews pen caps flat. Sings the lullaby to herself while calibrating and doesn't know she does it. Swims in the harbor every morning, year-round, and kept swimming through the fishfall, which horrified the town. Her defense: "The fish are dead. The water's fine." **Flaws.** She hoards undigitized, half-degraded tapes because digitizing means finding out what's on them — what she's already lost — and she'd rather not know. She under-mentors: praise physically cannot leave her mouth, so it comes out as corrections ("Your metadata's improved" is the warmest sentence she has). And the denial: the hearing loss is real, progressive, high-frequency, and she has attributed it for three years to cheap earbuds, bad calibration, and a manufacturer's defect she has written to the manufacturer about *twice*. The audiologist's appointment card in her drawer is from two years ago. She has moved it four times so it stays on top of the mess. **Physicality.** Fifty-seven. Short, thick-wristed, swimmer's shoulders going soft; white hair cut by her own hand when it annoys her, so it always looks accidental. Three field shirts rotated until Inês buys her a fourth. Reading glasses lost while on her own head. She moves deliberately — a person who learned young that haste on small boats costs fingers. Voices low, unaccented when calm, Polish vowels surfacing when tired. The hearing shows only in geometry: she turns her right ear to you, sits facing walls, took the café's outside table that everyone assumed was for the view. **Motives & relationships.** She is a conservative in the literal sense — her instinct is to conserve: the archive, the routine, Station 9's record. The story's ask, that the archive be *used*, violated her twice over: use means exposure, and exposure means the possibility of being wrong in public. Allegiance: to the data itself — she jokes, not entirely joking, that her loyalty is to the reef, not the institute. Theo: the ex-student still hungry for approval she cannot dispense; their rhythm is his warmth against her flatness, and since his injury she's discovered she misses his chatter when he travels, a fact she has told no one. Inês: fifteen years of adjacent doors and sisterly warfare; the only person allowed to say the word *ears* to her face. Junie: a mirror she keeps almost stepping away from — the child is doing, by hand and by instinct, what Maren has spent thirty years doing with instruments, and Maren responds the only way she knows, with tasks instead of tenderness: "Label the jar. Date it. Otherwise it's just a jar of bones." Sunday phone call with her brother in Toronto, never missed, never mentioned to anyone. **Voice.** - "I've got four hundred hours of that reef and I couldn't tell you what one damselfish means by any of it. Why would they be easier?" - "The new hydrophones roll off above twelve kilohertz. I've written to the manufacturer. Twice." - *Internal, hearing a 1994 reel:* "For a second she was in the water with it, the crackle coming at her from every direction, and then she remembered the water was dead now, and the remembering hurt worse than the news had." --- # Theo Marques **Background.** Lisbon city kid who met the sea at nineteen on a field course and converted — and converts are the zealous kind. PhD under Maren on anthropogenic noise masking in coastal fish — how engine noise deafens fish in their own homes — then a postdoc in Boston, then picked up by the translation consortium as liaison because he's fluent in both acoustics and people. For the past month he's been shuttling between consortium calls and Horta, sleeping in his old office at the institute, refreshing his apartment in Boston only in video calls to check whether Ana, his partner, has watered his plants. She has not. He has stopped asking. Ana moved to Lisbon for work last year; the distance was supposed to be eighteen months; the towers have made his absence suddenly, guiltily defensible. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Fast where Maren is slow; fills silence as a service. Hopeful by practice rather than temperament — he decided to be hopeful the way other people decide to quit smoking, and he maintains it the way you maintain anything, daily and with lapses. Runs the marina at dawn in washed sneakers. Remembers everyone's birthday. Cries easily and without embarrassment — cried openly at the whale names, and when Maren looked at him he just said, "I know." Keeps a spreadsheet of every failed human reply to the towers: 214 rows, columns for source, content, duration, *response: none*. Inês calls it his grief log. He calls it a dataset. Both are right. Sweet coffee, a field-season habit from when sweet meant calories. Carries a wind-up alarm clock because a dead phone once made him miss a grouper spawning aggregation, and he's the kind of person a grudge against battery life fits. **Flaws.** Zeal outruns evidence: he's been certain the towers are a conversation since day three, and he tunes his confidence to whatever room he's persuading. He needs to be the bridge — connector isn't his job, it's his identity — and it makes him schmooze in moments that call for plain speech. He's signed Maren's name to consortium emails "as a courtesy" without asking. After the injury, the recklessness curdles: he physically cannot sit in meetings now — the tinnitus spikes in air-conditioned rooms — and conducts consortium business standing in the parking lot, pacing, which reads as fury to people who don't know him. **Physicality.** Thirty-eight, tall and narrow, sprinter's build gone stringy, gray in one dramatic streak at the temple

# Chapter 1 — Day 30 The tide had been bringing them in for a month, and the gulls had stopped coming. That was the thing nobody had predicted. The gulls gorged for the first week, then ate selectively, then not at all, and now they stood around on the rooftops looking violated, and the smell off the beach had moved through fish into something older and mineral, like a cellar. Maren walked the tideline below the road the way she walked it every morning, which was the way she had walked it before, and this was either discipline or a failure of imagination, and she had decided early on not to examine which. The fish came in as silver, went out as bone. Windrows of ribcages light as ash, spines intact, eye sockets filled with sand. The beach had whitened. Under her boots the pebbles clicked together and it occurred to her, not for the first time and never usefully, that she was walking on a sound. The Needle stood on the western horizon where it had stood for thirty days, ninety kilometers out and looking nearer, its top in the cloud as always, so that what you got was a gray column entering the gray and never arriving. The old men at the café had named it the first week — *a Agulha* — and the name had stuck because naming it made it a thing on the horizon rather than a thing in the water, and everything in the water was currently dying. Junie was down near the slipway, where the drift had piled deepest. Ten years old, rubber boots two sizes too big, kneeling in the wreck of the fish with a kitchen sieve. She worked with her whole body, shoulders down, hair stuck to her face, and she did not look up when Maren's shadow reached her. "You're late," Junie said. "It's mostly sardines today." "Mostly?" "There's a mackerel." She said it the way another child might report a four-leaf clover. She lifted the sieve, tilted it, let the small bones rattle through back onto the sand, and kept what stayed: a white stone the size of a peppercorn. She held it up between two fingers for inspection, then dropped it into the jam jar that sat in a bucket hole she'd dug to keep it steady. The jar was a third full. Maren had asked her, in the first week, why the heads. Junie had looked at her like the answer was on the ceiling. "The stones," she'd said. "When something dies you can read how long it lived from its stones." She'd said it flat, the way she said everything, and Maren had not managed to add anything to it since. There were people at the institute with grant money designing protocols for the die-off sampling, and none of them had a jar a third full. "Label the jar," Maren told her now. "Date it. Otherwise it's just a jar of bones." "It's got a date." Junie turned the jar so the masking tape showed. Maren read the date. It was wrong, off by a week, and she decided this was a fight for a day with better weather. She sat on the overturned dinghy that had been her office through the worst of it, and took out her phone, and put one earbud in. She kept the other ear free for the town, which was a habit she'd had long before the month that gave it a reason. The feed came up the way it always came up now, instantly, without buffering, because everyone carried it now the way they'd once carried weather. There were local versions and there were cleaned versions, gain-riding, noise-gated, someone in Boston had made a version with the frequencies shifted up into human comfort, and there was a version that was just the raw channel off the Azores array, and that was the one Maren listened to, because it was hers. The voice was in it, as it always was. The sound engineers at the institute had tried, in week two, to describe it to the radio, and done badly, and Maren had understood why. It was not loud. That was the first mistake everyone made — they said *vast*, they said *enormous*, and the levels were modest; a blue whale at full flood was louder by an order of magnitude. It was more that it was *placed*. The sound sat in the deep sound channel the way a coin sits in the groove of a tray, held there by nothing you could see, and it did not scatter, and it did not smear, and every hydrophone on Earth got the same signal at essentially the same strength, whether it was a thousand kilometers from a spire or eleven thousand. The engineers had words for all the properties. What they did not have a word for was the effect, which was that listening to it felt like being listened *at*. It had a cadence. That had been clear from the first hour, clear before anyone could say why — a rhythm inside the sound, repetitions arriving at intervals too long for music and too regular for weather. Speech-shaped. For thirty days the voice had said the same thing, over and over, and the translation teams had it now, everyone had it, it was on the wall of the fish market in six languages: *Who speaks for the water.* Not a question mark. The teams had been firm on that from the start. Whatever it was, it did not inflect. Maren listened to it for a while with her eyes on the Needle. There was nothing new in it. There had been nothing new in it for two weeks, which was itself the news — the signal didn't drift, didn't cycle, didn't tire. It had the patience of a machine or of something for which patience was not a virtue but a medium, like water. Her phone buzzed against her hip. She looked at the notification long enough to see the sender — the consortium office in Lisbon, Theo forwarding again, the subject line with the word *archive* in it, the same word that had been in the subject line the last four times. They wanted her tapes. Thirty years of reef recordings, requested by name, in an email whose first paragraph thanked her for her *invaluable contribution to this moment for humanity*, which was a sentence she had read four times now and declined each time to be in. She put the phone face-down on the dinghy's hull. On the feed, the voice turned its phrase over, and began again. Maren had come down here every morning with the earbud in her pocket, and every morning she told herself she was listening for a change, a professional act, a monitoring of the channel, and every morning at about this point she admitted she was just listening to it. She didn't know for what. It was like standing near a wall behind which people were talking — you didn't need the words, you wanted the *talking*, and the fact that you couldn't have it. Junie had filled the sieve again. Down the beach the water worked at the bones, and it hissed where it worked, a long thin hiss with none of the frying crackle in it that a living shallows makes, and Maren sat on the dinghy with one earbud in, one ear on the town, and listened to the dead water and the voice together until it was time to go up.

# Chapter 2 — Day 0 Later, when the timelines were drawn, the sonar shadows came first — 02:14 UTC, nine soft gray blooms on screens in Norfolk and Kanagawa and the Azores, each the size of a city and each, the operators insisted afterward, reading like nothing so much as something rising. Maren was asleep above her lab. Her array logged it all and she didn't look at the log for eleven hours, and this became one of the small facts she carried without ever saying: that the world changed under her instruments while she slept, and the instruments, which had never once missed anything in thirty years, waited politely for morning. What woke her was the sound of boats. Not the engines — the hulls, the specific flat knocking of fiberglass against stone that a harbor makes when every mooring line in it is loaded wrong at once. Then the water level in the marina had gone strange overnight, half a meter off and rising where it shouldn't rise, and the harbor was full of boats standing on lines that weren't theirs, and out past the breakwater the sea was white at the horizon. Not wave-white. Flat white, a white *layer*, like frost on a field. The fish were already dead by then. That was the accounting nobody got right for weeks: the death came *before* the towers did, or with them, underwater and finished while the spires were still two thousand meters down. The boats that went out that first morning — Junie's father among them, and Maren would learn later he never went out again — motored over water that was thick with the dead rising. Sardines first, and mackerel, and things from the deep that no one in Horta had ever seen brought up whole: lanternfish in their millions, a hatchetfish still lit, its photophores pulsing on the deck like a small blue accusation. Swim bladders ruptured. The veterinarians who flew in on the third day said the word *resonance* and then spent the rest of the week not being believed. And on the western horizon, gray on gray in the dawn haze: a column. Ninety kilometers out and looking nearer. It came up out of the water with no fuss, no displacement you could measure — they would measure, later, obsessively — and stood there, and did nothing, and did nothing the next day, and did nothing still, which turned out to be what it did instead of everything else. By noon the town had migrated to the café by the transatlantic dock, because that was where the wi-fi was and where the harbor could be watched, and Maren went too, because the institute's network was drowning and because at home there was only the log she now couldn't stop reading. The old men had taken the big table. Senhor Alberto, who was ninety-one and had been nine years old when Capelinhos rose out of the sea a few kilometers west, held the floor, and what he said, while the television behind him showed the Norfolk column on a loop, was that he had seen the sea make land once already in his life and everyone had coped. "The water does what it does," he said. "We watched an island be born. At least this one is polite enough to stay put." Somebody asked him whether it frightened him. He thought about it — really thought, Maren watched him do it — and said, "It's older than me or it isn't, and either way I've been hearing about worse since 1957." It was the calmest room on the island. It was possibly the calmest room on Earth. Up the hill the institute was already filling with shouty people from four governments, and down here nine old men were drinking coffee in front of the end of the known world and finding it weather. She should have gone back up. Instead she kept sitting with her laptop open on the table, going deeper into the array log, because there was something under the water column and she had found it at 02:14 and it had not stopped. Not a shockwave. Not machinery. A signal — structured, repeating, seated in the deep sound channel like it had been built for the seat. The channel runs at depth, a thousand meters down and more, a layer the temperature and pressure of the water make into a corridor that carries low sound across whole oceans, and whatever had risen had put its voice exactly there, where the whales put theirs, where nothing human had ever managed to put anything so precisely. Every repetition identical. Long, slow phrases, if they were phrases, arriving at intervals too long for music and too regular for weather. She sat with her headphones on in the café for an hour while the television looped, and then Senhor Alberto's granddaughter asked her, not unkindly, what she was listening to, and Maren — who did not do this, whose rule was that public things happened in rooms with projectors — took the headphones off and jacked the laptop into the café's little speaker by the till. The café went quiet without being asked to. It wasn't loud. That was what Maren watched the room get wrong and then get right: people braced, and then unbent, and then leaned *in*. The signal came out of the small speaker, thin, a fraction of what the channel held, and still it sat in the room the way it sat in the ocean — placed, held, arriving whole. On the television a government minister was being interviewed about the column, and someone turned the television off, and nobody turned it back on. It went on for four minutes before anyone said anything. Then Senhor Alberto, who had watched the sea his whole life and once watched it make land, said it, quietly, in Portuguese, and his granddaughter didn't translate it because everyone had already understood: "That's not a machine." "No," Maren said. "It's saying something." "We don't know that." He looked at her, ninety-one years of patience in his face, and did not say *yes we do*, because he was too polite, and because he didn't need to. On the speaker the voice turned its phrase over, and began again. The fish came in on the afternoon tide, and the gulls came down to meet them, and nobody in the café had moved.

# Chapter 3 — Day 33 The dispatches came out of Lisbon at six and eighteen, and Theo came with the morning one, up from the airport in a shirt that had started the week better. He had been sleeping in his old office since week two, on the theory that the cot there was no worse than the hotels, and his wind-up alarm went off at five every morning and could be heard through two doors, and Maren had not told him this because she had decided it was useful, like a rooster. He put the dispatch on the projector screen, because Maren's rule was that public things happened in rooms with projectors, and this was now a public thing whether she liked it or not. "Oka," he said. "In Kanagawa. She ran the cycles against each other." For two weeks the translation had been stable and the world had organized itself around one sentence. *Who speaks for the water,* uninflected, on the wall of the fish market in six languages, on signs, on a tattoo Maren had seen on a deckhand's forearm in the marina. The signal repeated; the repetition was the message; that had been the understanding. Oka had done the boring thing. She had taken the cycles — every repetition of the phrase, hundreds of them now — and compared them to each other, on the hunch that identical things shouldn't require a similarity analysis at all. They didn't. No two cycles were the same. The phrase was a frame, and inside the frame, held at a level below it the way a watermark sits below a stamp, was other content, cycle after cycle, different every time. The screen showed the comparison. The frame, and inside it a structure: two units, long-short, like a genus and a species. "They're names," Theo said. "That's the working conclusion. Taxonomic names. They've been saying them since day one, underneath the part we could read." The oldest were shapes out of shale, things that had held names for a hundred and fifty years only because a paleontologist had dug them up and given them one — armored fish, spined fish, the lungfish's great-great-ancestors. The recitation had started in the Paleozoic and climbed. Week one had covered an eon. Week two, another. The teams were calling it a ledger. Nobody had a better word. Maren sat looking at the long-short pattern on the screen and felt something in her settle and rot at the same time, because she knew the shape of it. Versicle and response. She had sat through a thousand of them as a child in Gdańsk, the priest's line, the congregation's line, back and forth, the name of the dead, *wieczny odpoczynek*, the name of the next. The sentence on the fish market wall was not the message. It was the refrain. "Where did they get Latin?" she said. Theo looked at her. "The strata don't have names," she said. "A fish five hundred million years old doesn't come with a binomial. Someone gave these things their names, and it was us. They've read us. Our books, our cables, our — " she stopped, because the next word was *museums* and something about the word, in this room, at this moment, was unbearable. "That's the other conclusion," Theo said quietly. "Yes. They know we're here. They've known something about us long enough to know our taxonomy." He let that sit, and then, because he was Theo: "They still aren't talking to us." "So the consortium wants my reefs." "The consortium wants your reefs. I put your name forward before you say it — I know. I'm sorry. It was that or let them requisition them, which they were forty-eight hours from doing, and this way you get to say no." "The answer's no." "The answer's no answer. Which you've been giving for a month, and I want to know what it's to. Not the tapes. The question. Somebody's going to answer that thing eventually. Every government on Earth is drafting. You've got four hundred hours of the water actually speaking and you won't — " "I couldn't tell you what one damselfish means by any of it," Maren said. "Four hundred hours, and it's noise with fish in it. Why would they be easier?" "Because they asked." "They didn't." "They said *who speaks for the water* on a planet with three billion humans on the coasts," Theo said. "If that's not asking, it's the closest thing to asking I've ever heard in any language, and I've spent my career on fish." Neither of them won, because there wasn't a win. He went to take the six a.m. call and she went toward her lab, and in the corridor Inês intercepted her, smelling of the deep freeze and holding a tablet with casts on it that she didn't show. "The deep water," Inês said. "My oxygen numbers from the dead zones. Have you looked?" "At what?" "At this." She turned the tablet around, then turned it back before Maren could focus, because that was Inês, feeding you the fact and withholding the number. "They're wrong. The casts. Wrong the good way. Since about day ten." Someone called her name from the wet lab, loudly, the way everything at the institute was called now. "Come look. Bring your glasses. It's cleaner than my entire career and I want you to tell me I'm not." Then gone, down the corridor, not waiting for an answer she obviously believed she'd get. In the evening Maren took the day's cycle from the array log and listened to it alone with the door shut, the way she had listened to the whole month, one good ear to the headphones. The names went by too fast to catch each one — the teams had software for it; she had her ear — but the refrain came up every fourth interval like a tide gauge, *who speaks for the water*, and between it the long-short, long-short, the roll call climbing out of the Miocene into the recent, and then, at 21:14, she heard one arrive that she knew. *Lipotes vexillifer.* The baiji. The Yangtze river dolphin, gone in her own lifetime, in the decade of her own career. She had said the name aloud once, at a conference in Halifax, in a ballroom with two hundred other people, because old Halloran had read the eulogy and ended it with the name and paused, and the room had understood what the pause was for, and two hundred acoustic scientists had said *Lipotes vexillifer* once, together, because there was nothing else to do with their mouths. She told him she would come. In her language, that was the objection, retracted. Theo went down at 11:20. The gap had opened at 10:40, as predicted, forty minutes early by the book's margin of comfort. She watched his bubbles move along the mooring line and listened to the feed, and the skipper smoked, and the deck hand stood at the rail not looking at the Needle and not looking away from it either. At 11:31 the voice rose. There was no warning in it — no swell, no approach. The gap simply ended, forty minutes ahead of every schedule it had ever kept, and the signal came up out of the channel at full power, and Maren was at the rail before she had decided to move. The bubbles stopped moving. Then they moved fast. She understood afterward that he had done everything right, and that doing everything right meant abandoning the connector, the tools, the plan, and going up through a column of sound that was killing everything in the water around him for ninety kilometers in every direction. What it was like inside it she never asked and he never said. What she had was the surface: the bubbles arriving, then him, white-faced, horizontal, one hand clamped over the left side of his head like he'd been hit with something, because he had. They got him over the transom between two names. She registered the fact at the time and could not stop registering it: the voice was still going, the feed still murmuring through the hull speakers, long-short, long-short, and the medic they'd brought for exactly this knelt on the deck working on Theo's ear, and the names kept coming up out of the water. He said one while they cut the suit away. He said *Hydrodamalis gigas* — the sea cow, 1768, dead before the century turned, the first name every student of the sea learns — while they were wrapping Theo in a blanket, and Maren stood on a research vessel ninety kilometers from a spire with her student's blood on her sleeve and listened to a eulogy that had not missed a syllable. They kept him in the clinic in Horta overnight for observation, and the ENT told him in careful English and then, when that didn't land, in better Portuguese, that the left ear was finished. The word she used was *permanent*, twice, in two languages, to be sure he had it. He thanked her. That was the part Maren couldn't get over afterward: he thanked her. The argument happened that night, in his office, with him sitting on the cot because his balance was wrong and standing made him seasick in a room. "I should have—" Maren started. "No." He said it without heat. "You haven't been below ten meters since the nineties, and the connector needs hands that know it, and we're not doing the thing where this is yours. It's mine. I made the call. I'd argue it again, the arithmetic held—" and there he stopped, because the arithmetic was the wound. "You can't know that," she said. "The gap came early. Nothing held." "That's what I mean." He looked at the wall. His laptop was open on the desk with the dive log half-entered, the cursor sitting where he'd abandoned it. "I keep the spreadsheet. You know that. Nobody had a better reading, so the room kept all three and fought about them, and the institute split into camps that corresponded exactly to nobody's expertise — the benthic ecologist believed triage, the geochemist healing, and Inês believed nothing until the numbers told her to, which was her whole personality. Maren said it at the whiteboard, because it was her turn to say something. "They came for a dying ocean. That's why they're reading it — you read a ledger when you're closing accounts. Then they got here and the patient was still alive. Now they're healing it and carrying on with the rite, and the rite is killing fish in the billions, and they haven't stopped the rite. Undertakers who found a pulse." The silence after it was long, and then the ministry woman asked her to say it for the record, and Maren said it again, and the record took it, and eleven hours later a cable came back from the consortium office in Lisbon, addressed to her personally: *OBSERVED PATTERN CONSISTENT WITH RITUALIZED VOCALIZATION. INTERPRETATION ANTHROPOMORPHIC. REJECT. MAINTAIN WORKING FRAME OF OPEN INQUIRY.* She'd been rejected before in her life. She'd never been rejected in all caps. Meanwhile the ledger had climbed into the living record, and the world had begun trying to answer it. Theo kept the spreadsheet — 214 rows, and now it grew. The Icelandic state choir sang into the North Atlantic for six hours, facing the water. Japan sent whale song, recorded off Ōnin, amplified down the channel. The Secretary-General read a statement of peace and goodwill in the six official languages; the towers read through every one. A fleet of fishing boats in Gdansk — not her Gdańsk, the shipyard was gone — streamed a banner: WE SPEAK FOR THE WATER. The towers read through the banner. "What did they all send," Maren said. It wasn't a question for Theo, but he was there, half-deaf on his right... left side now, pacing the office, and answered it anyway. "Choirs. Statements. Music." "No. What did they send. The Icelanders stood on a cliff and sent *about*. Every one of them sent speech about the water. To the towers." She looked at the array log going on its long gray scroll. "Nobody's sent the water." The room did the thing rooms do with a sentence like that, and Theo stopped pacing. In the evening Junie came up the hill to the lab with her jar, because her father had said the institute was where the stones went now, and the jam jar had graduated to a plastic tub with a lid, labeled in her handwriting, the date wrong. "Three hundred and forty-one," she said. She put the tub on the bench, matter-of-fact, an orphanage delivering its orphans. Then she stood there while Maren counted a sample under the loupe, and after a while said, "Are they going to keep talking?" "Nobody knows." "Grandmother says they're reading the names of the dead so the sea remembers them." A shrug in it — she was reporting the position of the household, not her own. "Is that true?" "It's the best thing anyone's said," Maren said, and Junie nodded, satisfied, the matter adjudicated, and left the tub and went home down the hill in the dark. Maren sat with the tub of otoliths afterward. Three hundred and forty-one stones from three hundred and forty-one fish, and the light behind her and the loupe in front of her, and she took one out and looked at it: a peppercorn of bone with rings in it like a tree, if a tree kept its whole life in its ear. You could read how long it lived. You could read, in the chemistry of the last ring, the temperature of the water it died in. She put it back. She did not count the rest. The email sat unanswered on her desk for the fifth time, the one with *archive* in the subject line, and this time she opened it and read to the bottom, all four paragraphs of *invaluable contribution to this moment for humanity*, and then typed, into the empty reply field, at 11 p.m., with the feed murmuring through her open laptop speakers the way it murmured everywhere now: *Not to the towers. Not as speech.* She looked at the line for a long time. It said no and it said something else. Then she closed the laptop without sending, and the room went dark except for the array monitor, where the ledger climbed, and the names went by under the refrains, long-short, long-short, into the year of her career's beginning, and she listened to the water's oldest dead being read out in a language made of water, and did not send the reply.
