He said it without drama, standing at her right shoulder — he stood there always now, so his good ear faced her, and they had both quietly rebuilt their bodies around the month without discussing it. "Nobody stops a thing on Faial. Nobody believes a thing on Faial matters. The projector's being serviced Thursday." It was not being serviced. It was being signed out, under maintenance, by two people whose names were on the sign-out sheet and would remain on the sign-out sheet, and there was a workboat, and there was the cable station. She went to the archive on Wednesday, because the question had stopped being whether to send and become what, and the what could not be answered by anyone who hadn't listened. She started with the shelves. Thirty-one Junes of Station 9, the patch reef off Pico that nobody had funded since 2003 and that she had kept recording anyway with borrowed gear and her own money, and before Station 9 there were the working years, the Caribbean transects, the Canaries, the two grim weeks in the Baltic in '98 she had never once replayed because she knew what they held, and she worked down the shelves and the inventory became a walk through her own life conducted by sound: here the 1994 reels, the first summer, the tape healthier than she'd feared, the reef at full afternoon crackle — snapping shrimp, thousands of them, the sound every textbook calls noise and every one of us knows is a city talking — here the box marked PICO?? with a question mark in her own hand that she wanted to reach back thirty years and scold, here the June the hydrophone dragged its mooring and recorded six hours of sand, here the reel she had labeled GOOD ONE and distrusted ever since, here 2011, the humpback that came through Station 9 at dusk and the damselfish stopped, all of them, mid-note, better discipline than any orchestra she had heard, and here 2016, and here 2020, and she could hear it going quiet without checking the dates, the crackle thinning year over year the way a fire goes out in the next room, and she sat with the loupe lamp on and her right ear to the monitor and listened to thirty years die in the space of an afternoon, and digitized all of it, and labeled every file, and did not stop, because stopping was a thing she had decided, that day, not to do. Junie drifted in on Saturday with her tub, because the institute was where the stones went now. She stood in the doorway a while, listening to the monitor. "Bacon," she said. "What?" "It sounds like bacon." The 1994 reel was playing. Maren had written *broadband crackle consistent with alpheid snapping shrimp* across four hundred hours of analysis in her life, and here was the most accurate description the institute had ever produced, delivered by a ten-year-old in rubber boots. "Is this what you're sending?" "Yes." "Good," Junie said. "It's better than the singing." The Icelandic choir had been on the television. The matter was adjudicated, and she put her tub on the shelf next to the ones from the week before, and went back down the hill. The cable station was the old building by the transatlantic dock, brick, 1890s, the room where the world's messages had once come ashore before going anywhere, and it had power and it had the terminus racks, and on Sunday the workboat would take the calibration projector out and lower it into the channel, and that was the whole of the engineering: a borrowed source, a room built for messages, thirty years of tape. The content took longer than the rigging. Theo came in the evening with the harbor hydrophone — the little one off the marina wall, the one whose feed the tourists liked — and set it on the bench. "Live," he said. "Put the harbor in it. Not speech. But if the archive is all we send, we're sending a museum. It should hear the water now, with the engines in it. With us in it. No speech, but no hiding either." "No speech," Maren said, and Theo wrote it on the whiteboard by the racks, the only rule, and under it the order of service, which she had decided that afternoon and not told him yet: Station 9, oldest to newest, all thirty-one Junes, in order, the way it had happened. Not the best reef. Not the cleanest recordings. One place, one lifetime, going quiet. "When?" Theo said. He meant the cycle. The voice rose every eleven hours and the gaps had been coming early all week, the schedule falling apart as the ledger climbed. "In the gap," Maren said, "if the gap comes." "And if it doesn't." "During." Theo looked at the whiteboard, at the one rule, and nodded slowly, and she understood that this was the thing he'd been turned into by the column of sound and his ruined ear — that the man who'd spent a month believing it was a conversation no longer needed it to be one. "During," he said. "All right." They loaded the reels into the car in the dark, boxes stacked in the back seat like the family silver, and the harbor lay below them with its lights on the water, engines and church bells and water working the stone, all of it going quietly onto tape. On the western horizon the Needle stood where it had stood for forty-four days, and tomorrow, in the gap if there was one and during the voice if there wasn't, the water was going to hear itself.

Junie was there because her father had brought the week's tub up at suppertime and she had carried it herself, and then nobody had noticed the hour, and it had got late, and nobody had noticed that either. She sat on the floor in the corner with her coat as a pillow, doing whatever ten-year-olds did with a phone in the corner of a room where history was about to be attempted, and the tub of stones beside her like luggage. The voice rose at 23:50. The gap had come at 22:00 and lasted barely two hours, the schedule collapsing exactly as it had been collapsing all week, and they had known by midnight that the choice had made itself: during. "Roll it," Maren said. The first reel was 1994, the first June, the dusk hour. The tape hiss came up through the racks and out of the channel and into the sea, and then, under the hiss, the crackle began — Station 9 at full flood, the snapping shrimp in their thousands, the fish talking over them, the whole reef at once, bacon, the most accurate description the institute had ever produced — and it went out into the deep sound channel where it sat beside the voice the way a coin sits beside a coin in a tray. For eleven minutes, the world's dead and one living hour of water occupied the same channel. Theo stood at the gain with his hand flat on the board, not adjusting anything, just touching it. On the monitor the voice went on under the reef — long-short, long-short, the refrain, the next name — and the two sounds ran together without touching, and Maren listened with her right ear to the headphones and heard what she had known for a month and never once heard: that the ledger was a voice too, that it had timbre, that the names came faster or slower in its mouth — if it had a mouth — as if the reading cost something. At 00:03 the voice stopped. Not trailed. Not faded. Stopped, mid-name — a genus given whole, a species begun, and then the first syllable of the species unfinished, and then nothing. Maren's hand wrote the time before she had decided to write it. Junie looked up from the corner. "It stopped." "Yes." "Did we do that?" "Nobody knows," Maren said, and Junie accepted it, the way she accepted everything, and lay back down on her coat. The silence went out over the Earth. Every feed on the planet carried it — every earbud, every harbor speaker, every monitoring station from Norfolk to Kanagawa — and for the first time in forty-five days the deep sound channel held nothing human and nothing otherwise, and the world sat in it. The whales noticed. The biologists would spend years on this part: the humpbacks off the Azores went quiet mid-phrase, all of them, at once, and stayed quiet. Somewhere a radio announcer stopped talking. In the channel, the crackle of Station 9 went on, the only sound on Earth's floor, one reef at dusk in 1994, talking to an ocean that had stopped to hear it. Theo's hand had not moved from the board. The reels turned. Junie's breathing had gone slow and even in the corner, and Maren let her sleep, because the girl had school, and there was nothing for her to do here, and because someone in the building asleep was a load-bearing thing. The silence lasted four minutes. Then the channel took sound again, and it was not the voice, and it was not the reef. It was waves. That was the first fact and it arrived whole: wave noise, the long wash and drag of water against a shore, running under them through the deep channel — but the period was wrong, wrong the way a familiar room is wrong when you come home to it, the intervals too long, the wash too slow, a sea keeping time with some other sky. There was rain in it, or what stood where rain stands — a fine, even percussion on water, unbroken, patient. There were clicks in it, thousands of them, at intervals nothing in her thirty years had taught her, not shrimp, not cetacean, not sonar, life of some kind clicking in a shallows that was not hers. And under all of it a low tone, almost a hum, the sound a whole ocean makes against its own floor, a sound Earth's own sea made and no ear had ever lifted out of the noise floor. It was not speech. There was no refrain in it, no ledger, no address. It was a place. They had been sent, by something, the sound of a place. Maren did not move. Neither did Theo. The ninety seconds ran, and neither of them reached for a recorder, and both of them knew they were failing their professions in real time and could not lift a hand to save them. It ended the way it had come, without ceremony, mid-wash, and the channel held the reef again, and then only the reef, and then the hiss. Afterward Theo sat down on the floor next to Junie, slowly, because his balance was bad now, and put his good ear against the speaker grille, and stayed there. He did not say it was a reply. He did not say it was theirs, the drowned thing everyone at the institute had half-believed in, their ocean, their loss. He sat with his ear against the sound of Station 9 and let it be unexplained, and Maren understood that the column of sound and the ruined ear had made him this, finally: a man who could hear a thing without owning it. The reels went on turning. June of 1994 ran out and June of 1995 began, and the harbor feed murmured underneath it, live — engines and church bells and water on stone — and none of it was speech, and all of it was going out. Before dawn, one of the projectors in the racks clicked its gain lamp out and back on, and that was all. Junie slept through the whole second half of the night, through the ninety seconds and the silence after, and Maren never told her, not that week, not ever — that the sea had answered, and the only person in the room to sleep through it had been the one with the jar of stones.

# Chapter 8 — Day 46 The voice came back the next evening at the old hour, and the whole world's instruments measured it, and the measurement said: quieter. A tenth of the power. The engineers argued about whether the source had moved deeper or simply lowered itself, and settled, the way engineers settle, on describing the phenomenon rather than choosing: the register had dropped. The broadcasts ran eleven hours and held forty minutes, and the ledger went on underneath the refrain, long-short, long-short, slower now, a name every few minutes where there had been a name every few seconds. Whether it was still climbing toward the present, or had turned around, or had begun again at the Paleozoic, no one could say. The channel kept it the way it kept everything, seated, patient, at a volume the water could survive. Because that was the other fact, and it took three days for anyone to say it out loud at the institute, the way it takes days to say the thing too large to check: nothing new was dying. The tide came in on the forty-sixth day and brought wrack and plastic and a pallet lid and no fish, and came in the next day and brought none, and the beach lay white under its month of bone and began, slowly, to be a beach. On the fiftieth day a gull landed on the slipway, pulled something silver out of the shallows, and ate it standing up, and Senhor Alberto's granddaughter cried at the café, and Maren couldn't have said why that was the moment and not any of the others. The inquiry arrived on Day 47 as a cable in the usual capitals — *UNAUTHORIZED TRANSMISSION, SOURCE IDENTIFIED, REVIEW INITIATED* — and dissolved by Day 53 into a second cable noting that monitoring infrastructure had been operated *within local discretion* and that the register drop was *attributable to consortium observation protocols*. Theo read it twice and laughed the not-warm laugh, and then opened the spreadsheet, and Maren watched him do it. Row 215 was theirs: source, Horta; content, thirty-one Junes and the live harbor; duration, eleven hours. He moved the cursor to the last column, the one that said *response*, and sat there a while, and then closed the laptop without typing anything, which was the most accurate entry anyone had ever made in it. The sardines came back off the marina on Day 58. A fisherman reported them on the radio, annoyed, because they were interfering with something, and then apologized for being annoyed. The institute asked for footage; the ministry asked for footage; a research vessel anchored off the marina for a week and mostly photographed the mural wall. The sardines stayed or they moved, no one agreed, they were a handful of fish or they were the beginning of everything, and Horta, which had watched an island be born and coped, held both opinions at once without strain. Junie went down to the slipway the first morning and came back up reporting, as ever, the facts: "They're early." Nothing in her face adjudicated the matter. On Day 60 a humpback sang off the south coast, and the hydrophone caught it, and Inês printed the spectrogram and brought it to Maren's lab the way you bring wine. Maren put the print on the bench and looked a long time at the shape of it, the stacked harmonics rising through the frequency scale, up past four kilohertz, past six, into the fine high reaches where the whale keeps the top of its voice. She looked at it and heard nothing. The room was quiet around her, and the paper sang the whole time, and she read it measure by measure the way she'd read the ledger, and it was the first thing in two months she was grateful to take on faith. The email with *archive* in the subject line she answered on Day 61, at eleven at night, a month late, which was her way. She typed two words — *Come and get them* — and sent it before it could turn into a paragraph, and then copied the drives twice, because data you love lives in three places, and gave one copy to the institute and one to the archive in Lisbon, and kept Station 9 on the shelf by the window where the sun got to it, which was bad for tape and she did it anyway. The mural went up in the last week, on the wall by the transatlantic dock, where the crews paint. Not one of theirs — no flag, no boat name. Someone, at night, with permission from nobody: a gray column rising out of gray water into gray cloud, and below it, small, in silver, a shoal of fish going sideways into the dark, and nothing else, no letters, no faces. The town left it alone. The tourists photographed it. She walked the tideline with Junie at the end of that week, out past the slipway, over the whitened pebbles. Junie carried the new tub, mostly empty now, a week's stones, because she kept coming and nobody had told her to stop. The masking-tape label had a date on it. The date was wrong again, and Maren looked at it, and this time did not say anything, and Junie, who noticed everything flat, noticed that too. On the last morning she went down before the light, the way she had gone down for thirty years, and left the headphones on the bench by the door. No feed. No earbuds. One ear free for the town and the other for whatever was left. The water took her the way it always took her, cold at the temples, then nowhere. She swam out past the moorings, and the harbor woke around her — first engine, gulls coming off the roofs, a bell somewhere finding the hour, water working the stone of the breakwater with its long drag — and she rolled onto her back and lay in it with her ears under the surface, where the world went round and held. The deep channel murmured below her, carrying its quiet voice out toward the Needle. She couldn't have said what it was saying. She couldn't have said she wasn't meant to. Somewhere past the breakwater, holding her place in the swell, she realized she was singing, and kept on.

# Intention **Core concept.** The 🩸🩸🩸 is an emergency signal from a childhood "blood pact" — four girls, aged eleven, swore an oath over a sewing needle and a horror film: *three blood drops means come now, no questions asked, blood sisters forever.* The pact has lain dormant for five years, because the friendship has quietly collapsed. Then, at 00:04, Bex — the sister who blanked them all eight months ago — sends the emoji. Our narrator, Nell, goes. She has to. Those were the terms. **Tone & voice.** First-person, past tense, confessional and dry — the sensible, funny, slightly swotty narrator of British YA (think Holly Bourne by way of Caitlin Moran). Nell treats a midnight distress call with the grave operational seriousness of a war film, while the story lets the real, quieter darkness — family breakdown, shame, the slow rot of a friendship — leak in underneath. Comedy on top, ache underneath. The joke is never at Bex's expense; the comedy punches at Craig-with-a-K, the NHS vending machine, and Nell's own melodrama. **Structure.** Mostly one night, told against a literal clock (chapter timestamps from 00:04 to dawn), then an aftermath chapter and a coda weeks later. This keeps 8,000 words propulsive — it's a rescue story with a time-stamped engine — while the flashbacks to the original pact supply the emotional archaeology. Each chapter gets one comic set piece and one reveal. **Darkness dial.** Real but survivable: Bex's home has imploded (mum's boyfriend, dad gone), she's put her hand through a door's glass panel, and the house isn't somewhere she can be. No death, no supernatural, no graphic gore. The dark heart of the story is that teenagers ghost their friends out of *shame*, and the pact — silly, melodramatic, sworn over a sliver of a sewing needle — turns out to be the one thing that outlived the shame. **Setting.** A middling English town: ring road, retail park, recreation ground, a spinney behind Daisy's old garden, a 24-hour garage staffed by the unshockable Gurdeep, rain, a screaming fox. Mum's ancient bicycle, named Doris. **Things to avoid:** Americanisms; mean-spirited humour about the girl in trouble; mawkish sentiment (no group hugs scored to imaginary violins); phones as filler; adults as pure idiots. The ending should be warm but honest — not everything is fixed, but the safety net is back up. **Motif.** The emoji itself. It opens the story, it's misread, it's honoured, and it returns transformed in the final line — the pact downgraded from blood oath to ridiculous ongoing alarm system, which is somehow better. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — "The Terms & Conditions" (00:04, ~1,000 words)** The text arrives. Nell's phone glows; three blood drops from BEX, who blanked her at the bus stop in March. Compact flashback to the original sleepover: the horror film, the sewing needle, Daisy fainting, Priya admitting she'd assumed the pact was about periods, the oath ("come now, no questions, blood sisters forever"). Nell rationalises, catastrophises, changes out of pyjamas into "competent" clothes, leaves a note for her dad, and exits via the extension roof. **Function:** hook, voice, the pact's rules, the fracture line established. Ends with her on the patio, heart hammering, absurdly proud of herself. **Ch. 2 — "Doris" (00:41)** The night town. The gauntlet of neighbours' motion-sensor lights; a stand-off with a fox that Nell loses. She liberates Mum's bike, Doris, whose brakes are advisory. Interior backstory: how the Coven of four became two and a bit — Priya still texts, Daisy's wrapped up in am-dram, Bex went to college and evaporated. Nell realises she's obeying a rule drafted by eleven-year-olds and keeps pedalling anyway. **Function:** texture, comic set piece, the friendship's decline mapped. Ends as she reaches Bex's street and sees the front door wide open at 1am. **Ch. 3 — "Craig" (01:17)** Discovery. The house half-dark, bin bags on the drive, Bex on the kerb with a tea-towel wrapped round her hand and blood on it — not a massacre, but not nothing. Craig-with-a-K's silhouette in the doorway; the mum nowhere; a volume of rowing still ringing. Bex's shame is the obstacle, not the injury: she can't even look at Nell. Nell does paramedic-nerd triage (she wants to be a paramedic; this finally pays off) and decides: A&E, now. Bex: "You actually came." Nell: "Those were the terms." **Function:** the reveal — the darkness is domestic, the blood both literal and the least of it. **Ch. 4 — "Gurdeep Has Seen Everything" (01:50)** The ride to hospital, doubling as a second set piece: Gurdeep's 24-hour garage, where Nell buys plasters, Lucozade and the last two sausage rolls; he does not blink. Nell texts Priya the emoji; Priya replies "omw. this is either an emergency or the best night of my life." On a bench outside, Bex starts talking — in fragments — about the last eight months: why she cut them off, the shame, Craig, the dad who texts fortnightly. Nell breaks the only rule and asks questions. **Function:** the emotional centre begins; comedy keeps it buoyant. Ends at the A&E sliding doors. **Ch. 5 — "Minor Injuries, Major Drama" (02:30)** A&E waiting room at 2am: a man with a fork-related incident, a telly bolted to the ceiling showing shopping channels, a vending machine that eats £1.20. Priya arrives like a small weather system; Daisy's mum turns out to be the night nurse (Daisy barrels in twenty minutes later with party rings). The four of them together for the first time in a year, doing what they do: taking the mick with surgical precision. Bex gets seven stitches and a referral; the social-realist machinery hums in the background. **Function:** the reassembly of the Coven; belly laughs mid-worry; the girls' affection resurfacing through banter. **Ch. 6 — "Bin Lorry O'Clock" (05:00)** Dawn walk home through the waking town: milk float, bin lorry, bakers' van, the town looking scrubbed and simple. They detour to Daisy's old garden and the tree-fort where the oath was sworn. Ceremony 2.0 — botched, funny (Pritt Stick instead of blood; Daisy faints again, for tradition). But underneath: the real conversation. The pact can't survive unchanged — oaths written at eleven don't account for GCSEs, shame, or Craig — so they amend it. New terms: questions *allowed*, coming anyway still mandatory. **Function:** theme made explicit without a sermon; sunrise catharsis. **Ch. 7 — "The Summit" (four days later)** Aftermath and consequences. Nell's dad discovered the note and Doris; grounding delivered with, confusingly, a flicker of pride. The parents' summit at Nell's kitchen table — Bex's gran up from Skegness, Craig's name spoken like a verdict. Bex lands at her gran's for now; counselling booked; nothing fixed, but the floor is back under her. A wobble: Bex goes quiet again for two days, and Nell has to decide whether to crowd her or wait — chooses waiting, hates it, it works. **Function:** consequences are real; the story resists a magic fix; comedy from parents, party rings, and geography (Skegness). **Ch. 8 — "🧇🧇🧇" (six weeks later)** Coda. The Coven 2.0 in its realistic, unglamorous form: a group chat that's mostly memes and logistics; Daisy's am-dram panto; Priya's new girlfriend; Bex's stitches out, her attendance back up, her laugh returning in instalments. Nell on work experience with a paramedic crew, seeing what emergencies actually look like. Then, just after midnight, a new text: 🧇🧇🧇 from Priya. Nell groans, gets up, grabs her coat — grinning all the way to the door. **Function:** callback; the pact revealed as a ridiculous, load-bearing thing; warm, honest ending. Final line lands on Nell going, again, because those are the terms.
With a view to making the writing more human, discuss how a human might approach this particular piece (given the original prompt). Discuss telltale LLM approaches to writing (generally) and ways they might not serve this particular piece. For example, common LLM failings are to write safely, or to always wrap things up with a bow, or trying to write impressively at the expense of readability. Then do a deep dive on the intention & plan, critiquing ways it might be falling into typical LLM tropes & pitfalls. Brainstorm ideas to make it more human. Be comprehensive. We aren't doing any rewriting of the plan yet, just critique & brainstorming.
Model Output:
# How a Human Would Approach This Before critiquing the plan, it's worth imagining what a human writer — say, an actual mid-career British YA author — would do with this prompt, because the differences start before a word is written. **They'd write from a wound, not a concept.** A human doesn't pick "friendship decay and shame" as a theme; they pick it because they *were* ghosted at fifteen, or because they *did* the ghosting, and it still itches. The story would be tilted toward whatever that wound is. If the author was the Bex, the story might be told from inside the shame. If the author was the Nell, the narrator would be less heroically loyal and more compromised — she'd have stopped trying too, and she'd know it, and the midnight text would partly be an accusation aimed at her. **They'd draft out of order.** A human writes the scene with heat in it first — probably Chapter 3, the kerb, the tea-towel — and builds outward, discovering what the story is by writing it. They'd happily discover that Gurdeep is more interesting than the tree-fort ceremony and give him more room, and cut the ceremony to two lines. The plan's chapter-by-chapter "Function:" labels are the opposite of this: they treat each chapter as a deliverable that must justify itself to the project manager. **They'd know the world from the inside.** The details would be stolen from life: the specific despair of a hot cabinet in a 24-hour garage at 2am; the way A&E at night smells of hand gel and, faintly, of crisps; the fact that milk floats barely exist anymore and a modern human writer would know that, because they'd have *checked*, or more likely never thought of a milk float because they've never seen one. The plan's town — milk float, bin lorry, bakers' van — is a 1987 postcard. That's the pastiche problem: it's Britain assembled from other books about Britain. **They'd let it be uneven.** One chapter 500 words, another 1,500. One character very funny, one nearly silent. One joke that doesn't quite land, left in, because the rhythm needed it. A joke at the exact wrong moment that the narrator is ashamed of. Humans leave seams showing. **They'd resist the coda.** The wholesome-six-weeks-later ending is the thing a human author's editor would have to *talk them into*. Instinctively, novelists distrust epilogues where everyone's attendance has improved. They'd rather end on something smaller and stranger — a detail that aches without explaining itself. # Telltale LLM Approaches (and How They'd Hurt This Piece) **Over-engineering.** LLMs plan like civil engineers: "one comic set piece and one reveal per chapter," every motif deployed, recovered, and "returned transformed." The plan literally schedules catharsis ("sunrise catharsis," Ch. 6). Humans trust some scenes to do nothing except be funny or true; not everything is load-bearing. **Everything rhymes too hard.** The emoji opens, is misread, is honoured, returns as waffles. Daisy faints in the flashback, then faints again "for tradition." The paramedic ambition is planted in Ch. 3 and "finally pays off." Runners and callbacks are sitcom machinery; used at this density they make the story feel written by a very organised ghost. **Slick dialogue.** "You actually came." / "Those were the terms." That's trailer dialogue — the exchange you'd put in the film's teaser. Real teenagers, and especially a real Bex in real shame, are more likely to say "you're such a mug" and mean *I love you*. Affection transmitted as insult is the actual language of British teens; the plan's dialogue is currently the language of book jackets. **Curated quirk.** Skegness, sausage rolls, Pritt Stick, party rings, ring road, Lucozade, "Bin Lorry O'Clock." Individually fine; collectively it's "how do you do, fellow Britons." A human scatters three of these across a whole book. The plan has roughly all of them, per chapter. **Safety rendered as good taste.** Keeping the darkness survivable is the *right* call for this story. But LLM safety also manifests as vagueness: Craig is "a silhouette," the rowing is "a volume of rowing still ringing." The dark stuff is kept artfully off-stage, which risks making it decorative. A human would let one specific ugly thing through the door — one sentence Craig actually said, still replaying in Bex's head, that she repeats flatly on the bench. Not graphic. Just true, and therefore worse than any silhouette. **The efficient system.** Ch. 7 has "a referral," "counselling booked," "the floor is back under her" within four days. Real CAMHS waiting lists are months. Real social services lose files. A human wouldn't turn this into a social-policy rant, but they'd know the gran-from-Skegness solution happens *because* the system is slow, and that honesty would make the ending warmer, not colder, because it's earned. **The bow, wearing the costume of "honest but hopeful."** The plan *says* "not everything is fixed" and then fixes nearly everything: stitches out, attendance up, laugh returning "in instalments," group chat thriving, mum presumably History's Greatest Monster defeated off-page. "The laugh returning in instalments" is a lovely phrase doing the work of a full recovery montage. # Deep Dive: Critique of the Intention & Plan **The Intention.** Mostly sound — the pact-as-premise is good, the one-night clock is genuinely propulsive, and "comedy on top, ache underneath" is the right brief. The problems are in the fine print: - *"Nell treats a midnight distress call with the grave operational seriousness of a war film."* This is the plan's best joke and also its trap: it commits the narrator to performing wit in every paragraph. If every paragraph is a bit, there's no floor for the ache to land on. The narration needs dead patches — plain sentences at the moments that matter. - *"Each chapter gets one comic set piece and one reveal."* A formula, stated as one. By Ch. 5 the reader can feel the rotation. - *The narrator is too competent and too kind.* Nell goes out at midnight out of pure loyalty and handles everything well. Where's her guilt about March? Her secret relief at being needed? Humans let narrators be slightly self-serving and half-aware of it. Right now Nell's only flaw is being delightfully melodramatic, which is a trait, not a flaw. - *Bex has shame but no anger.* The plan gives her one note. The most human version of Ch. 3 is Bex being *furious* that Nell came — because being rescued in front of witnesses is humiliating, and because the pact obliges her to be grateful when she wants to disappear. The gratitude, if it comes, should come late and sideways. - *The Mum-shaped hole.* Doris is "Mum's ancient bicycle" and Mum is otherwise unaccounted for. Nell's household has a dad who dispenses a grounding. Every character needs a household with its own weather; right now Nell's is a stage set. (Also: one bike, two girls, one with a hole in her hand — the plan hand-waves the logistics of getting to hospital. Logistics are where truth and comedy live. Two girls walking one bike between them at 2am, arguing about who steers, is a better scene than anything currently in Ch. 4.) **Chapter by chapter:** - **Ch. 1** — Explains the pact, the emoji, the rules, the fracture line, *and* the theme, all before 1am. The reader assembles nothing. The flashback should be a shard here, not a summary: Nell knows what 🩸🩸🩸 means before we do, and doesn't tell us for a page and a half. Also, the plan claims the emoji "is misread" but never stages the misreading — a missed opportunity: let Nell's first guess be *wrong* (she assumes drama, attention-seeking, a period emergency) and let the wrongness sting later. - **Ch. 2** — The fox stand-off is good; the motion-sensor lights are good. But "interior backstory: how the Coven became two and a bit" is an essay inserted into a bike ride. A human would deliver the friendship's death in objects and specific memories — the last message Bex ever replied to, the birthday she didn't acknowledge — not a status report. This chapter also misses the single most human phone-texture available: Nell scrolling back through the dead chat, months of one-sided blue bubbles, to find exactly when it went cold. That's the wound, in an iPhone. - **Ch. 3** — The best chapter in the plan, but it resolves too fast. Bex resists, Nell decides "A&E, now," and off they go. Real version: Bex *refuses* the hospital. She's terrified of questions, of her mum being called, of it going on record. The negotiation — Nell bargaining her into the car park of the hospital "just to look at it" — is drama; compliance is logistics. - **Ch. 4** — Gurdeep the unshockable wise cashier is a borderline trope (the magical all-seeing shopkeeper). Keep him, but demote the wisdom: he doesn't dispense life lessons, he just doesn't blink, and maybe overcharges her for the Lucozade by accident. Also this chapter dawdles for people with an open wound — it works *only* if Bex is refusing treatment, per above. Otherwise it's a snack montage en route to minor surgery. - **Ch. 5** — Daisy's mum being tonight's A&E nurse is a colossal convenience the plan doesn't notice. Either cut, or lampshade so hard it becomes the joke ("Is this a miracle?" "She *works* here, Nell."). The fork-man and the vending machine are keepers — that's human observation. But "the four of them together doing what they do: taking the mick with surgical precision" is the plan describing chemistry it hasn't earned yet; four girls who haven't spoken in a year should be *awkward* first, and the awkwardness is the good material. - **Ch. 6** — The Pritt Stick re-oath is the group hug in disguise. The plan bans mawkishness and then schedules a ceremony. Strongest alternative: the ceremony *fails*. The tree-fort's been demolished (the spinney got fenced off for new builds — thematically convenient, but also just true of how towns work), or it's there and it's tiny and damp and they can't all fit in it because they're sixteen now, not eleven. The pact renews itself anyway, accidentally, via a stupid message in the group chat — which is how sixteen-year-olds actually conduct sacraments. - **Ch. 7** — "The Summit" is a plan-shaped word; nobody's kitchen-table crisis meeting is a summit except in fiction. The two-day silence is the most human beat in the entire plan — keep it, and make it cost more. But "counselling booked" is doing fantasy work; change it to "on a list" and the chapter gets more honest for free. Dad's "confusingly, a flicker of pride" is nice; the grounding should also be properly boring and slightly unfair, because real consequences are. - **Ch. 8** — 🧇🧇🧇 is a genuinely good ending image and I'd fight for it. But "grinning all the way to the door" is sugar. The human version: she goes *grumbling*. It's a school night. There's a mock exam at nine. She goes anyway, furious about it, and the fury *is* the love. Also, "Priya's new girlfriend" listed alongside "Daisy's panto" is identity-as-character-note — a plan-shaped bullet. If Priya's girlfriend exists, she exists in scenes, or not at all. # Brainstorming: Making It More Human **Voice & prose** 1. **Let Nell be wrong.** Her first interpretation of the text is uncharitable ("attention-seeking, classic Bex") and she has to live with having thought it. Narrators who briefly think the worst are human; narrators who are instantly, gravely loyal are characters in an insurance advert. 2. **Dead patches.** Two or three moments per chapter where the narration goes plain and small. The line after Bex shows her hand should be six words long. 3. **Jokes that fail.** Let Nell make a joke at the exact wrong moment on the kerb and watch it die. Have her be funny *to cope*, and know it isn't working. That's more darkly comic than a hit-rate. 4. **Banter with uneven distribution.** Priya funny, Daisy earnest and occasionally accidentally hilarious, Bex barely speaking for two chapters. Not everyone quips. A group where everyone's witty is a writers' room. **Character & relationship** 5. **Bex's anger before gratitude.** Her first line to Nell should push her away. The "you actually came" beat, if kept, arrives much later, possibly in text message form three days afterwards, because that's how shame communicates. 6. **Give Nell a stake in March.** Maybe she was the last one to text Bex and got left on read and *never followed up* — one attempt, then pride. Her going tonight is also atonement, and she only admits this to herself somewhere around Ch. 6. 7. **Mum exists.** Give Nell's household one live wire of its own — even a small one (Dad's new shift pattern; Mum working nights, hence Doris going unused). The note Nell leaves gains weight if there's a person who'll actually read it at 6am. 8. **Craig gets one sentence.** One line of his actual dialogue, reported by Bex, flatly, on the bench. Not a rant. The specificity is the horror. 9. **Gurdeep demoted from oracle to man.** He watches the hand, says "hope it's not your dominant one, mate," and gets her flavour of crisps wrong. Unshockable is funnier without wisdom. **Structure & scene** 10. **Break the clock once.** Seven chapters time-stamped, then one chapter drops the timestamp entirely and is just the sleepover, told in full, dropped into the middle of the night — the past interrupting the present like a memory actually does. (Or interleave: two-page flashback slabs, not summaries.) 11. **Fail the ceremony.** Tree-fort demolished or too small. The re-oath happens by accident, in the group chat, at 4am, as a joke — and nobody says it's a joke. 12. **The bike carries two.** Solve the transport logistics on the page. Two girls and one bike, three miles, 2am. It's the love scene of the story and it currently isn't in the plan. 13. **Awkwardness before chemistry in Ch. 5.** The reunion should have a limp opening five minutes — wrong hugs, a "you look well" that's a lie — before the old rhythm kicks in. 14. **Uneven chapters.** Let Ch. 3 run long and Ch. 7 run short and terse. The timestamp structure will hold the reader regardless; uniform 1,000-word blocks are a plan artefact, not a story rhythm. **Ending** 15. **End on the grudge, not the grin.** Final chapter: she's annoyed. It's Wednesday. She goes. Maybe final line is her muttering the terms like a complaint. "Those were the terms" lands *harder* as a grumble than as a vow. 16. **Leave one thread genuinely loose.** Bex is *better*, not recovered — one bad week still ahead, one thing (her mum) unresolved and honestly maybe unresolvable, said once, plainly, and not fixed. Hope with an unsolved corner is what "darkly comic" actually means; the current plan solves the corner and then calls itself honest. None of this requires abandoning the plan — the skeleton is good, and the premise is genuinely strong. It requires demoting the engineer and letting the mess back in: the wrong first guesses, the failed ceremony, the angry girl, the bike built for one, the joke that dies, the grumbled ending.
Ok now with these considerations in mind, formulate the final plan for the a humanlike, compelling short piece in {n_chapters} chapters. Bear in mind the constraints of the piece (each chapter is just 1000 words). Above all things, the plan must serve the original prompt. We will use the same format as before: # Intention <State your formulated intentions for the piece, synthesised from the the parts of the brainstorming session that worked, and avoiding the parts that didn't. Be explicit about the choices you have made about plot, voice, stylistic choices, things you intend to aim for & avoid.> # Chapter Planning <Write a brief chapter plan for all {n_chapters} chapters.>
Model Output:
# Intention **Core concept (unchanged in skeleton, changed in blood).** At 00:04, Nell receives 🩸🩸🩸 from Bex — a distress signal devised by four eleven-year-olds over a horror film and a sewing needle: *come now, no questions asked, blood sisters forever.* The friendship died eight months ago; Nell goes anyway, because those were the terms. The pact is the premise, but the story's real subject is shame — the shame that made Bex vanish, and the smaller, quieter shame Nell is carrying about the text she never followed up in March. **Voice.** First person, past tense, dry and confessional — the voice of a swotty sixteen-year-old who copes with fear by narrating herself as the hero of a war film. Crucially, the narration has *dead patches*: at the moments that matter most (the tea-towel coming off, Craig's one sentence, Bex's first word) the prose goes plain and short. Wit is Nell's coping mechanism, and the story occasionally catches it failing — she makes a joke on the kerb and it dies in the air, and she has to sit in the silence she's made. Not everyone quips: Priya is funny, Daisy is earnest and accidentally hilarious, Bex says almost nothing for two chapters. Affection between these girls is transmitted via insult: "you're such a mug" is the love language, and it's what Bex says on the kerb instead of "you came." **Nell is wrong, and it stings.** Her first interpretation of 🩸🩸🩸 is uncharitable — she runs through the options (period emergency, Bex being dramatic, a wind-up) and nearly talks herself out of going. She went anyway for the wrong mixture of reasons: duty, melodrama, and something she won't name until Chapter 6 — that she texted Bex once in March, got left on read, and let pride do the rest. The going is loyalty and atonement at once, and the story lets her be half-aware of this rather than announcing it. In the aftermath, Bex tells her she almost didn't send the emoji because she assumed Nell would think it was a joke. Both girls were wrong about each other. That's the wound and the repair. **Bex's order of operations: anger, then nothing, then — much later, sideways — gratitude.** Being rescued in front of witnesses is humiliation on top of humiliation. She resists the hospital (terrified of questions, of her mum being called, of it going on record) and Nell has to bargain her there. Craig exists as exactly one sentence of quoted dialogue, reported flatly by Bex on the walk: *"He said Dad was right to leave."* That's why her hand went through the glass panel. No rant, no silhouette-melodrama — one specific, ugly, ordinary line. **Logistics are where the love lives.** One bike, one girl with a hole in her hand, three miles: they walk Doris between them, arguing about who steers, and it's the love scene of the piece. Gurdeep's 24-hour garage stays, demoted from oracle to man: he doesn't blink, hopes it isn't her dominant hand, and gets her crisps wrong. Daisy's mum is *cut* as the A&E nurse — no miracle staffing. The tree-fort ceremony *fails*: the spinney's been fenced off for a new estate, the fort is half-demolished, and the pact renews itself by accident, in the group chat, at 4am, proposed as a joke that nobody treats as one. The reassembly of the four is awkward before it clicks — wrong hugs, a "you look well" that's a lie, five limp minutes. **The world.** A middling English town rendered in roughly six true details, not twenty curated ones: motion-sensor security lights, a screaming fox, the dead group chat, a vending machine, party rings, a gran in Skegness. Nell's household has weather of its own: Mum works nights at a care home (which is why Doris has gone unridden, and why the note Nell leaves will be read at 7am by someone who loves her). The system is honest and slow: counselling is *a list*, not a booking; Bex lands at her gran's because the machinery grinds slowly, not around it. **Ending.** No bow, one unsolved corner (Bex's mum, said once, plainly, unresolved). Six weeks on: the Coven 2.0 is unglamorous — memes, logistics, a panto — and Bex is better, not recovered. Then 🧇🧇🧇 from Priya, just after midnight, on a school night. Nell goes *grumbling*, furious about it, and the fury is the love. Final line is "those were the terms," muttered as a complaint, which lands harder than any vow. **Aims:** the emoji as engine, misread, honoured, and finally ridiculous; comedy on top, ache underneath; uneven rhythm (Ch. 3 tense and long-feeling, Ch. 7 terse); timestamps holding the shape while chapters vary in texture; plain sentences where it counts. **Avoids:** trailer dialogue ("You actually came"/"Those were the terms" as an exchange — the line moves to the end, grumbled); quips in every paragraph; the magical shopkeeper; the group hug scored to violins; recovered-in-six-weeks; Americanisms; British-ness as a prop list; every scene load-bearing. Some scenes exist only to be funny or only to be true. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — 00:04.** Open on the exact prompt line: the text, three blood drops, Bex, who blanked her at the bus stop in March. Nell's guesses run charitable-to-uncharitable: period emergency, then *classic Bex drama*, then a wind-up — and she nearly stays in bed. Shard-flashback only (half a page, no full anatomy): the sleepover, the needle, the oath, one friend having to sit down. She doesn't explain the rules to the reader yet — we understand she *has* to go before we understand why. She changes out of pyjamas into "competent" clothes, writes a note propped on the microwave (Mum, nights, care home — established in one line), leaves via the extension roof. Ends on the patio, heart hammering, absurdly proud, already composing how she'll tell this story someday. **Ch. 2 — 00:41.** Doris the bicycle, liberated from the shed; brakes advisory. Night town as gauntlet: security lights snapping on one by one like judgement; a fox stand-off that Nell loses. No friendship status-report — instead the wound in an iPhone: parked behind the leisure centre, she scrolls the dead group chat back to March, finds her own last message to Bex ("you about this weekend?"), reads at 14:52, never followed up, and counts how many messages since are hers alone. She realises she's obeying a rule drafted by eleven-year-olds and keeps pedalling. Ends as she turns into Bex's road and sees, at 1am, the front door standing open. **Ch. 3 — 01:17.** The longest-feeling, tensest chapter. Bin bags on the drive; the row still ringing off the walls inside; Bex on the kerb with a tea-towel around her hand. Nell's joke lands wrong and dies — Bex's first words are "go home, you mug," meaning *don't look at me*, meaning everything else. The tea-towel comes off: the sentence after it is six words long. Triage via Nell's casualty-documentary habit. Bex *refuses* the hospital — questions, records, her mum being phoned — and Nell bargains: just to the car park, just to look at it. Bex stands up. That's the yes. Ends with the two of them and one bike at the end of the drive. **Ch. 4 — 01:50.** Gurdeep's garage: plasters, Lucozade, the last two sausage rolls; he does not blink, and gives her cheese-and-onion when she asked for salt-and-vinegar, and this is somehow the kindest thing all night. Then the walk: Doris wheeled between them, Bex's good hand on the saddle, an argument about who steers, the town utterly empty except a taxi and a fox (the same fox; Nell's sure of it). Bex talks in fragments, without being asked — the eight months, the shame, Craig. One quoted line, flat: *"He said Dad was right to leave."* Nell breaks the pact's only rule and asks a question. Bex answers. Ends at the sliding doors of A&E, neither of them moving for a second, then moving. **Ch. 5 — 02:30.** Minor injuries, major drama. Waiting-room census: a man with a fork-related incident he's exhaustedly refusing to explain; a ceiling TV selling jewellery; a vending machine that eats £1.20 with the serenity of a religion. Priya arrives like weather. Daisy arrives with party rings and goes very quiet and sits down slowly when she sees the hand. The reunion is awkward first — a wrong hug, "you look well" (a lie) — and the old rhythm only kicks in over the stitches: seven of them, a tired and unspectacular nurse who has seen four of these tonight, a plaster, a leaflet. The four of them in plastic chairs, taking the mick, catching each other not doing it too hard. No miracle. Ends with Bex, in the middle of everyone's noise, laughing once, by accident. **Ch. 6 — 05:00.** Dawn walk home wheeling Doris; bin lorry; town looking scrubbed and simple, like it's apologising. Detour to Daisy's old garden and the spinney: the fort is half-demolished behind a new-build fence, and they stand in the drizzle looking at it like people at a graveside, until Daisy says something accidentally perfect and awful and they laugh so hard it hurts. The re-oath they'd half-planned doesn't happen — there's nothing to swear it on, and they're sixteen, and Pritt Stick would be insane. Instead, later, on Nell's bed at 4-something-PM of the same day: Priya renames the group chat and posts the amended terms as a joke — *come anyway, questions allowed* — and nobody replies "lol," which is how they know. Also here, plainly, once: Nell admits the March thing to herself. Ends on Bex typing, stopping, typing: "thanks for coming. mug." Something unsaid, said. **Ch. 7 — Four days later.** Terse, clipped, the shortest-feeling chapter. Consequences, boring and slightly unfair: Dad's grounding (delivered with one confusing flicker of pride), Mum finding the note at 7am, Doris confiscated then quietly returned. The kitchen-table meeting — Nell's mum, Priya's dad, Bex's gran up from Skegness, who says two devastating sentences about Craig and takes Bex home with her. Counselling: a list, weeks long; the gran doesn't fuss about it, which tells Nell she's done this before, for someone. Then the wobble: two days of Bex-silence, and Nell choosing — hating it — not to crowd. On the third day a message arrives: "u up?" at 11pm. She was. Ends with the fact that Bex nearly didn't send the emoji that night, because she'd assumed Nell would think it was a joke. Nell's wrong first guess, handed back to her. **Ch. 8 — Six weeks later.** 🧇🧇🧇 — but first, the unglamorous coda: the group chat running on memes and bus times; Daisy's panto (Nell attends, twice, out of love); Bex's stitches out, one bad week in the middle of the six, her laugh returning in instalments she doesn't notice anyone counting; Nell's paramedic work experience, which is mostly lifting people and being kind, and nothing like the war film. Bex's mum: one plain sentence, unresolved, left unresolved. Then, just after midnight on a school night with a mock exam at nine: the text. Priya. Three waffles. Nell lies there, furious, already reaching for her jeans, grumbling the terms out loud to an empty room like a woman much older than sixteen, and goes — because those were the terms.

# Nell (narrator) **Background.** Nell Shaw, sixteen, Year 11 at the comp. Lives with both parents in a house that functions but is always tired: Mum works nights at a care home (which is why Doris, Mum's ancient bicycle, has hung unridden in the shed for three years), Dad does early shifts and falls asleep during films at 8:40pm. Nell has been Bex's best friend since Reception — they were the original two, the pact's inner circle, before Priya and Daisy were co-opted at juniors. The wound in her ambition: her grandad had a stroke on Boxing Day when she was twelve, and the paramedics were the only calm people in the room. She has been chasing that specific feeling — being useful in the worst moment — ever since. She watches *24 Hours in A&E* the way other girls watch romance: attentively, repeatedly, with opinions. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** Dry, swotty, organised to the point of pathology. Carries a first-aid kit in her school bag the size of a submarine — eyewash, burn gel, two triangular bandages, for a girl who has never used a plaster on anyone but herself. Names inanimate objects (Doris was her christening, age nine). Counts in fours when panicked — a breaststroke rhythm she's never examined. Keeps a mental ledger of slights and pretends she doesn't: she can tell you exactly who didn't reply to which message and when, a talent she treats as a character flaw she's chosen not to correct. Walks fast, on the outsides of her feet; her shoe heels wear at an angle the shoe shop man has commented on. Cannot read an analogue clock quickly under pressure, a fact she'd deny. **Flaws.** Brave in emergencies, avoidant in maintenance: she will cycle three miles at midnight but could not, in April, send a second *"you okay?"* after Bex left her on read. Pride dressed as busyness. Jokes at exactly the wrong moment — the kerb, Chapter 3 — and then has to sit in the silence her joke made. Half-aware that she may prefer being *needed* to being loved, and would rather not finish that thought. **Physicality.** Middling height, practical self-cut bob (fringe slightly longer on the left), school blazer sleeves short since a Year 9 growth spurt her parents optimistically called temporary. Eyebrows do live commentary. Carries her bag like it's an expedition. Changes into "competent clothes" for the rescue: walking boots, cagoule, head-torch — dressed for the Somme, going to a semi in Marsh Lane. **Motives & relationships (from inside her).** To be useful; to matter when it counts; to find out if the pact was real or just something children say to each other. She'd tell you she's going because those were the terms. The truer answer — that she went because she stopped trying once and it's been eating her since March — doesn't surface until Chapter 6, and she'd resist it even then. To Bex: the lost other half, whose blanking at the bus stop she replayed for a fortnight and then filed under *people change*. To Priya: mutual appreciation society of the quick-witted, though Nell is the straight man and knows it. To Daisy: fond, faintly exasperated, protective. To her parents: loved, seen, slightly misunderstood (they think the paramedic thing is a phase; it is the opposite of a phase). **Voice samples.** - *(Internal, war-film mode.)* "Behind enemy lines. Or, as the residents of Fern Close insist on calling it, the cul-de-sac." - *(Internal, ledger mode.)* "In April I did not send a second text. I keep this fact in the same drawer as the time I told a supply teacher my name was Constantine, which is to say: I know where it is." - *(Internal, dead patch — the tea-towel comes off.)* "The towel was stuck. She pulled it. Underneath, the hand. It needed stitches. It needed them an hour ago." # Bex **Background.** Rebecca — Bex, always Bex — sixteen. Only child of Carol and Dave. Until March she was the loudest girl in Year 10: the one who could do eyeliner on a moving bus, argue a teacher down on a technicality, and get the tuck-shop woman to add extras out of pure charm. Then Dad left in the spring for a woman with a Volvo and a job at the garden centre, and the whole school knew within a week because this is a small town, and Bex spent a month watching pity faces assemble in corridors. She blanked Nell at the bus stop in March — pre-emptive, because being abandoned and being pitied in the same term was too much — and let the group chat die with a final "mad one x." By summer, Craig had moved in. The pact was *hers*: her eleventh birthday sleepover, her cousin's bootleg 15-rated slasher, her mum's sewing tin, her liturgy. The girl who wrote the terms is the girl who typed 🩸🩸🩸 four times, deleted it three, and hit send at 00:04 on the fifth attempt. **Personality & idiosyncrasies.** A ringleader turned ghost. Formerly the priestess of the Coven — organiser of rituals, bylaws, secret handshakes; the child who founded a witch coven and gave it a constitution. Still does her eyeliner in one unbroken stroke, no mirror; it's the one front she maintains, and Nell understands by Chapter 3 that the eyeliner is load-bearing. Hates being thanked. Says "to be fair" when she's lying and knows it. Taps things twice without noticing. Has started agreeing with Craig about things she doesn't believe — the house does eat money, her mum does fuss — because agreement keeps the temperature down, and she despises herself for it in a way she can't say out loud. **Flaws.** Pre-emptive cruelty: pushes people away before they can leave, because leaving is the thing she now expects from everyone. Would rather bleed than be pitied. Lies by omission as a lifestyle. Anger arrives before anything else — the first thing she says to her rescuer is an insult, and she means it in at least three directions at once. **Physicality.** Tall — used to take up space, loudest laugh on the corridor — now folded: hood up, sleeves pulled over her hands, chin down, walking fast like she's escaping a crime scene she witnessed rather than lives in. Sits on kerbs with the ease of someone who's done a lot of it recently. Chipped black nail polish she hasn't redone. In Chapters 3–5: one hand wrapped in a tea-towel gone rust-coloured, held against her body like a bird that might fly. **Motives & relationships (from inside her).** Get to Year 11's end without anyone seeing the whole picture; get to college, where nobody knows; keep the eyeliner on. Sending the emoji was the last card she had, played at 00:04 because everyone knows nothing counts after midnight — if it went wrong she could claim it was a wind-up, delete it, die quietly. From her side: she assumed Nell would think it was a joke, because Nell has her life together and Craig says people like that don't come back for people like this. She loves her mum and is so angry at her that the two feelings have fused into something she can't hand to anyone. Her dad texts fortnightly, sometimes with £20 and once with a photo of a gazebo, and she doesn't know which she'd rather stop. The Coven is the one context in which she ever asked for help and wasn't weaker for it — which is exactly why she nearly couldn't. **Voice samples.** - *(First words on the kerb.)* "Go home, you mug. I mean it. Don't — just don't look at me like that." - *(The reported line, flat, on the walk.)* "He said Dad was right to leave. That's all. That's the whole thing. He wasn't even shouting when he said it." - *(Sideways, days later, by text.)* "thanks for coming. mug." - *(To Nell, once, when it's nearly okay.)* "I'm not doing a bit, Nell. I just can't be anyone tonight." # Priya **Background.** Priya Nair, sixteen, the youngest of a big loud household and the only one quiet enough at school to be underestimated for a week. **1.** The text came just after midnight: 🩸🩸🩸 From Bex. I want to be clear about the order of my thoughts, because I've had cause to review them many times since, and I don't come out of it well. The first thought was: someone's started their period at a sleepover. Honest to God, that was it. Three blood drops, middle of the night — some poor cow stranded at Ruby Parton's with a rolled-up sock situation, and Bex, who knew everybody, sending out the general distress call. I was already mentally drafting the reply. *Hold on. I've got supplies. Which house?* Except it wasn't Ruby Parton's number. It was Bex's. The second thought — and this is the one I have to live with — was: *classic Bex.* Because that's what eight months of nothing does to you. Eight months since she blanked me at the bus stop outside Somerfield, looked straight through me like I was weather, and got on the 12A. Eight months of the group chat dying on its feet, and the last message in it being hers, *mad one x*, sent into nothing. You build a version of a person out of that, and my version of Bex was someone who sent three blood drops at midnight the way she'd once claimed a seagull stole her homework: dramatically, and for attention. The third thought was the sleepover. I was eleven. It was Bex's birthday, and her cousin had supplied a film we absolutely weren't allowed to watch, and by the end of it we were sitting in her mum's spare room with a sewing needle and a sense of occasion. I won't pretend I remember every word of what was said. I remember the shape of it. I remember that Bex had written actual terms, on paper, beforehand, like a lunatic, and read them out in a voice she'd borrowed from the film. I remember Priya saying she'd thought this whole thing was going to be about periods, and being told firmly that it was not. I remember Daisy having to sit down before the needle came out, and then again after. I remember that I went second, and it hurt more than anyone had admitted it would, and that I'd have done it again straight away if asked. And I remember the signal. Three drops. It meant: *come now. No questions asked. Blood sisters forever.* We were eleven. It was a game with the lights off, basically. But games have rules and the rules were these, and no one had ever once used the signal in five years, and now, at 00:04, on a Tuesday in November, Bex had. I sat up in bed with my phone glowing on the duvet and did the maths of staying put. The maths were excellent. It was probably nothing. It was *definitely* probably nothing. Period emergency at a sleepover I'd already ruled out. Drama, attention, a wind-up, a pocket-dial of the soul. Eleven-year-olds don't get to requisition sixteen-year-olds. Nobody has honoured a pact since the Mitchell report. I had a mock exam in three weeks and a bag packed for tomorrow and a mother coming off nights at seven. I counted to sixteen, in fours, which is a thing I do and don't examine. Then I got up. I'd love to tell you I got up out of pure loyalty. Some of it was loyalty. Some of it was that I'd spent eight months being the girl who got blanked at the bus stop and then, in April, sent one text — *you about this weekend?* — watched it sit on *read*, and never sent another, because pride is easier to wear than rejection and almost nobody can tell them apart at a distance. If Bex was actually in trouble, then tonight was the bill for April coming due. And some tiny remaining part of it, I admit, was that I've always secretly wanted something to happen to me, and I knew, even then, that this was a disgusting reason to get out of bed, and I got out of bed anyway. The clothes were a genuine problem. You can't answer a distress call in pyjamas with penguins on them; nobody in the history of rescue has been taken seriously in penguins. In the end I went with walking boots, jogging bottoms, my school fleece, and the cagoule, plus the head-torch, which in fairness to me is kept in the shed and not, as has been suggested since, carried on my person. I looked in the wardrobe mirror and saw a girl dressed for the Somme, reporting to a semi in Marsh Lane. The note took two drafts. The first said *gone to help Bex, back soon, don't panic* — all right for Mum, who'd read it at seven with a brew, but it would fall to Dad to see it at half five if he woke, and Dad panics in the mornings the way other people panic at funerals. The second just said *out. safe. phone on. love you, N.* I propped it against the microwave where it couldn't be missed and felt, briefly, like a soldier's widow. The window was the only hard part. Officially my window doesn't open far enough, which is true, for safety, for burglars. But the extension roof underneath it is a shallow slope of mossy felt, and if you go out feet first, flat on your front, trusting the felt, you can shuffle down to the gutter, hang, and drop into the flowerbed that Mum has been threatening to replant since 2019. I'd done it twice before. Both times at fourteen, for reasons I won't go into, and both times it had gone perfectly, discounting the drainage issue the second time. Tonight my hands were shaking, which I noticed from a strange distance, the way you notice it's started raining. The felt was wet. The gutter held. The flowerbed took me with its usual soft *whump*, and I stood up in the dark at 00:19 in my own back garden, heart going like the bins have come, one boot print in the bed, phone in my pocket, alive and out. And I'll be honest about this too, because it was the last fully stupid thing I did before any of it became real. Standing there on the patio, in the drizzle, in the Somme outfit, I caught myself already telling the story. To Priya, someday. *So I got this text at midnight—* I'd got no further than that, had already cast myself as the calm one, the one who came, when I didn't yet know what I was coming *to*, and that's the bit that frightens me looking back. You can get all the way out of the window on the strength of how it's going to sound later. Then I fetched Doris, and stopped performing, and went.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished opening chapter that demonstrates genuine literary craft. Let me work through its qualities systematically. **Voice and Character** The narrator's voice is the chapter's greatest achievement. Nell's dry, self-aware confessionalism is established immediately and maintained with impressive consistency. The line "pride is easier to wear than rejection and almost nobody can tell them apart at a distance" is genuinely good — it earns its insight rather than announcing it. The self-deprecating honesty about her motivations ("some tiny remaining part of it, I admit, was that I've always secretly wanted something to happen to me") is exactly the kind of uncomfortable truth that distinguishes literary YA from its lesser cousins. The character is fully consistent with the profile: the ledger-keeping, the war-film self-narration, the counting in fours, the competent-clothes instinct. **Structure and Pacing** The chapter follows its plan faithfully. The three-thought sequence (period emergency → classic Bex drama → the sleepover) is well-executed and does exactly what the plan intended: we understand she has to go before we understand why. The flashback to the sleepover is appropriately brief — a "shard," as planned — and efficiently establishes the pact's emotional weight without over-explaining. The note-writing scene is a small gem of characterisation (Dad panics in the mornings the way other people panic at funerals). **Prose Quality** The prose is largely excellent. Metaphors land consistently: "pocket-dial of the soul" is inventive and funny; "pride is easier to wear than rejection" is clean and true; "heart going like the bins have come" is perfectly British and specific. The Somme joke is deployed twice without becoming tiresome. The final paragraph — catching herself already composing the story before she knows what she's going to — is the chapter's emotional peak and it earns it. **Weaknesses** The chapter is almost entirely interior monologue, which is appropriate for an opening but means there's no dialogue to assess. The plan called for Nell to be "absurdly proud" on the patio, which is delivered, but the self-awareness about the storytelling instinct is perhaps slightly over-explained — the reader gets it before the final sentence lands. "Heart going like the bins have come" is excellent but "the way you notice it's started raining" (for the shaking hands) is slightly less precise. The Mitchell report reference is a bit opaque — it's a nice joke but may not land for all readers, and it's the one moment where the Britishness feels slightly performed rather than inhabited. **Tonal Balance** The darkly comic register is well-calibrated. The comedy never undercuts the genuine stakes; the ache underneath is present throughout. The chapter avoids the trap of being too clever — the wit serves the character rather than the author's desire to impress. **Faithfulness to Plan** The chapter hits every planned beat: the three-thought sequence, the shard-flashback, the competent clothes, the note, the extension roof, the patio moment of self-awareness, ending on fetching Doris. The plan's instruction that "we understand she has to go before we understand why" is executed well. **Minor Quibbles** "Nobody has honoured a pact since the Mitchell report" — the Mitchell report is a real thing (the 2012 report on child abuse in Rochdale) and using it as a throwaway joke about pacts is slightly jarring, possibly unintentionally. This may be a different Mitchell report the author intends, but it's unclear. The drainage issue reference is funny but slightly rushed. Overall this is a high-quality opening chapter that demonstrates genuine command of voice, structure, and tonal balance. It's not quite a masterpiece — the interiority is occasionally over-explained, and there are one or two moments where the cleverness slightly outpaces the naturalness — but it's well above average literary YA. **2.** The shed was locked, which was a formality, because the shed has been locked since 2016 and the key has hung on the same nail since 2016, two feet from the lock, because we are not a family that burglars would find challenging. Doris is my mum's bike. Mum bought her second-hand when I was in Year 4, rode her to the care home for maybe four months, then went on nights and never touched her again, and now Doris hangs on the shed wall like a museum exhibit: *bicycle of the late 2010s, note the basket.* Getting her down in the dark without waking the street was a two-person job executed by one person, and there was a moment — Doris airborne, me folded under her, a rake beginning its slow slide — when I genuinely considered just lying there until morning and letting whoever found me explain it. The tyres held air in the technical sense. The front brake did nothing at all and the back brake made a sound like a kestrel, and I want it on record that I considered this fine. In casualty documentaries there's always a moment where someone says, *the bike just went from under her,* and the camera pans to a folded bicycle, and everyone at home thinks: that will be the bike's fault. It is never entirely the bike's fault. The bike has been in a shed for three years. Nobody asks the bike. I did the back lane first, standing on the pedals, because the lane has no houses and therefore no lights, and no lights means no witnesses. There's a specific feeling you get cycling through your own town at half midnight, which is that you've died and it's carrying on without you. Everything's where you left it — the postbox, the chippy, the phone box that's now a defibrillator — but running on some economy setting, streetlights doing the minimum. The only moving thing was a taxi on the ring road, and I recognised it, actually. Mr Nair. Priya's dad. I had a mad urge to wave, and then a much saner one to be a stranger. Then came the gauntlet: Harrow Crescent, which is a cul-de-sac of new houses, all of them rigged with security lights set, apparently, to *moth*. You can't cycle Harrow Crescent quietly. You take one house and the light comes on like judgement — that flat white stare — and then the next one triggers, and the next, so that you ride the whole street at the centre of a slow wave of exposure, a girl on a squealing bike lit up in instalments, absolutely guilty of nothing, feeling guilty of everything. Number 14 has two lights and a camera. I did the rest of the Crescent freewheeling, knees out, like something from a hostage video. The fox was at the bottom, by the garages. I need you to understand that this fox and I have history. It's been through our bins since forever, and it sits on the wall by the cut-through like it pays rent, and every time it sees me it gives me this look — not scared, not interested. Assessed. Tonight it was sitting in the middle of the road, in the exact middle, and it watched me come and did not move, and I braked — kestrel noise — and we had a stand-off, me and this fox, at one in the morning, and I want to tell you I won. What actually happened is I went round it. On the pavement. Slowly, with eye contact, the way you'd pass a bouncer. It turned its head to keep me in view the whole way past, and when I looked back from the corner it was still looking, and I would file that under *things I'll be embarrassed about at dawn* if I filed things, which I don't, apparently, because they all resurface anyway. I stopped behind the leisure centre. Officially, this was a routing decision — the cut through to Marsh Lane is quicker — but really I'd realised something and needed to not be pedalling for it. The text was from Bex. Bex. And since March I had spoken to Bex exactly once, which was the bus stop, and she looked through me, and since then — this is the bit I needed to sit still for — since then I hadn't once opened our old chat. Not once. I'd gone into it the way you don't go into a room after something's happened in it. I sat on the wall under the leisure centre's one sad light and I opened it. It's all still there, isn't it. That's the thing nobody warns you about. Two years of it, scrolling down through the ages: voice notes from when we were fourteen, forty-second shrieking about *some boy or other*; a photo of Daisy asleep at a sleepover with her thumb in her mouth, captioned *the queen rests*; the summer of the pedalos. Whole civilisations down there. And then March, and the archaeology changes. The messages go grey at the edges, the way grass does where nobody walks. Mine was there. *you about this weekend?* Tuesday, 14 March, 2:52pm. Read at 14:52 — she read it in ten seconds, she was holding her phone, she must have stood somewhere reading it — and then nothing, from her, ever. And then the bit I sat on the wall for. After that, every message in the chat was mine. I counted them. I didn't mean to count them, the way you don't mean to check the time when you're waiting, and then you've done it, and now you know. Seven. Seven messages over eight months — a meme in April, a *happy birthday* in June that I made myself keep short and casual, *saw this and thought of you* in front of a sheep in September. Little brass plaques, put up in an empty building, by me, alone. Seven's not nothing, I told myself. Seven is me trying. Seven spread over eight months is one message every five weeks, said the other half of me, the half that keeps the ledger. That's not trying. That's *noticing*. Trying is the second text, the *are you okay*, the walk to Marsh Lane in daylight — all the things available to a person with legs in a town this size, for eight months, while she told the Somme story to nobody. So that was the arithmetic I did on the wall, at 00:52, in the drizzle, on my mum's resurrection of a bike, on the way to honour a treaty drafted by children. Because that's what I was doing — that had started to sink in, pedals or no pedals. Eleven-year-olds had drawn up terms, and eleven-year-olds don't know about reading at 14:52, or Craigs, or any of it, they just know *come now, no questions*, and every adult part of me knew the pact was a game, and here I was anyway, cycling, like the game had turned out to be the only law on the books. I got back on Doris. Marsh Lane has a bend at the bottom and then you can see the whole street, bollard to cul-de-sac, and I want you to picture it as I saw it: nothing moving, every window dark or doing that blue nightshift flicker, one cat, bins out early. And Bex's front door, wide open, at one in the morning.

Judge Response:
[Analysis] Chapter 2 is a remarkably accomplished piece of YA fiction that demonstrates genuine craft across nearly every dimension. Let me work through its qualities and weaknesses systematically. VOICE AND CHARACTER: The first-person voice is exceptionally well-realized. Nell's dry, self-aware narration ("I want it on record that I considered this fine") is consistent throughout and never tips into self-parody. The parenthetical asides feel earned rather than performative — the shed key hanging two feet from the lock is a perfect, specific detail that tells us about the family without announcing it. The ledger-keeping personality trait is beautifully dramatized in the phone-chat scene: "I didn't mean to count them, the way you don't mean to check the time when you're waiting, and then you've done it, and now you know. Seven." This is exactly the kind of interiority the character profile calls for, and it lands without being labored. The fox stand-off is a genuine comic set-piece that also does character work — Nell's admission that she went around it, on the pavement, slowly, "the way you'd pass a bouncer," is funny and self-deprecating in exactly the right register. The follow-up ("I would file that under things I'll be embarrassed about at dawn if I filed things, which I don't, apparently, because they all resurface anyway") is a small masterpiece of voice — it's funny, it's true to the character, and it quietly foreshadows the ledger scene that follows. EMOTIONAL ENGAGEMENT: The chapter's emotional core — the phone chat archaeology — is handled with real restraint and precision. That "she must have stood somewhere reading it" is the kind of imaginative leap that actually lands, because it's grounded in the specific and the human. The self-indictment that follows ("Seven spread over eight months is one message every five weeks... That's not trying. That's noticing") is genuinely moving without being sentimental.
