**3.** I dropped Doris on the pavement on purpose, quietly, like the bike might set something off. The house did the talking first. You could hear it from the gate, that ringing you get after loud — the way a room holds an argument even when the argument's over. A television somewhere inside was on and being ignored. Bin bags stood on the drive in a line, four of them, and one had tipped and bled contents into the gutter: egg box, a mirror, clothes on hangers, still on their hangers. There's a thing your brain does with a sight like that, which is refuse to arrange it into what it means. And on the kerb, sitting with her knees up, hood forward so far I could mostly just see the hood, was Bex. Her right hand was wrapped in a tea-towel. Kilt-patterned. The kind every kitchen in this country has folded in a drawer, and I remember thinking, absurdly, *Bex's mum has that same tea-towel*, and then remembering whose house I was standing outside. She'd heard the bike. She didn't look up. I did the thing I do. I said, "Special delivery," because the silence was enormous and my mouth wanted to be helpful, the way it always wants to be helpful, and I'd like to formally apologise to it here, because the joke came out of me sounding exactly like a joke, cheerful, bright, insanely wrong, and it dropped dead on the pavement between us, and Bex flinched, actually flinched, like I'd shone a light on her. "Go home, you mug." Voice wrecked. She still didn't look up. "I mean it. Just — don't. Don't look at me like that." "I'm not looking at you like anything." "You are. You've got your *rescue* face on." And here's where I could have said something true. Something about the pact, or April, or the fact that I'd cycled through a fox's sovereign territory to get here. What I actually said was "You texted me," which came out like an accusation, because apparently even my soul has a filing system and *why did you text me, you ignored me for eight months, you don't get to* was sitting nearer the front than anything useful. Bex laughed. One syllable, no humour in it, the driest sound I've ever heard come out of someone I used to know. "Five times," she said, to the road. "Typed it five times." "Typed what?" "You know what." Her chin came up an inch, and under the hood I could see the eyeliner, and I want to explain about the eyeliner. Perfect wing, corner to corner, both sides, unbroken. Nobody does their eyeliner at midnight in the middle of a family detonation unless the eyeliner is load-bearing. It was the only bit of her still running at full strength, and I made a decision right then, silently, that we would not be commenting on the eyeliner, the hood, the time, the door, or any of it, because I understood that I was watching someone hold a shape together with their face. "What happened to your hand?" I said instead. "Nothing." "Bex." "It's fine. It's *nothing*, it looks worse than—" She stopped. The door of the house made a sound, some internal door, someone moving around inside, and her whole body did a thing I've only ever seen birds do. She stood up. Fast, away from the house, closer to me, hood still down over her face, and said, "Can we not be here? Can we just — not be *here*." "Yeah," I said. "Yes. Course. Down the road, there's a bench by the—" "Just move." We moved. I wheeled Doris between us like a shield with a basket, and neither of us said anything until the second lamppost, and then she stopped, and held the hand out. "Look, then. Since you've come all this way on your *mum's* bike." The tea-towel was stuck. That's the detail. It had dried on, along the line of the cut, and she pulled it, and made no sound at all about it, which was somehow worse than any sound. Underneath, the hand. It needed stitches. It needed them an hour ago. It wasn't a film. There wasn't a lot of blood by then, that's not why my chest went strange — it was the *shape*, the length of it across the heel of her palm, held shut by her own other hand, and the way she kept it facing herself, tilted away from me, an angle you'd only use if you'd been looking at it privately for hours, deciding. "Door," she said, before I could. "I hit a door." "Doors don't—" "The little glass panel. At the top. I was— it doesn't matter what I was." Then, flatly, in the voice people use for reading out a train time: "I don't even remember deciding to hit it. I just heard it go." I did what I've watched a hundred paramedics do on television at my nana's on a Sunday, which is: be calm, ask boring questions. Which hand do you write with. Can you bend the fingers — she could, all of them, and something in me sat down with relief. How long ago. An hour, maybe. Any dizziness. No. Any of it still in there, any glass — I didn't know, I wasn't going to know, that was a hospital question, everything important was turning out to be a hospital question. "So that's that, then," I said. "Minor injuries. It's open till — it's open. We cycle, I walk it up the hills, you sit on the—" "No." "Bex." "No *hospital*. They ask what happened, and it goes on a form, and they phone your mum to come and get you, and she's *busy*, she's— " The hood turned towards the house, back down the street, out of sight. "It's my hand, Nell. I'll keep it clean. People keep things clean." "People get infections." "People get *phoned*." I stood there. And I'd like to tell you that I said something wise, or laid down the law, or was in any way the girl from the story I'd been writing in my head since the patio. What I actually did was bargain, because it was the only currency she'd accept. "We walk to the car park," I said. "That's all. The car park by the Northgate entrance. We sit on the wall, we look at the doors, and if you still want to go home, we go home. Nobody has to go in. We just — go and look at it." "You're such a—" "Say yes, Bex." She looked at the hand. Then at me, properly, the first time all the way through the whole thing: eyeliner, wrecked, sixteen, furious, her whole face asking if I was going to be one more person who left the room. She didn't say yes. She picked up her half of the bike.

**4.** Garages at night are run by men who have seen everything, and the one on Northgate is run by the king of them. Gurdeep. I've bought emergency crisps off him at every hour God sends and never once seen him surprised, and I was counting on that now, because we were a sight: two girls at 1:50am, one bleeding through a fresh tea-towel, one in full Somme dress, wheeling a bike with a basket between them. I made Bex wait outside. She didn't argue, which told me more about how much the walk had cost than anything she'd said. Inside, the shop did its fluorescent hum. Gurdeep looked up from his phone, looked at me, looked through the window at Bex and the bike, and looked back at me. Nothing. Not a flicker. A man could walk in on fire and Gurdeep would ask if he was paying card. "Plasters," I said. "The big ones. And, um. Bandage-y things?" "First aid's on the right of the magazines," he said. "You want the big box, not the travel one. Travel one's for show." Lucozade, because I've watched enough casualty programmes to know about Lucozade. Sausage rolls — there were two left in the hot cabinet, lying there like the last survivors of something — so both of those. And salt-and-vinegar, because Bex is a salt-and-vinegar person, it's one of the founding facts of her. He gave me cheese-and-onion. I didn't notice till we were outside. When I did, I opened my mouth to go back in, and then didn't, because Bex had opened the cheese-and-onion and started eating, methodically, staring at the middle distance, and I've thought about it since and decided Gurdeep did it on purpose. He'd seen everything, and he'd clocked her hand, and there's a kind of man who can't say *look after yourselves* so he mis-shelves the crisps instead. It remains the kindest thing anyone did all night that didn't require a licence. The walk was three miles. Doris went between us, Bex's good hand on the saddle, and this raised a question that occupied us for most of Northgate. "I should steer it," I said. "I know the bike." "You're walking it like it's a wheelbarrow. I'll steer, you push." "You've got a hole in your hand." "Not on that side, have I." It's the stupidest argument I've ever had and I would not trade a second of it. Because here's what it was, underneath: it was two girls who haven't spoken in eight months, negotiating a physical arrangement — *her* hand on *my* mum's saddle, our paces syncing up, the bike wanting to wobble between us like a shopping trolley — and every inch of the negotiation was a message, and we both knew it, and neither of us said so. She steered. I pushed. By the pelican crossing we'd stopped being careful about it. The town was empty in a way day never permits. One taxi passed us on the ring road — Mr Nair again, I'm almost sure, second pass of the night, though this time I didn't get the urge to wave. And at the bottom of Baker Street, sitting on the wall outside the butchers like it owned the wall, the fox. Same fox. I know it was the same fox; I'd know that face in a parade. It watched us the whole length of the street, and Bex, who hadn't laughed at anything in a year, exhaled through her nose at it, almost a laugh, and said, "What's *his* problem," and I said, "We've met," and she looked at me sideways — *you've met a fox* — and the old rhythm came back for four whole seconds before she remembered to put it away. Then, somewhere past the church, without being asked, she started talking. Not in order. That's how I'd describe it. In paragraphs that didn't connect, like she was emptying pockets. The house had been going since spring. Dad leaving hadn't been an ending, it had been a starting pistol — everything that was wrong got to be *his* fault, and her mum liked that, needed it, and then Craig moved in by summer, right into the gap, and Craig had opinions. About the house eating money. About her mum fussing. About the telly being on all hours. And you keep the temperature down, that's the whole job, you just keep agreeing, and then one day you hear yourself agreeing that your dad — She stopped there. Checked her pocket for a lighter she didn't have. "That's the bit," she said, flat. Flat like a train time. "He said Dad was right to leave. That's all. That's the whole thing. He wasn't even shouting when he said it. It was just — a thing he thought everyone knew." And the panel went, and her hand went through, and everything after that had been kitchen roll and websites about glass and sitting on the kerb deciding. Here is where I broke the only rule. Five years, one rule, *no questions asked*, written in Bex's eleven-year-old handwriting on paper her mum still has in a drawer somewhere. I broke it on Baker Street at two in the morning. "Why not Priya?" I said. "Or Daisy. Why me?" Because it had been sitting in me since the kerb. Because Priya is easier to talk to and Daisy is kinder, and everyone knows this, it's practically their job titles. Bex was quiet long enough that I started composing the apology. Then she said, "Priya'd have told her mum. Daisy's mum works at the hospital." Which were sensible answers, tactical answers, and I'd have accepted them, except she went on pushing the bike for a few steps and then said, to the road, "And you wouldn't think it was a joke." "What?" "The signal. I nearly didn't send it, because I thought — " a breath, steadying, done in one — "I thought you'd think I was being a drama queen. I did it in the end because it was after midnight and nothing counts after midnight. If you'd laughed, I'd have said it got sent by accident." "I wouldn't've laughed." "You laughed at the fox." "That's — the fox is *funny*, Bex, that's different—" It was the hospital. That's the last thing. The building came up on us out of the dark, lit the way hospitals are at night, like an ocean liner that's run aground and decided to stay. And the sliding doors at the Northgate entrance, glowing, humming, opening for a man with his arm in a sling who didn't look at us either. We stopped at the edge of the car park. Neither of us moved. Bex looked at the doors, and at the hand, and held the towel a bit tighter, and I understood that we were at the exact edge of the thing she'd agreed to — *just to the car park, just to look at it* — and everything after this was going to be questions, and forms, and a phone call, and there was no version of me that could push her another inch. Then she moved.

**5.** Minor injuries at half two in the morning has its own ecosystem. There was a man of about fifty with a tea-towel on his hand — *not* kilt-patterned, I checked — who had told the receptionist one word, *fork*, and was now refusing, with the calm of a man beyond embarrassment, to elaborate. There was a television bolted to the ceiling selling jewellery to nobody, a presenter describing a bracelet with a sincerity that belonged in a better-paid job. And there was a vending machine by the water cooler which I will come back to, because it had a religion. I sat Bex two seats away from fork man and went to the desk, and while the receptionist typed — name, date of birth, *and what's happened tonight, love* — I did the thing I'd decided on over the road. I opened the group chat. The dead one. The one where my last seven messages were brass plaques in an empty building. And into it, at 02:31, I sent 🩸🩸🩸 It felt insane. It felt like setting off a flare over a field where everyone's moved away. Priya's reply came in eleven seconds: *WHO IS BLEEDING.* Then: *don't answer. omw.* Then, a minute later, from her dad's taxi, apparently already at the Baker Street lights: *collecting daisy. she doesn't know she's coming yet.* Doris went on the racks outside, locked with the lock that lives in her own basket, which felt like the bike doing its own homework. Bex got called through at five to three. That's when they asked the question she'd been dreading, the one the whole car park bargain had been about — parent or guardian to contact — and Bex stood very still at the little desk and then said, "My gran," and reeled off a Skegness number she clearly knew by heart, the way you know things you've had to use before. The receptionist rang it. Gran answered on the second ring at three in the morning, which I've thought about a lot since — you don't answer that fast unless you sit up. Bex didn't get the phone. She got to stand there while the receptionist said "she's fine, we're just stitching a hand, she's with friends," and whatever Gran said back made Bex's face do something complicated, and then it was done, and nobody had phoned Marsh Lane, and Bex sat down in the cubicle looking like she'd been let off a cliff. I went in with her. Through the curtain I could hear Priya arrive like weather. The nurse was called Annabel and she was magnificent in the way of people on their ninth hour. She unwrapped the hand, looked at it under the good light, and said, "Right then." That was the whole assessment. "How did this happen?" "I hit a door." "Glass panel?" "Yeah." "It's the third one tonight." She said it the way you'd say *rain's coming* — no suspicion, no interest, just the weather. "It's always the little panel. People think it'll take the force. Nothing takes the force." Then she looked at Bex, properly, once, and asked, quietly, sideways, "Nobody did this to you?" — and Bex said no, and it was the truth, and Annabel nodded and got the needle, and that was that. Seven stitches. She talked Bex through each one in the same tone she'd have used for a bus timetable. A dressing. A leaflet about keeping it dry, which she described as "optimistic." Through the curtain, Daisy had arrived. I heard the whole thing. "You look well," Daisy said to Bex, before anything else, before *hello* even, and there was a silence the length of a held breath, because it was a lie, and everyone could hear it lying, and Daisy could hear it too, the second too late. "She's fought a door, Daisy," Priya said. "Nobody looks well." "I just meant—" "I know what you meant. Sit down. Give me a party ring." They came through the curtain while Annabel was taping the dressing — Priya, and Daisy in pyjamas under her mum's parka, holding the packet of party rings she'd grabbed from her own cupboard because Daisy cannot process an emergency without provisions. Daisy saw the hand and went very quiet and sat down slowly on the cubicle stool, like slow sitting was a form of respect. Priya hugged me instead of Bex, hard, sideways, a hug that had originally been aimed at Bex and diverted at the last second like traffic. And then we were four, in plastic chairs, at ten past three, and it was awkward for about ninety seconds — long enough for one wrong hug, one lie about looking well, and a silence in which all of us could hear the year we hadn't spoken — and then the old rhythm came back, the way speech comes back after a coughing fit. Not all at once. Carefully. We took the mick, and I could hear us all taking the mick *carefully*, each joke set down like a glass on a wobbly table. "You cycled here," Priya said to me. "On *Doris*. In that coat." "There's nothing wrong with the coat." "There's nothing wrong with the coat the way there's nothing wrong with the Titanic, it was fine until—" "Your dad drove past me twice." "He's circling. He's on nights anyway, he said, and I quote, *may as well be nosy on the clock*." And it built, gradually, and by half three the cubicle curtain was no defence against it. Which brings me to the vending machine. I went out for a coffee and it ate my £1.20 — took it, considered it, offered nothing, lights steady, the serenity of a religion. And I don't know what it was exactly — the hour, the stitches, the party rings, the sheer injustice — but the campaign against that machine became the funniest thing that has ever happened. Priya addressed it formally, as *the defendant*, and outlined her case. Daisy suggested turning it off and on again, and then knelt in her mum's parka and found the plug, and the machine rebooted, thought about its life, and dispensed two coffees, which is theft in reverse. Bex laughed. Once, by accident, in the middle of it — a real one, the old one, gone as soon as it came, and her hand came up to her mouth like she could catch it. Nobody said anything. Everybody heard.

I put the phone face-down on the desk and did a Biology past paper, badly, and hated every minute of the waiting, and would like the record to show I sat still. **8.** Six weeks on, here's the state of things, honestly, because I've promised accuracy and accuracy is mostly admin. COVEN 2.0 runs on bus times. That's what it is now — a weather service with jokes in it. Daisy's panto was *Aladdin*, at the arts centre, and I went twice, which is once more than strictly required by love, and I'd go again. Daisy played a lemon tree in the background of a market scene — a non-speaking lemon tree, her idea, she fought the director for the role — and on the second night she did a small wave in the middle of someone else's big solo, and Priya laughed so loudly that a man three rows down turned around, and we let him. Bex gets the 09:14 in on Fridays. The stitches are out; the scar is a line across the heel of her hand that she claims is "barely a legal scar." The counselling list has moved from "the spring" to "late March," which is technically spring and doesn't feel like it. She had one bad week in the middle of the six — I'm putting it in, because we agreed not to do the other thing — a week where the chat went flat and she didn't come on the Friday. Nobody cured it. Priya sent her the fox. I sent her a past paper. She came the following Friday and said nothing about it, and we said nothing about it, and that's the whole story of that week. Her mum is still at Marsh Lane. That's the sentence. There are visits being discussed, and a phone call every Sunday that Bex does in the hall with the door shut, and I don't know what's in them and haven't asked, because questions are allowed now but so is waiting. Some things, it turns out, you just stand next to. Her laugh's come back in instalments. She doesn't know anyone's counting. I'm counting. And me — I did the work experience. Two weeks riding with a paramedic crew, which I'd wanted since Boxing Day three years ago, since the only calm people in my nana's front room, and I want to report the following from the far side of it. Nobody said *special delivery*. There was no music. It was mostly lifting — a lot of lifting, there is so much lifting in that job, nobody puts that in the adverts — and being kind to confused people at 4am, and forms, and a man called Kelvin who'd rather talk about fishing than his heart, and I sat on the step of the ambulance with an old woman's hand in mine while we waited for her son, and it was nothing like the war film. It was better. It was quieter than the war film and braver than the war film and I want it more than I did before, which I hadn't thought possible. I've started the application. Mum cried. Dad said, "Paramedics can't spell," which in our house is a ribbon and a trophy. So: the Coven, mended, is four girls on a group chat, a lemon tree, a spreadsheet of chip shops, a scar, a list. Nobody's life got rescued. Nothing was solved that the world would notice. I notice. Which brings me to last night. Wednesday. Mock at nine. I'd revised until my eyes fizzed — I now know four things about osmosis and have retained none of them — and I was in bed by eleven, in the penguin pyjamas, an adult, a model citizen, asleep. The text came just after midnight: 🧇🧇🧇 From Priya. I lay there and read it four times. Three waffles. Waffles, which in our house, our street, our four-person nation, have exactly one meaning, ever since Priya's wind-up amendment to the terms got ratified by silence on a Tuesday afternoon in November: *come now. no questions asked.* I want to explain the fury. It was 00:06. I had a mock exam. I had *osmosis*. It was raining — properly raining, sideways, the rain this town does as a specialty — and Priya lives the other side of the ring road, and Doris is technically un-confiscated but has a front brake that kestrels. And on top of all this sensible fury was another layer of fury, which was that I was already, underneath it, doing the maths of the route. Harrow Crescent and its judgement lights. The cut-through. Fox country. Because that's the thing nobody tells you about pacts. You think you're keeping them. You think, *I honour the treaty, the treaty is lucky to have me.* And then it's raining, and it's Wednesday, and a girl you love sends three waffles, and you find out that the treaty keeps *you*. It's load-bearing in both directions. Ask the eyeliner. I got up. Competent clothes. Not the full Somme — there are grades of emergency, I've learned that on the ambulances; this graded a cagoule. The window doesn't open far enough, officially, but the extension roof takes the shuffle and the gutter holds and the flowerbed did its soft *whump*, and I stood up in my own back garden at 00:19, exactly like last time, heart going like the bins, and I didn't compose any story about it, which is how I know I've grown, slightly, in the manner of a scar. I stopped at the shed only to get Doris, and there on the wall, on the flat top of the gate, in the exact middle, sitting in the rain like it paid rent, was the fox. Assessed. It watched me wheel the bike out. I watched it back. Neither of us moved for a moment. I like to think some respect passed between us, veterans both. "Come on then," I said to it, or possibly to the night, possibly to myself. And I cycled out of the garden, into the empty economy-setting town, grumbling, wet, furious, out loud, alone, sixteen — a girl muttering the law of her own nation to nobody, on a school night, towards three waffles and whatever they turned out to be. "Those were the terms."

The prose has the quality of someone who has thought hard about how to be funny without trying to seem like they're trying to be funny, which is the hardest trick. The "dead patches" the plan calls for are present: "Her mum is still at Marsh Lane. That's the sentence." This is exactly right — plain, short, devastating in its restraint. The plan specified one plain sentence about Bex's mum, unresolved, and the chapter delivers it with precision. **Following the Plan** The chapter follows its plan closely. The unglamorous coda is there: bus times, panto, stitches out, counselling list. The work experience section delivers on the plan's note about "mostly lifting people and being kind, and nothing like the war film." The 🧇🧇🧇 arrival, the fury-as-love, the grumbled final line — all present and executed well. The fox callback is a nice structural touch not explicitly in the plan but consistent with its spirit. **What Works Exceptionally Well** "The treaty keeps you. It's load-bearing in both directions. Ask the eyeliner." This is the chapter's best moment — it ties together the eyeliner as load-bearing (established in Bex's profile), the pact's reciprocity, and Nell's growth, in three short sentences. It earns its compression. The work experience passage is genuinely moving without being sentimental. "It was better. It was quieter than the war film and braver than the war film" — this lands because it's specific and because it pays off the war-film motif established throughout. "Her laugh's come back in instalments. She doesn't know anyone's counting. I'm counting." Three sentences, perfect rhythm, genuine ache. This is the kind of plain writing the plan called for at emotional peaks, and it works. **Weaknesses and Criticisms** The fox callback ("veterans both") is slightly too cute. The plan warned against "British-ness as a prop list" and the fox has been used enough that this third appearance risks becoming a quirky affectation rather than a genuine structural echo. "I like to think some respect passed between us, veterans both" is the chapter's most self-consciously whimsical moment and the one that feels most like it's performing rather than being. "Heart going like the bins" is a slightly strained simile — it's trying for the same register as the rest but doesn't quite land with the same precision. The osmosis joke ("I now know four things about osmosis and have retained none of them") is competent but the most predictable joke in the chapter — the kind of thing any YA narrator might say. The phrase "four-person nation" is a bit precious, though it's brief enough not to derail anything. The chapter is perhaps slightly too tidy in its accounting — the list format ("a lemon tree, a spreadsheet of chip shops, a scar, a list") is effective but the chapter does a lot of explicit summarising that occasionally tips toward telling rather than showing. The plan called for the coda to be "unglamorous," and it is, but some of the unglamour is reported rather than rendered. **Dialogue** There's almost no dialogue, which is appropriate for a closing chapter. The one line of reported speech ("Paramedics can't spell") is excellent. The fox exchange ("Come on then") is fine. **Overall** This is a strong closing chapter that executes its plan faithfully, maintains voice consistency, earns its emotional beats, and lands its final line without overselling it. The weaknesses are minor — a slightly strained simile, one too-cute fox moment, some tell-over-show in the summary passages. It's not a masterpiece but it's genuinely accomplished work that knows what it's doing and mostly does it. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is a remarkably accomplished piece of darkly comic British YA fiction. The narrator's voice is the story's greatest achievement: self-aware, funny, precise, and emotionally honest without ever tipping into sentimentality. The opening chapter establishes the voice immediately and sustains it across all eight chapters with impressive consistency. **Strengths:** The voice is genuinely distinctive. Lines like "pride is easier to wear than rejection and almost nobody can tell them apart at a distance" and "seven spread over eight months is one message every five weeks — that's not trying, that's noticing" are earned observations, not decorative flourishes. The narrator's self-examination is rigorous and funny simultaneously, which is the hardest tonal balance to maintain. The comedy is genuinely dark and genuinely comic. The Somme coat, Doris the museum-exhibit bicycle, the kestrel brake, the fox as recurring sovereign presence, Gurdeep's deliberate cheese-and-onion misdirection — these are specific, consistent, and funny without undercutting the emotional weight. The vending machine scene in the hospital is a perfect example of well-earned lightness: it arrives at exactly the right moment and the laughter it produces from Bex is the emotional payoff of the whole hospital sequence. The pacing is controlled. The story knows when to slow down (the wall outside the leisure centre, the archaeology of the chat history) and when to accelerate. Chapter 4's walk to the hospital, with the fox's second appearance and Bex's fragmented confession, is particularly well-handled — the information arrives in the right order, at the right pace. The dialogue is excellent. "You've got your rescue face on" is perfect characterisation in five words. The Daisy "you look well" exchange is painfully accurate. The negotiation over who steers Doris is the story's most quietly brilliant passage — the subtext is entirely clear without being stated. The structural decision to end on a mirror of the opening (three waffles, the same window exit, the same fox, the same "those were the terms") is elegant and earned. The story has genuinely transformed its central premise into something about the nature of commitment and friendship without announcing that it's doing so. **Weaknesses:** Some metaphors are slightly overworked. "Whole civilisations down there" about the chat history is fine but borders on the self-consciously literary. "Like an ocean liner that's run aground and decided to stay" for the hospital is a touch strained. The piece occasionally reaches for a poetic register that slightly exceeds what the narrator's voice would naturally produce — though this is infrequent and rarely badly misjudged. The resolution in chapters 6-8 is somewhat compressed. The summit scene with Gran is handled efficiently but the emotional weight of Bex's home situation — Craig, the mother — is resolved (or rather, deliberately not resolved) in ways that feel slightly rushed compared to the careful attention paid to the friendship dynamics. Gran is a wonderful minor character but her two sentences do a lot of heavy lifting. The "I've been circling for six chapters" moment in Chapter 6 is the one instance where the narrator's self-awareness becomes slightly too meta, too aware of its own structure. It's a small misstep in an otherwise well-controlled narrative. The "Unearned Transformations" question is interesting here: the reconciliation between Nell and Bex is not exactly unearned — the story works hard to justify it — but the speed at which the four-way friendship reconstitutes itself (party rings, the vending machine, the old rhythm) is slightly accelerated. Real estrangements don't dissolve quite this cleanly, even under pressure. The story acknowledges this somewhat ("it was awkward for about ninety seconds") but the acknowledgment is brief. The final chapter's explicit thematic statement ("the treaty keeps you") is the one moment where the story tells us what it's been showing us. It's not badly done, but it's slightly unnecessary given how well the preceding chapters have demonstrated the point. Overall, this is a genuinely impressive piece — confident, funny, emotionally intelligent, and technically accomplished. The voice is the kind that makes you want to read more, and the story earns its ending. # Brainstorming ## What's actually in the crate? 1. **A predator (horror route).** Something that shouldn't have survived the wreck it came from. Crew gets picked off in the dark of their own cargo bay. *Alien* in a Stetson. 2. **A person.** An escaped indentured laborer, a cryo-frozen outlaw with a bounty on his head, or a genetically engineered child — "the Asset" — fleeing a corporate lab. Moral dilemma: turn them in for the fee or burn the ship's future protecting them. 3. **A creature — the last of its kind.** A juvenile "drift-whale" / "void-bison," a species exterminated decades ago because its migration songs fouled the hyperspace lanes the mega-corporation was building. The buffalo slaughter mapped onto space. A collector or lab wants it back. 4. **A swarm / eggs.** Horror-adjacent, ravenous, possibly innocent. Harder to make a character out of. 5. **Subversion: livestock.** A space calf somebody lost. Comic or heartwarming, low stakes. ## Tone directions - **Firefly-esque:** found family, banter, warmth in the black, running from the law. Warm-blooded. - **Deadwood-esque:** grit, moral gray, profanity, the frontier as ugly and beautiful at once. - **Alien-esque:** dread, isolation, the ship as haunted house. - **True Grit / elegiac:** melancholy narration, the frontier already dying, a story about the cost of "civilization." First-person voice with western cadence. - **The Mandalorian-esque:** stoic protectors vs. bounty hunters over a small precious life. ## Crew options (keep to 4–5 for ~8,000 words) - **Captain:** older, war-scarred, on the losing side of an independence war; or — stronger — ex-corporate: she flew escort for the "Clearance Fleets" that culled the whales for the lanes, and has never told her crew. Guilt as engine. - **The vet:** a doctor trained on colony livestock (not people) — practical with big scared animals. Perfect if the cargo is a creature. Possible variant: she's a defected company lab tech who recognizes the asset tag. - **The engineer:** old-timer, superstitious, signs his welds; or dying of vac-lung and needs money. - **The pilot:** laconic war buddy of the captain. *Or* give the pilot the vulnerability — a brother indentured in a company mine — so the antagonist can buy him. - **The greenhorn deckhand:** new hire, POV candidate, the one who delivers the prompt line. Names the creature. - Names on the shelf: Voss, Calder, Reyes, Kade, Okonkwo; ship names: *The Jackalope*, *Dust Devil*, *Long Pull*, *Buckskin*

# Intention **The premise.** The crate holds the last known juvenile of the great drift-herds — the "thunderheads," space-bison whose songs used to roll through the hull like far-off storm — a species exterminated a generation ago when the Meridian Combine carved its hyperspace lanes straight through their calving grounds. The story is a cattle-drive in reverse: a broke crew of salvagers trying to move one small animal across the black to a rumored remnant herd, with the Combine's Asset Recovery man on their tail. **The engine.** Captain Voss's guilt. She flew escort for the Clearance Fleets that did the culling and has never told her crew. The crate forces her to choose, at fifty-something, which side of her own history she dies on. The calf is the plot; Voss is the story. **POV and voice.** Close third on Kit, the greenhorn deckhand — the outsider whose eyes justify the world-building, who delivers the prompt line in Chapter 1, and who names the calf (Biscuit). This keeps Voss mysterious until her confession, when it lands hardest. Prose carries western cadence: laconic dialogue, long elegiac sentences about the black, ship-as-ranch metaphors. The tone is *True Grit* melancholy warmed with *Firefly* found-family — dread where it's earned, but this is not a horror story. **Aiming for:** the buffalo-slaughter allegory worn lightly; a mid-story set piece where the dying calf stabilizes only when the engineer tunes the drive to the old herd frequency (the ship literally learns to sing); a vacuum duel on a derelict's spine as the climax; an ambiguous-but-hopeful release at the end. **Avoiding:** Alien-style body horror; snark-overload banter; POV on Voss (kills the reveal); a crew larger than five; deus ex machina — the Combine must be beaten with leverage and cost, not luck. **Cast.** Captain Ada Voss (ex-Clearance Fleet, guilty, quiet). Doc Reyes (colony livestock vet — better with scared animals than people). Grady (old engineer, superstitious, signs his welds). Kade (pilot; brother Rafe indentured in a Combine mine — the antagonist's leverage). Kit (deckhand, new hire, 19, POV). Mr. Orr (Combine Asset Recovery; polite, patient, worse than a villain — a process). Ship: *The Long Pull*. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — "Salvage Rights."** Kit's POV established on the *Long Pull*, towing a derelict hauler for scrap to cover a debt at Threshold Station. Introduce crew in motion; Grady's superstitions; Voss's economy of words; the hull-deep quiet of the black. They crack the derelict's sealed hold and winch aboard one crate the manifest lists as LIVESTOCK — PROBABLE LOSS. Last beat: Kit alone in the cargo bay hears it. Closes on the prompt line: *"Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up."* **Chapter 2 — "Livestock."** They open it: a starved, foil-tagged juvenile thunderhead, three meters of scarred hide and one wrecked wing. Wonder and danger in equal measure — it nearly kills Grady out of terror before Doc's ranch-hand calm settles it. Voss goes white and leaves the bay; Kade notices, Kit doesn't. Voss quietly orders the tag *not* pried off. End on Kit, feeding it by hand, christening it Biscuit. **Chapter 3 — "The Tag."** The tag is a beacon; Orr's message arrives politely: asset recovery, standard fee, no questions. Research logs in the derelict's slimed data-core reveal the Combine bred the calf from frozen stock — proof-of-concept for restocking the lanes' "biological infrastructure." Doc and Kade corner Voss when the vet recognizes Clearance Fleet protocol in the way Voss handles the animal. First fracture: Voss admits only that she "flew during the Clearance." Crew splits on selling versus running. **Chapter 4 — "Mr. Orr."** Threshold Station. Orr in person: courteous, exact, offers to erase the *Long Pull*'s debt — and to free Rafe from his indenture contract, looking at Kade the whole time. The bribe is aimed, and it lands; Kade doesn't say no. That night Biscuit sickens — the herd-song withdrawal the researchers never solved. Kit catches Kade quarter-packed and saying goodbye. Chapter ends with Voss announcing a heading nobody expected: the Cimarron Drift, the calving grounds the surveys never mapped — because she helped chart around them. **Chapter 5 — "The Hum."** The sick-calf chapter; the emotional core. Biscuit is dying of silence. Grady, half-mystic, recalls old hull-hands swearing the herds answered engine notes. Working from Voss's memory of the Clearance frequencies — her confession in full, told flat and terrible as she feeds numbers to the engine room — they detune the *Long Pull*'s drive until the ship's bones thrum with the herd's lost song. Biscuit rallies. Kade unpacks his bag. The crew votes to run for the Drift. **Chapter 6 — "Open Range."** The chase. Orr's cutter runs them down through a debris pasture; the *Long Pull* is slower but Grady knows the shallows. Cat-and-muster maneuvering, damage taken, first shots — western chase logic, low-tech and canny. Kit's growth beat: a risky EVA-winch trick saves them once. But Orr herds them exactly where he wants — onto the derelict spine of an old Clearance tender, dead in space, both ships forced to dock. He requests a meeting. Voss goes. **Chapter 7 — "High Noon, Hard Vacuum."** The duel-and-leverage climax on the derelict's hull, mag-boots down, two figures on a ridge of dead steel. Orr has the law's paper and a drawn iron. Voss has two cards: Kade's open channel broadcasting to Threshold's docks (bought back his brother's contract with the salvage claim and a lie), and thirty years of Clearance Fleet gun-camera footage she has kept — proof the lanes were routed through the calving grounds over surveyors' objections, and the extermination logs. The "draw" is short, ugly, and Voss takes a burn across the ribs — but Orr's employers cannot afford what she's queued to transmit. He withdraws: *the asset is recorded as unviable; there is no asset.* **Chapter 8 — "The Drift."** Release and elegy. The Cimarron Drift: a slow country of dust and dark where the instruments go strange. Voss, bandaged, coaxes the drive into the song one last time and Biscuit goes out the big doors into the black — small, then smaller. Long beat of nothing. Then the depth-finder registers mass, moving, *answering* — the remnant, or something like it; the story lets it be half-mystery. Voss drops her Clearance medal into the Drift. Final scene: the *Long Pull* turning for home, still in debt, crew whole; Kit listening to the hull and hearing, now and then, far-off thunder.

Model Output:
# How a Human Might Approach This Piece A human writer sitting down with "Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked up" would almost certainly start wrong, and the wrongness would be the making of it. They'd begin with a voice or an image — the smell of the cargo bay, the specific sound a frightened animal makes against a bulkhead — and discover the story in the drafting. They probably wouldn't know what's in the crate until they'd written 2,000 words, and some of that not-knowing would survive into the final draft as productive mystery. They'd trust the reader to assemble the buffalo allegory from fragments; if they stated it once, they'd cut the second statement. They'd let a chapter be lopsided — 900 words of Grady making coffee and forty words where everything changes — because human pacing is shaped by fascination, not by outline. Crucially, a human would let the story cost something and wouldn't be sure the ending worked. They'd write the release scene, feel it was too soft, and instead of adding a "still in debt" fig leaf, they'd consider killing something. They'd also write badly in places — a scene that goes nowhere, a joke that doesn't land — and leave some of it in, because it reads like a person made it. # Typical LLM Approaches and Why They'd Hurt This Piece **Completing the prompt as an exhibit.** LLMs love to reproduce the prompt line verbatim, polished, as the final sentence of the setup — the plan does exactly this, closing Chapter 1 on the line like a submitted receipt. It reads as obedience. A human would bury it mid-scene, crackling through a comms channel, stepped on by someone else talking. **Everything pays off, nothing is wasted.** The plan is a watch mechanism: Grady's superstitions pay off in Chapter 5, Kade's brother pays off in Chapters 4 and 7, the tag pays off in Chapter 3, the medal pays off in Chapter 8. Nothing is merely texture. Humans leave loaded guns that never fire and fire guns they never loaded, and the world feels bigger for it. **Announced emotion.** "Told flat and terrible." "Wonder and danger in equal measure." These are the plan *telling the future prose how to feel*. The LLM version of the confession will be a paragraph of weighty summary; the human version is Voss reading frequencies off a scrap of foil while the engine room smells like burnt coffee, and never once saying she's sorry. **The safe wound.** "Voss takes a burn across the ribs." Of course she survives; of course the crew is "whole" at the end. The LLM cannot bear to kill a named character it has made lovable. A human knows the story's price of admission might be Grady. **The tidy moral resolution.** Orr capitulates because leverage conveniently exists — thirty-year-old recordings Voss happened to keep, decisive enough that a corporation "cannot afford" the broadcast. This is leverage ex machina, and worse, it means the ending is won by *information* — the most bureaucratic possible victory — in a story that's supposedly about blood and guilt. **Everyone gets an arc, delivered on schedule.** "Kade unpacks his bag" is a one-line redemption, on time. Humans know people relapse, hedge, betray in small irreversible ways and then have to live adjacent to it. **Uniformity.** Eight chapters of ~1,000 words each, each ending on a button, each titled with a genre wink ("High Noon, Hard Vacuum"). The symmetry itself is machine-scented. Real short stories breathe unevenly. **Monovoice.** "Laconic dialogue" applied to all five crew members produces five cowboys with one larynx. And there's a pastiche-monotone risk in "long elegiac sentences about the black" sustained for 8,000 words. # Deep Critique of the Intention & Plan **1. Orr is a trope wearing an anti-trope badge.** "Polite, patient, worse than a villain — a process" is the polite corporate antagonist, one of the most heavily used figures of the last decade of SF. The plan congratulates itself for dodging the sneering villain and lands in a cliché anyway. Worse, "there is no asset" is a cinematic button — a line written to be quoted, not spoken. **2. The allegory is mapped 1:1 and then explained twice.** Exterminated herds for hyperspace lanes = buffalo for railroads; the Ch3 breeding-program logs *and* the Ch7 extermination footage both spell out the crime. Pick one, or better, let the crew piece it together incompletely and wrongly. **3. Kade's arc resolves too cleanly and too conveniently.** He wavers at Quarter-packed in Ch4, repents by Ch5, and his brother is bought free *offstage* in Ch7 "with the salvage claim and a lie." The one genuinely humanizing element — the crew staying in debt *because Kade spent their payday on Rafe* — is currently an accident of the plan, not a dramatized cost. **4. Kit is a camera.** He witnesses everyone else's story and gets one rule-of-cool EVA save. He has no want of his own, no reason to be on this ship, no fault in the debt. Passive-witness POV is the classic LLM choice because it's the safest: observation, never agency. **5. Biscuit is a symbol, not an animal.** The calf exists to be precious. Real animals are inconvenient: they panic at the wrong moment, bond with the wrong person, damage the ship, nearly kill someone *accidentally and without malice* — and that's more frightening than malice. "Biscuit rallies" when the ship sings is the song working on cue, first try. Tidy. **6. The ending is a bow with a knot left in it on purpose.** Calf released, herd confirmed ("mass, moving, answering" — the reader is even told the answer), medal ritually discarded, crew whole, thunder heard. The "still in debt" and "lets it be half-mystery" are gestures at imperfection that don't cost anyone anything. The dropped medal is symbolism performed at the audience. **7. The vote.** "The crew votes to run for the Drift" is found-family democracy, a TV beat. Real ships aren't votes; tension is better if Voss sets the heading and two people don't speak to her for a day. **8. Front-loaded clarity.** By Chapter 3 the reader knows what Biscuit is, who made it, and why it matters. Every mystery is spent in the first third; Chapters 5–8 run on pure logistics. # Brainstorm: Making It More Human - **Make Kade's betrayal actually happen, small and irreversible.** He sends one message to Orr in Ch4 — not to sell them out, just to ask about Rafe's contract — and can't unsend it. Now Orr's uncanny tracking in Ch6 isn't a beacon, it's a person's weakness. Kade confesses; the crew has to keep flying with him. "Kade unpacks his bag" becomes nothing so simple. - **Give Kit a fault and a cover story.** Let the Threshold debt be partly his — he mis-signed the salvage contract, or he's a station kid who lied about having vacuum hours. Best twist: he learned "cowboy" entirely from old vids, and his western-tinged narration is a performance he drops under stress. The genre voice becomes characterization. - **Let the song trick half-fail.** Detuning the drive gets a response — the wrong response. Biscuit panics, breaches an interior bulkhead, someone (Grady?) gets hurt, and the second attempt is done grieving, not hoping. - **Cut one explanation.** Lose either the breeding logs or the gun-camera footage. Let Voss's confession be her only testimony, unverifiable, and let the crew take the Drift heading on faith in her word — that's what the story's actually about. - **End without confirmation — or pay for it.** Either the depth-finder reads nothing, the doors close, and the story ends on not-knowing (the harder, more human ending), or confirmation comes at a real price. Consider: Biscuit, imprinted on Kit, won't leave — and the last scene is Kit being cruel enough to close the door on it. Earning the ending instead of decorating it. - **The medal, fumbled.** She means to drop it into the Drift, and can't. Keeps it. That's a person. Or she throws it and it just tumbles off-screen with no ceremony and no description. - **Let Orr win something.** He withdraws, but he takes a price or leaves a splinter — a remark that shows the recording won't protect them forever, or he gets the salvage claim after all, or he's simply *reassigned* and everyone knows there's another him. The "process" should feel undented. - **Vary the architecture.** Let one chapter be a single 1,000-word scene in real time (the opening of the crate, or the confession); let one be half-length and jagged. Ditch the jokey chapter titles or make them plain. - **Give Grady one detail that never pays off** — the signed welds stay just a habit, or the superstition is *wrong* — and let the successful idea come from Doc, the least mystical person aboard. - **Break the prompt line.** Deliver it mid-sentence, interrupted, misheard over comms static; or have Kit say it wrong and get corrected. Show the seams. - **Consider the darker door.** The calf dies in Ch5–6, and they go to the Drift anyway with nothing but a recording of its voice — and the ending is them playing it into the dark. Grief instead of triumph. This may be too much for a warm story, but a human would at least weigh it.

# Intention **The premise stands.** A broke salvage crew wins a crate off a derelict hauler and finds the last juvenile thunderhead — space-bison exterminated a generation ago when the Meridian Combine cut its hyperspace lanes through the calving grounds. A cattle-drive in reverse: five people moving one small animal across the black toward the Cimarron Drift, the calving grounds the surveys never mapped, while the Combine's Asset Recovery man, Mr. Orr, follows. **The engine is Voss's guilt, and now it's spent, not displayed.** She flew escort for the Clearance Fleets. Her confession comes once, in the engine room at the story's lowest moment, flat and without apology — and it is *not* the thing that saves the calf. When the ending needs leverage, the weapon is the confession itself, broadcast on the open channel with her own name and her own crimes in it. She wins by spending the secret she kept for thirty years. The crew's choice to back her story is the found-family proof; no vote, no speech — they just don't contradict her. **POV and voice: Kit, and the voice is the arc.** He's nineteen, a station kid who learned "cowboy" entirely from old vids, and his western-tinged narration is a performance — the prose is ornate and borrowed in Chapter 1 and strips down, chapter by chapter, under pressure, until Chapter 8 is nearly plain. He got hired on a lie about vacuum hours; his EVA set piece in Chapter 6 is him doing the thing he lied about being able to do, terrified, and afterward he confesses the lie — a small echo of Voss, learned by watching her. He names the calf (Biscuit). The tag he pries off at the end and keeps in his pocket: the kid souvenirs the thing Voss can't shed. **Kade's betrayal is real, small, and irreversible.** At Threshold he sends one message from a public terminal — not selling anyone out, just asking Orr's office what it would take to transfer his brother's indenture. The reply carries a handshake ping that marks the *Long Pull*'s transponder. That's how the cutter keeps finding them in Chapter 6 — not the beacon, a person's weakness. He confesses in Chapter 5 because someone got hurt and he can't carry it. Nobody forgives him; they just keep flying with him. In Chapter 7, Voss quietly folds Rafe's contract into her trade with Orr — and Kade learns of it afterward, and the mercy shames him worse than the anger did. **The calf is an animal, not a symbol.** It nearly kills Grady in Chapter 2 out of pure terror. The song trick *half-fails*: Grady's folk-tale frequency is wrong, Biscuit panics, and Grady's hand is crushed against a bulkhead — the engineer who signs his welds loses the hand he signed with. The fix comes from Doc, the least mystical person aboard: she records Biscuit's own distress cry and detunes the drive to answer it. The ship becomes herd by singing the calf's voice back to it. No mysticism rewarded; observation is. **Cut to one explanation.** No gun-camera archive, no extermination footage. The derelict's data-core (breeding-program logs) survives as the story's single piece of hard proof — and in Chapter 7 Voss trades it away, along with the salvage claim that would have cleared the debt, for Orr's withdrawal and Rafe's contract. A trade, not a triumph. They end the story *poorer* than they started. **Orr is not defeated; he is adjusted.** He files the asset as unviable, takes the core, erases one indenture as a line-item, and leaves a splinter: a remark that this changes nothing about the lanes, and that her confession is now on record with him personally. He is undented. One shot is fired on the hull — brief, ugly, a burn across Voss's ribs — almost incidental to the meeting it interrupts. **The ending is earned hope, not confirmation.** Biscuit, imprinted on Kit, won't leave the ship; the release only works when Kit is cruel enough to have the singing stopped. The depth-finder reads nothing for a long, long time. They have to go — fuel, Grady's hand, the debt — and Voss orders the heading home before anything resolves. Then, once, far off, the scope ticks. One contact, ambiguous, rock-or-animal, and the story does not settle it. Voss takes out her Clearance medal to drop into the Drift, stands too long, and puts it back in her pocket. Nobody says anything. **The prompt is served by staging, not enshrinement.** The line arrives mid-scene in Chapter 1 — Kit keying the channel, saying it, getting talked over by Grady, having to say it again plainly — a moment of transmission, not a curtain line. **Aiming for:** interrupted dialogue; scenes that start late and leave early; uneven chapter interiors (one long real-time scene, one compressed montage night, one jagged crisis); specific hands-on detail (welds, manifests, feed, frequencies); the buffalo allegory carried in fragments and never named. **Avoiding:** the prompt line as a polished chapter button; leverage ex machina; on-schedule redemption; five characters with one laconic larynx; jokey chapter titles; the crew vote; the safe wound; the confirmed miracle; symbolism performed at the audience. # Chapter Planning **Chapter 1 — "Salvage."** Kit's borrowed, ornate narration establishes the *Long Pull*, the debt at Threshold, the crew in motion: Voss's economy, Grady's signed welds, Doc's bluntness, Kade's quiet. They crack the derelict hauler's sealed hold; one crate, manifest: LIVESTOCK — PROBABLE LOSS. Kit alone in the bay hears it, keys the channel, delivers the line — and Grady talks over him; he has to say it twice. End on the crate's foil tag glinting, not on the sentence. **Chapter 2 — "Livestock."** One continuous real-time scene, ~1,000 words, no time-cuts: opening the crate. The animal — three meters, scarred, one wrecked wing — nearly kills Grady out of terror; Doc settles it ranch-hand slow. Voss watches from the door, says nothing, leaves; Kade notices, Kit doesn't. Kit feeds it by hand; names it Biscuit. Nobody decides anything yet. **Chapter 3 — "The Tag."** They leave the tag on. Orr's message arrives: asset recovery, standard fee, no questions. Doc recognizes Clearance Fleet protocol in the way Voss handled the animal; cornered, Voss admits only that she "flew during the Clearance." An argument, not a vote — silence and hard headings instead of speeches. Kade says almost nothing. **Chapter 4 — "Threshold."** A compressed night at the station, montage-like. Orr in person: courteous, exact, offers to erase the debt while looking at Kade; mentions Rafe's mine by name. Biscuit begins sickening — withdrawal, the silence-sickness. Kade, at a public terminal, sends one message asking what a contract transfer would cost. Kit sees him send something and doesn't understand it. Voss sets the heading for the Cimarron Drift and doesn't ask permission. **Chapter 5 — "The Hum."** The jagged crisis chapter. Biscuit dying of quiet. Grady offers the old hull-hands' frequency; they try it; it's wrong — the calf panics, slams the bulkhead, Grady's hand is crushed. At the low point, Kade confesses the message. Then Voss confesses everything, flat, in the engine room — the cull, the numbers, the lanes. Doc, listening, records Biscuit's own cry on her med-kit and detunes the drive to answer it. The ship sings the calf's voice back; Biscuit settles. Nobody forgives Kade. They keep the heading. **Chapter 6 — "The Shallows."** The cutter finds them — and the crew knows why: the ping in the reply packet, Kade's message home. Bitter chase through the debris pasture; the *Long Pull* is slower, Grady's tracking, but Doc knows the shallows now. Kit does the EVA-winch trick he lied about being able to do, terrified the whole time, and confesses the lie after. It buys an hour, not escape: Orr herds them onto the dead spine of an old Clearance tender and requests a meeting. Voss goes out to meet him. **Chapter 7 — "The Meeting."** Two figures on the hull, mag-boots down. Voss opens a channel to the traffic bands and tells all of it — her name, her escort flights, the cull, the lanes. Her weapon is self-incrimination; the crew, one by one, keys in and doesn't contradict her. Orr's employers cannot want the story told, but Voss doesn't press the advantage into a victory: she trades — the data-core, the derelict claim, the quiet — for withdrawal and Rafe's contract. One shot, brief, ugly; a burn across her ribs. Orr files the asset as unviable, notes her confession is on record with him, and leaves undented. **Chapter 8 — "The Drift."** Quiet, spare, plain-narrated — Kit's borrowed voice mostly gone. The Cimarron: dust and dark, instruments strange. The song plays; Biscuit won't leave; Kit orders it stopped and the doors closed, and does not watch. The scope reads nothing, and nothing, and they have to go — and Voss orders home before anything resolves. Once, far off, the scope ticks. One contact, ambiguous. Nobody confirms anything; Voss takes out the medal, stands too long, pockets it. Final beat: the *Long Pull* turning home, deeper in debt, Grady's hand, Kade's brother, Kit in the empty bay that still smells like animal — the foil tag in his pocket, thunder in the hull that might be the drive.

# Kit (Arun Prabhu) **Who they are.** Nineteen, born on Threshold Station, Third Shift decks — grew up between the hydroponics racks and a mother who watched two-hundred-year-old western serials on a cracked slate to fall asleep. His given name is Arun Prabhu; "Kit" is a name he chose at sixteen off a serial box-art, and only the payroll ledger and Captain Voss know otherwise. He's done two supervised EVAs in training and logged forty; Grady clocked the lie within a week (engineers talk to other engineers) and never said a word, just started teaching him properly, which Kit understood was a kindness and has never acknowledged. His whole cowboy manner is costume — he practices "reckon" in his head before saying it, owns one tooled-leather belt bought at a dock stall, rolls cigarettes he never lights because you can't smoke aboard. Carries them anyway, like a prop. He alphabetizes cargo straps because station kids keep small orders to keep sane. He hates the smell of protein vats — he grew up next to them — and writes letters home to a mother who's been dead a year because he doesn't know how to stop. His flaw is the lie, but deeper: he wants to have *been* somewhere. The serials taught him the frontier is where you find out who you are, and he's terrified the answer is "a station kid who mis-signed a salvage contract." The Threshold debt is partly his — he countersigned the derelict claim without reading the penalty clauses, and only Voss knows that too. Two people on the ship know his two secrets, and both keep them. That's what the crew turns out to be. **Physicality.** Wiry, quick, hands always slightly too busy — he'll drum a knee, flip a strap-end. Stands with a hip cocked like he's leaning on a fence that isn't there; learned posture, straight off the screen. Under stress the drawl flattens out to plain station-standard, and the story tracks that flattening. When he's frightened his voice goes *smaller*, not bigger. **Motives & relationships.** Wants the crew's respect more than wages; wants to be the person the serials promised. He feeds Biscuit first out of curiosity and then because it answers his boot-steps — nobody has ever answered him before, specifically, by name. His arc is subtraction: the costume drops, and what's under it is a kid honest enough, at the end, to do the cruel necessary thing (ordering the song stopped, the doors closed) and honest enough to admit the lie out loud after the EVA. He keeps the foil tag in his pocket. Voss calls him "Mr. Prabhu" exactly once in the story — at the doors — and it lands like a medal. **Voice.** Early, ornate: *The black doesn't forgive a fool, which I knew from the serials, being only newly a fool and hoping to be excused on account of inexperience.* Late, plain: *The bay smelled like animal for days. I didn't clean it up right away. I don't know why I'm saying that except it's true.* # Captain Ada Voss **Who they are.** Mid-fifties. Ranch-kid off a settlement moon, family ran stock until the lanes collapsed the market — she took the Combine's training slot at twenty-two because it was flight hours and pay, and told herself the surveyors knew best. Clearance Fleet escort, six years: she flew the box patterns that herded the thunderheads into the kill zones. She was *trained to move stock*, which is the skill that betrays her in Chapter 2 — Doc recognizes the technique. Thirty years since, she's run freight and salvage on the margins, keeps meticulous paper logs, and has never once said the word "thunderhead" aloud. Drinks her coffee cold and won't say why. Her idiom is ranch-and-flight: she says "stock" for the cargo, "weather" for trouble, "fence" for the law's reach. Her flaw is that she manages people the way she manages guilt — by containment. Her kindnesses are covert operations: she sets the heading for the Drift without asking, folds Rafe's contract into the trade without telling Kade, quietly absorbs Kit's share of the debt. It denies everyone the chance to thank her, argue with her, or forgive her, and she prefers it that way, because gratitude would require her to explain. She'll spend herself before she'll spend anyone else — and she spends other people's *gratitude* without asking, which is its own quiet theft. **Physicality.** Gray-shot hair tied back with cargo line, a pilot's permanent squint, acceleration-habit of settling her head against bulkhead rests. Moves like someone conserving fuel. When she thinks, she does preflight touches — palm flat on surfaces, checking a ship she's flown for nine years. Hands scarred from cable work; the only time they're unsteady is around the animal. **Motives & relationships.** She flew with Kade once before hiring him and liked his silence; that's the whole extent of her vetting and it's how she does everything — one decisive reading, then loyalty without commentary. With Doc, the friction is professional and historical: both women know the Clearance era from opposite sides of the contract, and neither has said so until Chapter 3. Voss's motive isn't redemption — she doesn't believe in it — it's *balancing*. She's kept the account open for thirty years and this is the payment. She keeps the medal at the end because she doesn't get to close the account. She knows that. **Voice.** Clipped declaratives, no decoration. *"We're not stealing it. Manifest says probable loss. That's the nicest thing anyone's ever written about this crew."* And, flat, in the engine room: *"I flew the box patterns. You learn the patterns, and the animals learn them too, after a while. That was the part nobody wrote down."* # Doc (Pilar Reyes) **Who they are.** Mid-forties, colony stock vet from a ranching world — certified large-animal, cross-trained on humans because her colony had a doctor and then, for two years, didn't. She was offered a Clearance contract in the cull years: verification counts, stock-side. She turned it down, lost her colony posting over the refusal, and has spent thirty years being exactly angry enough about it that she can't mention it — which is why she corners Voss in Chapter 3 with a stock-handler's precision. She recognizes the technique before she recognizes the guilt, and would say she doesn't care about the guilt; she cares that it's *being handled badly*. Personality: blunt to the point of diagnosis. She'll tell you "it's an animal, it isn't grieving, it's deficient in something, and we're going to find out what" — and she's usually right, which annoys people more than being wrong would. Unsentimental about animals in a way that is actually respect: she refuses to lie to or about them. Despises pet names (friction with Kit over "Biscuit"); calls it "the calf," and by tag-number when she's working. Chews mint toothpicks split from cargo dunnage. Hums one off-key bar of something while she stitches — nobody has ever asked what, because it's clearly not a question she'd answer. Keeps a paper ledger of everything she's ever lost, numbered, species and date. Cold-comfort bookkeeping. At the end of the story she does not open it, and that's all we learn about that. Her flaw: bluntness as armor means she cannot do comfort — her bedside manner with humans is genuinely poor ("This will hurt and I don't care if you cry, but if you faint I'm making fun of you"). She says the true thing when the kind thing is needed, and sometimes the true thing is not the whole thing. **Physicality.** Broad-shouldered, forearms like a farrier's, calm hands — the calm travels up from the hands and is what settles terrified animals and men alike. Stands square. Looks animals in the eye; watches humans at the mouth. Claims she learned to read lips on cattle, which is impossible, and she knows it, and enjoys saying it. **Motives & relationships.** Loyal to the crew as *patients*, which is her version of family. Her professional pride is engaged by Biscuit — a case nobody's seen in thirty years — and she'd be embarrassed by how much that matters to her if anyone said it out loud. She is the story's empiricist: when Grady's folk frequency fails, she doesn't argue with it, she *records the calf's own distress cry and answers it*. Observation over folklore. She and Grady have a truce of unsaid things — she has heard his dry-air cough and said nothing, which is its own diagnosis. **Voice.** *"It's not dying of loneliness. Animals don't die of loneliness. They die of a deficit. We're going to find it."* To Grady, at the drive: *"Sing her own voice back to her. She doesn't want your granddad's song. She wants her own."* # Grady (Emmett Grady) **Who they are.** Sixty-eight, fifty-plus years on hulls. Started as a rivet-runner at the Palisade yard at fourteen under a falsified birth year — which is why he knew Kit's vacuum-hour lie on sight and covered for it without a word: he's played that hand himself. The drive is "the old girl"; he talks to her like a mule. Signs every weld with a small struck "G," and will tell you it isn't

# Chapter 1 — "Salvage" The black, as the serials had taught me, does not forgive a fool — and I was newly a fool that season, nineteen and flush with exactly one tooled-leather belt and a head full of borrowed sayings, signed aboard the *Long Pull* as deckhand and part-claimant to a debt I had not read closely enough to fear. I would learn to fear it. That is mostly what deep space is: the slow arrival of bad news you already signed for. The derelict hung off our port beam like something the dark had half-digested and given up on. Hauler-class, older than the captain, listing her cargo to the stars the way a dead man tips his hat. Grady swore she was a *Dunmore*-series and Voss said she was a payday, which ended the discussion, the captain's word being the shortest nail in any conversation she chose to swing at. "Eyes on the seal, Mr. Prabhu," she said. "We're not the first to look." We weren't. Someone had cut a survey hole in her flank years back — clean corporate work, healed over with vacuum-frost. But her hold was still sealed, and sealed meant somebody had paid to keep something in there, and the salvage math at Threshold Station ran simple: sealed holds paid debts, and ours was four months deep and growing teeth. I'll say this for the crew: each of them was exactly what they appeared to be, once you learned what they appeared to be, which took me the better part of a season. The captain ran the boat the way old ranchers are said to have run the weather — not by fighting it, but by being somewhere the weather had already agreed with. Ada Voss kept a paper log in a hand that never shook and never hurried, and she called cargo "stock" and trouble "weather" and the long arm of the law "the fence," and in four months I never once heard her raise her voice, though I heard her lower it to good effect twice. Grady was the engineer, sixty-eight if he was a day, and he talked to the drive like a mule that owed him money. Every weld he laid got a little struck G at the end of the seam, and when I asked him why, he said, "So I know which ones to apologize to," and looked at me like the joke was a test I'd failed. Doc Reyes I mostly avoided those first months, being as she diagnosed people for sport. She'd come aboard from some ranching colony with a vet's certificate and a farrier's forearms, chewing a mint toothpick split off the cargo dunnage, and she'd looked at my hands once and said, "Paper cuts. You'll do," and that was the warmest thing she ever said to anybody as far as I knew. Kade flew us. He was quiet in a way I mistook for peace, being green, and I'd learn the difference later — that some quiet is empty and some quiet is *full*, and Kade's was full the way a held note is full. He had a brother in a mine somewhere. He never said so. His face said so when he did his accounts. We cut the hold that shift, Kade holding the *Long Pull* off the derelict's shoulder in a breathless hover while Grady and I went across on tether. My fourth EVA. I logged it steady. Inside the glove my hands were doing what hands do, and I sang to myself an old theme from my mother's serials, the one about the ranger and the burned ranch, and got the words wrong, which in hindsight was the only honest thing about me that day. The hold was a tomb of ordinary riches — feed pallets burst and frosted, a loader with its arms up like a man surrendering — and aft of all of it, one crate, three meters of composite shell, strapped down like it had tried to leave. The manifest plate had weathered to lace, but I got my lamp on it and made out the old freight codes, and I'll own that my heart did something unprofessional. **LIVESTOCK, LIVE. PROBABLE LOSS.** Now, livestock needs life support, and life support runs on power, and dead ships don't pay that particular bill — so livestock, live, on a derelict this old, meant what salvage crews call a ghost entry: some clerk, some war ago, covering a loss. It happened. It would happen to our paperwork someday, if we were unlucky or lucky. We winched it aboard into Bay Two, set it soft, and the crew stood around it the way you'd stand around a coffin at a stranger's funeral — hats-in-hand without knowing the deceased. Doc read the shell tags and said the manufacturer's marks were Combine, which pulled the captain's mouth into a line I hadn't seen before and wouldn't learn to read until much later. "Well," said Grady, to the crate, in the voice he used on the drive. "Somebody paid for freight on you." Voss said, "Get the manifest squared. We're five days to Threshold." And they went to their stations, because the black waits for no one's feelings, and I stayed to dog down the bay — station kid, keeping small orders, straps squared and字母alphabetized, that being my way of praying. That's when I heard it. A sound like weight shifting in a hayloft. Like a big soft thing finding a new side to lie on. The strap over the crate's midpoint had gone taut as a guitar string, and the whole three meters of it *creaked*, once, settling. I stood there with my lamp on it longer than a sensible man would, and I'm not sensible, I'm nineteen and costumed, but I knew one thing from the serials and it happened to be true: the black does not forgive a fool, and a fool is any man who opens an alien box alone. I keyed the channel with a thumb that wouldn't hurry. "Captain, something's... moving in that crate we picked—" *"—confirm the aft straps are rated for tow, or do I have to—" *Grady, riding right over me from the engineering deck, irritable as a mule. I pressed the key again. My drawl, I notice in memory, had gone flat as Third Shift station-standard. "Captain. The crate moved." The lamp's beam lay on the manifest plate, and there, near the seam, something glinted that wasn't frost — a tag of foil, small as a playing card, stamped with numbers I couldn't read at that distance, blinking slow as a sleeping thing's heartbeat.

# Chapter 2 — "Livestock" I want to tell it in order, because out of order it sounds like a story somebody made up, and in order it only sounds like a mistake, which is what it was. They came down to Bay Two within the hour. Voss first, because it was her bay; then Doc with her kit; then Grady grumbling that if it was stock it was dead stock and if it wasn't stock it was worse, and Kade last, because somebody had to hold the boat and he'd put her on station-keep with the long tether to the derelict still out, our claim trailing behind us like a leash on a dog we weren't sure we owned. The crate had been quiet since the creak. That was the worst part, looking back. It waited. "Manifest says probable loss," Voss said. She'd pulled the plate and had it in two pieces like a biscuit. "Somebody wrote probable. That's a bet, not a fact." She handed the numbers to Doc, and Doc read them twice and said the manufacturer's code was old Combine, pre-war, and the tag was a livetag — bio-telemetry, the kind you bolt to something you expect to outlive your interest in it. "So it's alive or the tag's drunk," Grady said. "I've known tags both ways." "Open it," Voss said. I'll set the scene square, because I remember it square: Bay Two is nine meters fore-to-aft, and we had the crate amidships with the deck lights up full, which in hindsight was our first error, and the loading ramp down, which was our second. Grady had the cutter, because Grady would not trust a seal to anyone else's hands. Doc stood off the crate's head end — if a crate has a head end; she said after that they always do — with her palms open and down at her thighs, a stance I'd learn to call *the stance*, though nobody taught me its name, it was just the way she stood near big frightened things. Voss stood at the bay door with her hand flat on the frame. I never saw her touch the animal the whole voyage, and I never saw her farther than that door either, and I'm getting ahead, but that's the truth of her and I'd rather say it plain. Grady cut the seam. Slow, sparks sparing, the cutter talking back to him the way tools talk to men who listen. The shell parted along a factory line and the two halves sagged on their straps and a smell came out of it that nobody expected: *straw*. Warm animal straw, and under it the sweetish reek of sedation gel, yards of it, gone gummy with age. Then the gel moved. It came up out of the shell the way weather comes off a range — all at once and everywhere, three meters of it, hide scarred down one flank like something had raked it, a wing — a *wing*, folded wrong and dragging — and a head the size of a shipping drum swinging blind on a neck like a windlass. It got its legs, which were wrong for a beast that size, too long, made for hanging in something bigger than a bay, and it saw nine meters of bright walls and five small loud things, and it did the only sensible thing there is to do in a bright small loud place. It came for the door. Grady was between it and the door, because Grady was between it and everything, being sixty-eight and slow in the knees and quick nowhere. It didn't charge him the way a bull charges, lowered and mean. It *blundered* — a great terrified flinch the size of a wagon — and took him against the bulkhead with its shoulder, not a strike, a shrug, and a shrug from that much of anything will kill a man as dead as malice. He went down under the straw-reek with the cutter spinning away, and it turned in the space it had — it could barely turn, wings mantling the walls, tags and straps and gel everywhere — and lined up on him where he lay. And Doc walked in. Not around it. *At* it, palms down and open, saying nothing, and the beast swung that drum of a head down at her and huffed — a sound I felt in my teeth, a big soft bellows of a sound, all fear, no fight — and Doc huffed back. I swear it on the belt and the belt was expensive. She put her face nearly in its steam and breathed out slow through her mouth, the way you'd gentle a horse that's never seen a man, and the two of them stood there trading breaths while the wing dripped gel and Grady bled quietly on the deck and nobody moved but the animal's flank, in, and out, and in. "Nobody brightens anything," Doc said, quiet, not turning. "Nobody shouts. Captain, kill half those lamps. Kit — Grady. Slow, from behind me, no hurry in your hands." We got Grady out by his boots. Ribs, not skull, thank every cheap saint on Threshold — he'd tell it later as being run down by a hay baler with a grudge. Doc backed the beast — the calf, it was a calf, we could see it now, rangy and wrong-grown and young — into the crate's shadowed half, and it folded down into its own stink and gel with the sigh of something too tired for terror, and lay watching us with one eye like a well. Voss was not at the door anymore. Kade, holding the ramp, caught my eye and tipped his head after her, down the corridor — *you see that?* — and I didn't. I was watching the animal. I'd never stood next to anything that wasn't human and known it was a *somebody*, and my chest did a thing I don't have serial words for. It wouldn't eat feed. It would eat from my hand — Doc said later my hand was small and unhurried, which was the nicest lie anyone ever told about me. We had ship's biscuit from the galley, the hard kind, and it took the pieces one at a time, polite as you please, a tongue like warm rope. "Biscuit," I said, before I could costume the words.
