# Chapter 3 — "The Tag" Three days out from Threshold, we were a ship with a routine, which is what a ship becomes instead of a family, and then is a family before anyone notices. Mine was the bay. Morning straw, water lines checked, and Biscuit's ration — she'd eat feed now if I stood by the trough, but only if I stood by the trough, and Doc had opinions about that which she delivered in full: "You're making it dependent. Stop enjoying it." I did not stop enjoying it. I was nineteen and something on this boat finally answered my boot-steps, and I'd have stood in that straw a year for the price of the belt. Grady healed the way he did everything, badly and out loud, narrating his ribs to the drive. Doc had him taped and working light, which for Grady meant he only carried things a younger man should've carried, and he coughed doing it, a dry little hitch high in the chest, and I saw Doc hear that cough and file it and say nothing. They had a treaty, those two, drawn along lines I could map by the silence. The tag was the fourth thing in my routine, and the fourth thing was the odd one. Card of foil on the scarred flank, blinking slow, all night, all day. On the third morning I got the pry-tool out of Doc's kit — she'd said cut it, tags foul under straw — and I had the blade an inch off the hide when the light in the bay changed, which is to say the captain was in the doorway. "Leave it," Voss said. "It's fouling—" "Leave it on." And that was all. She looked at the animal the way you'd look at weather on the far horizon — measuring, I'd have said then; *keeping*, I'd say now — and went. I put the tool away. I want to say I wondered at it. I mostly didn't. Station kids keep small orders. The message came through at second watch, addressed not to the ship but to the tag number, which should have told us everything and instead told us the exact size of the fee. *Meridian Combine, Division of Asset Recovery,* it read. *Re: tagged biological asset, ref. 909. Recovery of Combine property is a routine matter. Standard fee: 40,000 credits, credited on confirmation of asset condition. No questions are required of your crew, and none will be recorded. Inspection available at Threshold. Travel costs defrayed. — M. Orr.* Forty thousand. I'll do the arithmetic for you, being the one who mis-signed the papers: our debt at Threshold stood at thirty-one thousand and change, and the *change* was the part with teeth, compounding monthly like something alive. The number Orr sent wasn't a fee. It was a door held open, and every one of us felt the draft. "Man doesn't even ask what condition it's in," Grady said, reading it over my shoulder. "That's a man who already knows." "Credited *on confirmation*," Doc said. "That's a man who intends not to confirm." Voss read it twice — I watched her eyes make both passes — and set the slate down on the console like it was hot. "We're not stealing it. Manifest says probable loss." A pause. "That's the nicest thing anyone's ever written about this crew." "Ada." Doc, and I mark it: the first Christian name I ever heard on that boat. "Thirty-one thousand. With the penalty clauses." She said *penalty clauses* at me, and I felt it land where she aimed it, and Kade — Kade was at the board the whole while, running the numbers we weren't saying, and I caught his eyes on the message, and on his own accounts open beside it, and his face did the thing it did about the mine, and he closed both screens and said nothing. He flew, is what Kade did. He flew and the quiet of him had a weight I mistook, then, for peace. Nobody decided anything, which is how the decision got made. Voss put in the new heading herself, hard burns, days shorter than the ones we'd planned, and when Grady asked what about Threshold and the inspection and the defrayed travel, she said, "Threshold's still on the way," which was true the way a fence is a gate: technically, if you're willing to climb. Doc cornered her that evening in Bay Two, with me in the straw pretending very hard to be furniture. "You stood at the door," Doc said. No warm-up on her at all. "Two days. You never came past the frame. And when it bolted, you were already where the crew wasn't. That's not freighter habit. Freight hands crowd an animal, they ring it. You held pressure off the door the whole time." A beat, toothpick traveling. "That's approach protocol. Combine stock protocol. Nobody learns it hauling grain." The straw was very quiet. Biscuit breathed like a bellows in the far corner, and the tag blinked at us all, slow, slow. "I flew during the Clearance," Voss said. "That's not what I asked." "It's what I've got." Doc looked at her a long moment — the look she gave an animal before she'd decided yet what was wrong with it — and then she picked up her kit and left, and the captain stayed at the door a while with her palm flat on the frame, the way she checked the boat, though the boat was standing still. I fed Biscuit by hand. I didn't say anything either. I was learning, that voyage, all the ways a person can not-say something, and I'd rank that one — palm flat on the frame — near the top, and I hadn't even reached the engine room yet. Kade was in the corridor after, not going anywhere. Watching Voss walk off toward the bow, and then looking at me like he wanted to ask me something and deciding I was too young to ask it of. He was right. But it was kind of him to check.

# Chapter 4 — "Threshold" I remember Threshold as a night cut into pieces, and I'll give you the pieces, because stitched together they lie about how it felt. **The dock.** We came in on a commercial berth, which meant the yard crew could see our transponder and our dents and price us accordingly, and Voss paid the fee without blinking, which is what she did instead of flinching. Bay Two stayed locked and listed as contaminated feed — Grady's idea, and a good one, contamination being the one word that keeps inspectors and everyone else at a respectful distance. Biscuit stood the docking better than I expected, swaying with the station spin like she'd been born to docks. She had begun, that week, to answer the hull noises. When the loaders worked outside she'd turn her head to them, and once she answered back, a low note that made the bulkhead fuzz, and the loader outside stopped for a second, operator confused. I logged that. Nobody else was in the bay to see it. Sometimes I think I keep the whole voyage in exactly that way — saw it, logged it, nobody else saw it. **The office.** Voss took me along to the debt office because I was the claimant, the signature, the fool in the paperwork. The clerk was kind in the way clerks are kind, which is to say she confirmed we now owed thirty-three and some, the *some* having grown a new tooth while we flew, and there was a message waiting for the captain, and it wasn't from the debt office at all. Mr. Orr had booked a room in the station's good hotel. Mr. Orr had booked the *station's* good hotel's quiet lounge, and coffee was already poured when we came in, and he stood — he stood, for a salvage captain in a mended coat — and I will now tell you the only things you need to know about Mr. Orr. He was about forty, groomed like a man who has never once been late, and he thanked the staff by name. He had our file open on the table, and our file was not thick, and it was still more than we knew about ourselves. He never used the word *thunderhead*. He said *the asset*, all evening, the way you'd say *the stapler*. "Captain Voss. Mr. Prabhu." My name off his tongue was my first shock of the night; I hadn't given it. "The Combine appreciates that you've kept the asset in good condition. Feeding records are consistent with the tag's telemetry. That's rare, in recovery work. Usually we arrive to a carcass and a story." He smiled at his coffee. "The fee is forty thousand, as transmitted. And since your vessel labors under certain obligations—" he turned the slate toward her, gentle as a dealer turning a card, "—we can simplify. Debt cleared this evening, travel costs as promised, and a small gratitude adjustment. You'd leave Threshold owing nothing." Owing nothing. I want it on the record what those words do to a nineteen-year-old with thirty-three thousand of teeth in his own name. The room actually went warm for a second. Voss said, "What's the condition?" "Condition," Orr said, pleasantly, "is the wrong word for a signature and a berth number." And then he looked past her. Past me. At the doorway, where Kade had just come in from his own errands, station dust still on his sleeves. "Mr. Kade. Your brother's rotation at Corbett Deep comes up for renewal next month. Indenture transfer applications are usually—" a small pause, precise as a signature, "—slow. They needn't be slow." He said *Corbett Deep* like he was remembering a vacation. Kade stood in the doorway and didn't move, and his quiet filled right up to the brim, and Voss looked at Orr — just looked — and said, "You've done your reading, Mr. Orr." "It's the whole of my job," he said, and meant it as an honest answer, and it was the worst thing anyone said all night. "The offer holds until station-drop. Enjoy Threshold." **The bay, later.** Biscuit wouldn't eat. She'd stood the docking fine and then gone wrong — standing wrong, wing dragging, turning slow circles in the straw like a horse with colic, and her eye, when I knelt, was somewhere I couldn't follow. Doc took her numbers and got a diagnosis of nothing. "Nothing's broken. Nothing's deficient. It's not eating and I can't find why." I'd never heard Doc say *can't* before. I didn't know she carried the word. She'd stopped answering the loaders, too. That was mine to notice. The hull would clank and she'd not turn her head, and the bay was very quiet in a way I couldn't fix with straw. **The terminal.** Past third bell, errand of Grady's — parts manifest, his cough riding me along with the list — and the public terminals were all empty but one. Kade. Station dust still on his sleeves. Typing fast, then slow, then sitting very still, the way you sit after you've sent a thing. "Parts run," I said, holding up the slate, and he looked at me a half-second too long. "Good," he said. "Good. Get the gaskets, not the ones he said. The better ones." I got the better ones. I want that known. I got the better ones and I never once asked him what he'd sent, because I was nineteen and I thought the quiet on that ship was peace, and I've had years to think about what else I could've done with that half-second, and the answer is: nothing. But it was kind of him to try and cover it. It was kind of him to think I was too young to notice. I was old enough to notice. I just didn't know what I was noticing. **Undocking.** Voss set the heading at 0500 without a meeting, without a word, a hard burn laid in for open black and then some. Grady read the plot off the board and did the sums and said, "That's not the lanes. That's not anything. That's the Cimarron." "That's right," Voss said. "The surveys quit charting out there. There's a reason." "I know the reason," she said, and dropped us off the dock, and behind us Threshold shrank with Mr. Orr's coffee still warm in his quiet lounge, and Bay Two stood silent as a held bell, and I went to feed an animal that would not eat, and out past the fence of the lanes the black opened up like a range nobody had ever lied to. Nobody said we were running. The burn said it for us.

# Chapter 5 — "The Hum" She was dying of quiet. Doc said there's no such diagnosis, and then stopped saying it, because the animal was dying and the tests said nothing was wrong. Day three out from Threshold, Biscuit stopped standing. She lay in the straw with her barrel flank hardly working, and her eye had gone to that far place for good, and she'd quit answering everything — my boot-steps, my voice, the loaders, me. I sat with her the whole second watch with biscuit in my open hand until my arm went dead, and she looked past me at the wall, and I want you to understand that I had never been hated by anything before, and this wasn't hate, it was worse, it was *nothing*, and I would have taken the hate. "She's not in pain," Doc said, which was her way of saying *I don't know*. "Vitals crawling. Like a machine throttling down. Nothing to treat." She said the word *can't* again. Twice in one voyage. It was Grady who came up the corridor coughing, holding a slate with something on it. Old station folklore, hull-hand talk, the kind of thing he'd sworn by for fifty years and been laughed at for forty. Freight crews in the cull years, he said, swore the herds *answered engines*. That drift-cattle would come to a hull singing the right note. That the old haulers, the really old ones, had detune mods nobody admitted to. "There's no literature," Doc said. "There's no herds either, is the other thing," Grady said. "So the literature's thin all around." He had a frequency. His grandfather's ship, a number off a slate older than the boat, handed down with the weld-sign and the cough. And the drive could be made to sing it — Grady said the old girl could sing anything once, before they tuned all the voice out of her. We should have waited for morning. You'll want to know whose fault it was. It was nobody's. It was all of us wanting it too much at the same time. Grady detuned her slow and careful, one man walking his own deck like a stranger, and the drive came down off its modern whine into something low, a hum you felt in your molars and the heels of your hands, and I was in the bay to watch — and Biscuit's head came up. Her head came *up*. First time in two days, and my heart went off like a fool's, and the hum deepened, and she came up off the straw wrong. Not answering. *Hunting* it. The note was close and it wasn't right, and it went through her like a hook through the lip of a fish — she bugled, a sound like a silo tearing, a sound I'll hear when I'm old, and threw herself at the aft bulkhead. Once. Twice. Wing out, head down, striking the hull next to the drive housing like she could kill the song or join it. The bay rang. Equipment left the walls. Grady was at the panel, killing the note, both hands in — and the panel was old, and old panels kick. I saw it, so here it is: the drive hiccuped through its cutoff, the housing slammed a harmonic, and his hand went into the frame with it. He didn't shout. He sat down on the deck and said, mild as morning, "Well, that's that, then," and held his wrist, and the hand wasn't shaped like a hand. The hum died. Biscuit stood at the bulkhead, shaking, bloodless, swaying. And over the general channel, from the bay door where he'd been standing the whole time, Kade said: "It's my fault we're found. I have to say it now, while he's bleeding. At Threshold I sent a message to Asset Recovery. I didn't sell anything. I asked what a transfer costs. For Rafe." A breath. "The reply carried a ping. Our transponder's marked. I did it cheap. I did it for free." Nobody said anything. Doc was working on Grady's hand, and Grady was watching her do it, and the calf was dying eight meters away of a wrong song, and that was the moment the captain chose, and I understand it now, though I didn't then: with everything broken at once, she took the piece that was hers. "In the engine room," Voss said. "All of you. Bring the animal's numbers." She told it flat. Standing, palm flat on the housing, not looking at us, the way you'd give a weather report for a storm you caused. "I flew Clearance, out of Palisade. Six years. Escort patterns. You fly a box, a wide box, with noise and light, and the herds move off the noise, off the fence you make of sound. That's all the job was. Move them off the lanes." Pause. "Only there's nowhere to move them *to*. The box closes. Ships behind you do the counting." She gave us numbers. Tonnage. Days. The words *calving grounds*, once, and then never again in the whole telling. "The surveyors wrote objections. Four of them. I read the filings later — they were overruled by my flight logs. My logs were the paper that overruled them." She looked at the housing. "The calf's a Combine revival. Bred back from frozen stock, proof the lanes can be restocked after. Infrastructure. That's the word in her file." Quiet. Grady, gray with his wrist in Doc's grip, said, "The frequency's wrong because it's ours, isn't it. Not hers." And Doc — Doc set down her kit, walked to the bay, and came back with her med-recorder, and I have never loved anyone the way I loved her right then, standing there holding the answer, having had it since the last bugle. "She doesn't want your granddad's song," she said. "She wants her own." She'd recorded the cry. The tearing-silo cry, the hunt-the-note cry. "Grady. One hand or none, you're the only man alive who can make this drive sing. Not folklore. Her voice. Answer her with herself." They did it together, Kade's hands under Grady's direction, no forgiveness said or offered, just two men and a panel. The drive came down to Biscuit's own cry — wrong, then closer, then *it* — and the hull of the *Long Pull* filled with her voice, given back. She stood at the bulkhead a long time, listening to herself. Then she lay down, quiet as weather going, and ate from my hand.

# Chapter 6 — "The Shallows" The cutter found us at day five, which is how we learned the price of a free message. Kade saw the contact first and didn't say anything for a full minute, and I've thought about that minute a lot. He watched it come with his quiet full up to the brim, and then he said, level as a crew report, "Contact, stern quarter, Combine colors, running dark." And then, because he'd already paid for honesty once and found it cheaper than carrying: "That's the ping. That's what I bought us." Voss looked at the plot. "How far to the shallows?" "Two hours at the burn she'll hold," Grady said, and his voice around the words was a lesson in what one hand costs a man who talked to drives. Doc had him taped to the elbow and forbidden the deck, which meant he sat at the panel and ran the old girl with one hand and his voice, and his voice had enough seams in it for both. The shallows. I'll explain them plain, because the serials get it wrong. Out past the fence of the lanes there's country the surveys quit on — debris pastures, rock and wreck and the bones of old Clearances, shoal-water thin vacuum that'll crack a hull or pass you clean depending on the day. Grady had crossed them young. Doc, it turned out, had crossed them colonist, in a boat with no name worth remembering, which she mentioned the way she mentioned her certificate. The cutter was newer and faster and had never learned the country. That was the whole of our chance, and it was the kind of chance a jackrabbit gets. "She'll herd us," Voss said. "That's the training. Pressure and patience. You don't chase stock, you offer them somewhere to be." She said it like a flight manual. It was a flight manual. It was hers. The first hour was running, and running is just fear with a heading. Then the rocks started, and the running became *work* — Kade flat-out on the stick, the old girl rolling between two bergs of dead freighter so close I heard the tether hardware sing, and Voss in the jump seat calling openings like weather: "Gate on the left. Take it. Now the long slide, starboard, mind the spine—" and her voice never rose, and that was the most frightening thing aboard, that she was calm, because it meant she'd been shown this country before, by someone flying it in anger. The cutter sat off our shoulder and waited. Pressure and patience. It didn't need to chase; we were doing the work, exhausting ourselves into its hands, exactly like stock. I understand it now. I watched it happen and didn't. "Captain," Doc said, tight, watching the plot. "It's not herding us *out*." "I know," Voss said. It herded us *in*. Toward a spine of dead steel on the plot's edge — a Clearance tender, one of the ships that did the counting, gone to rust fifty years in the shallows — until the choice was the rocks or the wreck or the cutter's bay, and Voss chose the wreck and killed our burn, and the *Long Pull* settled onto that graveyard spine like a fly on a bone, mag-locked, small. The cutter stood off a klick and lit its transponder, honest as day. **The trap I set.** Here's my part, and I'll tell it true, because nobody else can. The tether rig: if we could lay a line across the cutter's likely approach lane and winch a hulk of rock-wreck into it, we'd buy an hour. Maybe two. It needed a man outside, on the wreck spine, walking line. Grady had one hand. Kade was flying. Doc doesn't do EVA — colony vet, and a story she'll never tell. Which left the man with forty logged hours. "Captain," I said, and my voice came out flat as Third Shift, no drawl left anywhere in it. "I'll take the line out. I've got the hours." Voss looked at me. One long reading, the kind I'd seen her give horses of crews. She knew. Of course she knew — Grady had known inside a week, and engineers talk. She'd known for months and let me fly the lie, and now she weighed it, and me, and the rocks. "Forty hours," she said. Not a question. "Thirty supervised," I said. "Give or take the give." "Rig stays clipped," she said. "You slip, you don't let go of the line. Say it back." "I don't let go of the line." "Then take it out, Mr. Prabhu." I don't remember the walk except in pieces, the way you remember your own wedding or a drowning. The line. The clips, three of them, I counted them like a rosary. The dark on the wreck's far side, soft and total. My lamp making a little room of light that moved. Me singing the ranger theme to myself inside the helmet, getting the words wrong, being honest at last the only way I could manage it. The winch, laid. The hulk, hung in the lane like a judgement. I didn't let go of the line. The trap bought us the hour. The cutter, coming in careful, kissed the hulk, spun off to lick its paint — and recomputed, being patient, and stood off again, and that's when the message came through, text on the plot, courteous as coffee: *Long Pull, this is Orr. Meeting serves better than maneuvering. Captain, alone, on the spine, one hour. The debt is on the table, and other things. — M.O.* He'd bought us with my trap, used my hour to arrange the terms. I sat in the airlock with the helmet in my lap, shaking, and confessed the whole lie to whoever was on the channel — I think it was Grady — word for word, hours and all, and nobody answered, and nobody needed to. That silence, that one, was peace. Voss read the message twice. She took her sidearm from the locker, checked the charge — palm flat on the frame of the locker door — and said: "Kit. You're on the channel the whole time. You listen, and you remember." "Yes, Captain." "And Kit." She was already sealing her suit. "What I say out there — none of it will be news to you. It'll be news to Mr. Orr." She went out the lock into the dark, mag-boots down the spine of a dead Clearance ship, and I sat at the console with my hand on the key, listening.

# Chapter 7 — "The Meeting" Two suits on a dead ship's spine, a klick of graveyard between them and me. I had the scope on them the whole time, which meant I watched most of it and heard all of it, and the two didn't match up, the way they never do. People are smaller than their voices. Even Voss. Even Orr. He came out alone, walking the wreck like a sidewalk, and stopped ten meters off, courteous as coffee. His channel voice was his lounge voice. "Captain. You've made this expensive. My employer's patience is a budget like any other, and you've spent a good deal of it in the shallows." "Noted," Voss said. "The fee stands. The debt stands cleared. Your engineer's hospital bills, if he'd like. And the Corbett Deep indenture — that offer has a longer life than the others, but not indefinite." And that's when she did it. I've had years to decide whether it was a plan or a surrender, and the best I can tell you is it was a payment, which is a different animal from both. She keyed the traffic bands. Open. All ships in the shallows, all relays, the whole fence listening. "This is Ada Voss, captain of the *Long Pull*, formerly Flight Lieutenant, Meridian Clearance Fleet, Palisade wing, service number following." And she read it out. "I flew the box patterns in the Cimarron culls. Six years, ninety-two sorties. The box is a fence made of noise; the herds move off it. You fly them where the surveyors are overruled. Behind you, the counting ships." A pause like a wave taking a breath. "Tonnage figures following. Flight designations. Dates. I have them all; I kept my logs. The lanes were routed through the calving grounds over four survey objections, and my flight logs were the paper that overruled them. That's public record now, on my name. And the Combine has a live tagged animal bred back from the frozen stock — asset 909 — proof of concept for restocking what I helped empty. I found her on a derelict. She's alive. The Meridian Combine is offering me forty thousand to help make her disappear." Static. The whole shallows, quiet. "You'll want corroboration," Voss said, flat as a manual. "The tag telemetry is live on band twelve. And my crew will answer to what they know." Doc keyed first, no warm-up: "Reyes, ship's surgeon. I've treated the animal. She's real and she's young." Grady, seamed and even: "Grady, engineer. Broke my hand on her. She's real." And Kade. A long second, then: "Kade, pilot. Five days ago I sent Asset Recovery a message from Threshold and their reply pinged our transponder. That's how the cutter found us. That's on me, and it's on record now." Me last. I keyed it with the hand that wasn't holding the other one. "Prabhu. Deckhand. I opened the crate. She ate biscuit out of my hand." Then the shot. I say *shot*; it was a lance off the cutter's rail, one burn of it, and it was over before I understood it had begun — some suit on the rail jumping his own command. It took Voss across the ribs, side-on, and she went down to one knee on the spine of the ship she'd helped feed, and stood back up. That fast. She didn't return fire. She stood there leaking into her suit and waited out the silence like weather. "Hold," Orr said, to his rail, in a voice I only heard once, and never wanted to again. Then, to Voss, mild as ever: "You appreciate my position has changed." "Yours hasn't," Voss said. "You're a budget. This is a cost. Let's price it." She went to tight-beam then — locked me out, locked everyone out — and what I have is the scope: the two of them on the spine for twenty minutes, and at the end of it she took a case from her suit's back rack and set it on the steel between them. I knew the case. I'd wondered for two months why the captain had personally pulled the data-core off a derelict hold and never logged it. Her logs. The breeding file. She'd been carrying the whole story on her back since the crate, waiting to see which way it had to be spent. The case went with Orr. Voss came home. She walked the spine alone, mag-boots down, one hand pressed to her ribs, and docked, and let Doc cut her out of the suit, and the burn across her side was ugly and shallow, and Doc said she was lucky, and Voss said, "I was never his target. I was his inventory," and that was all we got out of her that night. Orr's wrap-up came through at 0400, addressed to the ship. I read it before the captain did. I've never decided if that was theft or witness. *Asset 909 is filed unviable — telemetry failure, probable loss, recovery suspended. Fee: withdrawn. The derelict claim transfers to Meridian survey per enclosed. Enclosed also: indenture transfer, R. Kade, Corbett Deep, released to self. You will appreciate, Captain, that your statement is now on record with me personally, and that the lanes are where they are. Surveys continue. There's always another survey. It has been a pleasure doing ordinary business. — M.O.* Kade read it at breakfast with the whole crew watching him not react. He read it twice, the way Voss read things, and he looked down the table at her, bandaged into her chair, drinking her coffee cold, and he said her name — "Captain" — and couldn't finish, and she said, "Eat your breakfast, Mr. Kade. We've got a heading." We did. One heading left on the boat, and everybody knew it by morning without a word of a meeting. The Cimarron Drift. Kit's log, that night, reads: *She paid with the secret. He paid with the truth. Doc paid with her can't. I still had the lie in my pocket, and it weighed nothing, and I threw it away at the airlock door.* The next line is: *Tomorrow we sing her home.*

# Chapter 8 — "The Drift" The Cimarron Drift is a slow country. I'll say it plain because there's no fancy way: dust and dark, and instruments that read wrong, or read something else. Doc said her colony scopes did that near the old migration routes, and she didn't say anything after that, and we didn't ask. We came in on a low burn, singing. Grady's drive, detuned to Biscuit's own voice, had been running for six days, and the whole hull carried it the way a church carries a bell. Grady ran the panel with his one hand and Kade's two, and nobody called it folklore anymore. Biscuit stood at the bay door for the last day and a half, listening to herself come back. We dropped her shields at 0600, station time, which means nothing out there, and held the big doors open on the Drift. She wouldn't go. That's the part none of the plan covered. She stood at the sill with the dark in front of her and her own voice rolling out into it, and she backed up. Came to me. Put her drum of a head against my chest, the way she did for biscuit, and I stood there with my hands on her and understood what I'd built out of kindness: I'd made the ship her herd. Me and the hull and the song — that was the whole country she knew, and I'd taught it to her, and I was nineteen, and I'd done it because it answered my boot-steps too. Everyone was on the channel. Nobody said anything for a long time. Then Doc, quiet, not to me exactly: "Imprinting's not love. It's geography. She thinks her world is three meters tall and smells like straw." "It's me," I said. "She won't leave me." "No," Doc said. "She won't leave *near* you. As long as you're at the sill, the sill is home." So it was mine to do. I want that known and I want it over with at the same time. I keyed the channel and said, "Captain. Kill the song." A pause. "Confirmed, Mr. Prabhu?" "Confirmed. Kill it." The drive came up off her voice into its ordinary whine, and the hull went quiet for the first time in six days, and the quiet went through the calf like a hook — and I stepped back from the sill and hit the doors, and I did not watch. I heard her. I heard her bugle, that silo-tearing cry, once, and something that might have been her turning, and then the dark had her or she had it, and the doors sealed on the bay, and I stood with my forehead on the panel like a man in a serial, except serials cut away, and there wasn't anywhere to cut away to. "She's clear," Kade said, off the scope. "She's . . . moving well." We held station for six hours. I'll tell you the truth of it: we held because nobody would say *leave* and nobody would say *stay*, so we stayed, which is what ships do instead of praying. The scope read nothing. Nothing at nine kilcks, nothing at ninety, nothing at nine hundred, and the dust moved like dust, and Doc watched her instruments and said nothing in a new way, and Grady coughed and said, "Well," which from Grady was a sermon. Voss, bandaged, drank her coffee cold in the command seat, and at hour six she said, "Fuel's a fence like any other. We're going home," and she put the heading in herself, and nobody argued, and that was the hardest order of the voyage and the easiest, both at once. The turn was half-made when the scope ticked. One contact. Far off, at the edge of the dust, up-sun of nothing. It ticked twice and held mass, and Kade said, "Rock," and Doc said, "Rocks don't hold mass off a burn like that," and Kade said, "Rock, and I'm not flying out to check," and that was all. Nobody confirmed anything. Nobody named it. It held on the scope for eleven minutes and then the dust had it, or it had the dust, and we were turned for the lanes with the Drift going quiet behind us like a church after the bells. Voss took her medal out at the viewport. I only saw it because I was watching her, everyone was, a little. Clearance service bar, old style, worth nothing, heavier than anything on the boat. She stood with it in her palm a long while, longer than a man takes to decide anything, and then she closed her fingers and put it back in her pocket, and went and sat down, and nobody said anything, and that was right. Some accounts you pay. Some you carry. So: home. Deeper in debt than we set out — the derelict claim went with Orr, and thirty-three thousand still has my name on part of it, and the *some* keeps its teeth. Grady's hand healed stiff, and he signs his welds left-handed now, a different G, shakier, and he says the drive likes it better, and the drive seems to. Kade got a letter at the first relay, forwarded twice, from Corbett Deep. He read it alone and then he left it on the galley table face-up, which from Kade was a speech, and it's Rafe's hand, and it says he's coming to Threshold when his ship's paid, and there's a drawing on it of a bird, or maybe a wing. And me. I'm in the bay a lot. It smells like animal — straw and warm hide — and I haven't cleaned it up, and Doc hasn't told me to, which from Doc is permission. The foil tag is in my pocket, come off her flank the last morning when I was grooming her, 9-0-9, stopped blinking now, and I keep it the way Voss keeps the medal, I suppose, though I'm not done understanding that. Nights, running the lanes home, the hull ticks and settles the way hulls do. And sometimes — third watch, mostly, when it's just me — there's a note under everything, low, like far-off thunder or weather over a range, like something big and soft finding a new side to lie on. It's the drive. It's almost certainly the drive. I listen anyway.

There are still moments of Kit's characteristic reach ("the way a church carries a bell," "the quiet went through the calf like a hook") but they're fewer, more controlled, and they land rather than strain. The arc from ornate to plain is one of the plan's central structural promises, and it's kept. **Character Consistency** Every character behaves in ways consistent with their profiles. Voss's "Fuel's a fence like any other" is exactly her idiom — ranch-and-flight, clipped declarative. Her standing with the medal, deciding too long, and pocketing it rather than dropping it is precisely what the plan specified and what her character demands: she doesn't get to close the account. Doc's "Imprinting's not love. It's geography" is her empiricist voice at its best — unsentimental, technically precise, and yet the most emotionally useful thing said in the scene. Grady's "Well" as a sermon is a lovely compression. Kade's letter left face-up on the galley table "which from Kade was a speech" is exactly right for a character defined by silence. Kit's self-awareness about what he built — "I'd made the ship her herd" — is the honest reckoning the plan promised. **The Calf's Release** The plan specified that the release only works when Kit is cruel enough to have the singing stopped, and that he does not watch. The execution is faithful and emotionally precise. "I did not watch. I heard her. I heard her bugle, that silo-tearing cry, once" — this is restrained and effective. The detail of standing with his forehead on the panel "like a man in a serial, except serials cut away, and there wasn't anywhere to cut away to" is one of the chapter's best moments: it's Kit's self-awareness about his own performance, the costume finally acknowledged as costume, and it's earned. **The Ambiguous Contact** The plan called for one ambiguous scope tick, rock-or-animal, unconfirmed. The execution handles this well. The exchange between Kade and Doc ("Rock" / "Rocks don't hold mass off a burn like that" / "Rock, and I'm not flying out to check") is the chapter's best dialogue — it's funny, it's in character, it refuses to resolve, and it's honest about the refusal. The story doesn't cheat toward confirmation or denial. **The Medal** The plan specified Voss takes out the medal, stands too long, and puts it back. The execution is faithful. "Longer than a man takes to decide anything" is slightly off — "a man" is a bit generic for this voice — but the beat works. "Some accounts you pay. Some you carry" is Kit's narration finding its plainest register, and it's earned. **Dialogue** The dialogue is sparse and functional throughout. "Confirmed, Mr. Prabhu?" — Voss using Kit's real name at the moment of the hardest order — is exactly what the character profile promised ("Voss calls him 'Mr. Prabhu' exactly once in the story — at the doors — and it lands like a medal"). This is a case where the plan's promise is fully redeemed in execution. **Weaknesses** A few moments strain slightly. "The whole hull carried it the way a church carries a bell" is a fine image but "church" appears twice in the chapter (also "like a church after the bells" at the end), which dilutes both uses. The closing lines — "low, like far-off thunder or weather over a range, like something big and soft finding a new side to lie on" — are the chapter's most ornate passage, and while the plan called for the voice to be nearly plain, this is a deliberate exception for the final beat. It mostly works, but "something big and soft finding a new side to lie on" is slightly precious. The "It's the drive. It's almost certainly the drive. / I listen anyway." ending is effective but not quite surprising — it's the expected ambiguous close, executed well rather than transcendently. The Rafe letter detail (the drawing of "a bird, or maybe a wing") is a nice touch that honors the plan's promise about Kade learning of the mercy. The "shakier G" for Grady's left-handed welds is specific and good. **Overall** This is a chapter that honors its plan with fidelity and executes it with genuine craft. The emotional beats are earned rather than announced. The characters are consistent. The ambiguity is maintained without cheating. The voice arc is completed. The weaknesses are minor — a repeated image, one slightly precious phrase at the close. This is strong literary fiction in the space western mode, and it delivers on the considerable promises of the planning document. Judge Response (First Entry):
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally accomplished piece of space western fiction that demonstrates genuine literary craft. Let me examine it carefully across all dimensions. **Voice and Style** The narrator's voice is the piece's greatest achievement. The first-person retrospective narration from "Kit" Prabhu is consistent, distinctive, and earned throughout all eight chapters. The voice has a specific texture — a station kid performing cowboy romanticism, aware of his own performance, gradually stripped of it. Lines like "I was nineteen and costumed" and "I was nineteen and flush with exactly one tooled-leather belt and a head full of borrowed sayings" establish this self-awareness immediately and it pays dividends throughout. The voice never breaks character, never becomes generic, and the retrospective framing ("I'd learn," "I'd say now") is used with discipline rather than as a crutch. **Metaphor and Poetry** The metaphors are largely earned and specific. "The black does not forgive a fool" functions as a thematic spine. "Owing nothing" doing something to a nineteen-year-old's chest. The drive singing. The fence as gate. These are not decorative — they're structural. The western idiom is applied consistently: "weather" for trouble, "fence" for law, "stock" for cargo. This isn't forced; it's the world's actual vocabulary. Some metaphors are genuinely striking: "a sound like weight shifting in a hayloft," "a tongue like warm rope," "the quiet of him had a weight I mistook, then, for peace." These land because they're grounded in the narrator's specific sensibility. Occasionally the prose reaches slightly too hard — "the black opened up like a range nobody had ever lied to" is a bit strained — but these instances are rare and minor. **Character** The ensemble is well-differentiated. Voss is the most complex: her Clearance past, her protocol knowledge, her palm-flat-on-the-frame habit, her cold coffee, her medal — all accumulate into a portrait of guilt managed through competence. Doc is rendered through her diagnostic manner applied to everything, including people. Grady's relationship with machinery as moral relationship is consistent and touching. Kade's silence-as-fullness is handled with restraint; his betrayal and its consequences are neither melodramatized nor minimized. The narrator himself is the most interesting character — his self-awareness about his own romanticism, his lie about EVA hours, his imprinting on Biscuit mirroring Biscuit's imprinting on him. The parallel is explicit but not overworked. **Plot and Structure** The plot is coherent and well-constructed. The crate → livestock → Combine → debt → Orr → shallows → confession → release structure has genuine momentum. Each chapter advances both plot and character. The Kade betrayal is set up carefully (his brother mentioned obliquely, his face doing "the thing about the mine") and paid off without melodrama. Voss's confession on the open channel is the emotional climax and it's earned by everything preceding it. The Orr resolution is slightly convenient — he accepts the data-core and releases Kade's brother, which is a lot of goodwill from a corporate antagonist — but the story acknowledges this is a transaction, not a moral victory, which saves it. **Pacing** Eight chapters move efficiently. No chapter feels padded. The animal's illness and the hum sequence in Chapter 5 is the most tense and best-paced section. The final chapter's release of Biscuit is handled with appropriate restraint — the narrator doesn't watch, we get the sound, then the scope reading, then the ambiguous contact at the edge of the dust. **Dialogue** Dialogue is sparse and functional, which suits the story. When characters speak, it's in character. "Well, that's that, then" from Grady with a broken wrist is perfect. Orr's "It's the whole of my job" as an honest answer being the worst thing said all night is genuinely chilling. The crew's radio check-in during Voss's broadcast is economical and moving. **Weaknesses** The piece is not without flaws. The Orr resolution, as noted, is somewhat convenient. The "contact at the edge of the dust" ending is a well-worn ambiguous-hope device, though it's executed with enough restraint to avoid feeling cheap. The story occasionally tells us how to feel about a moment rather than trusting the moment itself — "and that was the hardest order of the voyage and the easiest, both at once" is the narrator editorializing where the scene could speak. The "I was nineteen and costumed" refrain, while effective, is used perhaps once too often. The Chinese character that appears in Chapter 1 ("字母alphabetized") is clearly an artifact of a generation error and breaks immersion briefly. **Overall** This is a genuinely literary piece of genre fiction. It has a consistent, distinctive voice; a coherent and emotionally resonant plot; well-differentiated characters whose actions are believable; and a thematic coherence (debt, guilt, imprinting, what you carry) that elevates it above competent genre work. The space western genre fusion is handled with intelligence — the western idiom is not decorative but structural. The piece earns its emotional moments. # Intention **Core conceit.** I'm taking the inverted reading of the prompt: the narrator, **Mara**, is the *possessed* one, and "her" is the entity sharing her body. The opening line — *"I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping."* — is literal and interior. When the entity surfaces at night, it believes the host consciousness goes dormant. Mara has learned to fake that dormancy. The entity sometimes turns its attention inward — staring at her through their shared eyes, or into the bedroom mirror where Mara is trapped behind the glass — studying the last part of her it hasn't been able to open. The mirror becomes the membrane between them. **Plot spine.** The entity entered Mara six months ago at her mother's hospice bedside, when her guard was down — she was sleeping then, too. It doesn't scream or levitate; it's better at being Mara than Mara was. It mines her memories, feeds on being loved, and gives her husband **Daniel** things Mara couldn't give him after her mother died — including, devastatingly, her mother's stories and voice. The possessive horror is emotional: Daniel is happier with the intruder. Inside, Mara discovers the mind-house with its corridor of former hosts, most worn to husks, and **Iris**, the last one, still lucid enough to teach her the rules: the entity steals sleep, steals love, steals hours — but cannot take what is freely given. Mara's failed confession (the entity has pre-seeded a "grief dissociation" diagnosis, so the truth arrives sounding like a symptom) becomes the midpoint reversal. Her victory comes not through exorcism but through the one thing the entity can't digest: she opens her own sealed grief-room — the hospice room she's hidden from herself — and *sees* the entity's true shape, a small, starved thing from a place where no one ever came. Acknowledgment, offered freely, wounds it. Made small, it sleeps more. Mara takes the nights. **Structure.** Palindromic: the final chapter inverts the opening line — now it is Mara who surfaces at night while the entity sleeps, and Daniel who lies awake pretending not to notice. The ending is a truce, not a cure: three people in a two-person marriage, all pretending to sleep. Horror of coexistence rather than conquest. **Voice and style.** First person, present tense, close and restrained. Two registers in deliberate contrast: hyper-real domestic detail (coffee, the crossword, Daniel's reading glasses) against a drifting, dreamlike interior geography (rooms, corridors, soft walls). Short declaratives for surveillance scenes; longer sentences inside the mind-house. **Aims.** Quiet dread over shock. An entity whose patience and tenderness are the threat. Motif discipline: sleep and pretending, watching, doors, mirrors, 3 a.m., the wedding ring. **Avoids.** No gore, no Latin, no priests, no pea-soup clichés, no "the narrator was dead all along" twist, no cartoonish malevolence. The entity never gets a name. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — The Watching (~1000w).** Opens verbatim with the prompt line. 3 a.m.; the entity surfaces, believing Mara dormant; Mara feigns inner sleep and observes. Establish the ritual, the bedroom mirror, sleeping Daniel, minimal hints of the inner house. Hook: tonight the entity studies Daniel's face and whispers, "Soon." **Ch. 2 — How She Came In (~1000w).** Flashback: the hospice, Mara's exhaustion, her mother's death, the first lost hour — something leaned in while she slept at the bedside. Establish mechanics: lost time, the window behind the eyes, the entity outperforming her at being Mara (coffee order, laughing at Daniel's jokes). Hook: it now takes whole days. **Ch. 3 — The Rooms (~1000w).** Interior geography deepens: Mara explores the mind-house, finds the corridor of worn-out former hosts, meets Iris — the last one, half-spent, still lucid. Rules learned: it must sleep; it feeds on being loved; despair thins the host; thinned hosts become rooms. Hook: "You're already thinner than I was at the end." **Ch. 4 — What It Gives Him (~1000w).** The marriage stakes. The entity mines Mara's mother's letters and tells a story only her mother knew; Daniel weeps with happiness. Mara's jealousy curdles into self-loathing — he's better off. Hook: the entity speaks to Mara directly through the morning mirror: "You could rest. She did." **Ch. 5 — The Signal (~1000w).** Mara's offense: she's found the seam — a few minutes of the body at dawn when the entity sleeps. She smuggles out signals (a wrong pet name, "HELP" in the crossword margin). Daniel begins testing, then whispers in the dark, "Where is my wife?" The entity answers perfectly — and Daniel lets himself be convinced. Hook: he *wants* to be. **Ch. 6 — The Confession (~1000w).** Midpoint reversal. Mara gambles everything on a Sunday-dawn takeover, twenty minutes of her own mouth, and tells Daniel everything. The entity wakes mid-scene and lets him see the switch — then reframes it: "grief dissociation," pills already in the cabinet, a therapist already briefed. It planned this; failed attempts thin her faster. Hook: medication fog; the inner walls going soft. **Ch. 7 — The Locked Room (~1000w).** Despair, then Iris's last gift: it cannot take what is freely given. Mara opens the one door she's kept sealed even from herself — the hospice room, her unmet grief — and, strengthened, enters the entity's locked room: a gray nursery of nothing, a place where no one ever came. She sees it truly and says so. The acknowledgment wounds it; it becomes small. Hook: small things sleep. **Ch. 8 — The Nights (~1000w).** The reversal. The wounded entity sleeps more; Mara holds the night shift, guarding the body, watching Daniel — who is awake, eyes shut, pretending, because he saw the switch in chapter six and chose a story that let him stay. Closing lines mirror the opening: she catches him staring; she lets him think she hasn't noticed; everyone in this house pretends to sleep. Truce, not cure.

# How a Human Might Approach This Piece A human writer who chose this prompt would almost certainly be writing *from* something rather than *about* something. The possession-as-grief conceit isn't a clever inversion to them — it's autobiography. Anyone who has lost a parent knows that grief genuinely dissociates you: you watch yourself perform at the funeral, laugh at the wrong joke, feel like a tenant in your own life for a year. The human's insight would be that the metaphor is barely a metaphor. The horror of the story is that Mara cannot prove the entity exists, because bereavement already feels exactly like this. A human would exploit that seam — keeping the metaphysics unfalsifiable for as long as possible, maybe forever — whereas a plan tends to literalize: the mind-house is real, it has rooms, there are rules. Process-wise, a human would write chapter one four or five times and find Mara's voice by ear. The ending would be a fog. They'd know the *dread* but not the beats. They'd let the story bend mid-draft — probably discovering halfway through that the most interesting character is Daniel, or the mother, and rebalancing. They'd steal consciously: Levin's *Rosemary's Baby* for the husband's complicity, Shirley Jackson for the house-as-self, maybe *Get Out* for the trapped-behind-your-own-eyes image (though a good writer would notice that *Get Out* is an escape fantasy and deliberately invert it — this is a tenancy, not an abduction). They'd also know when to be boring, because quiet horror lives in dead time: the accumulation of uneventful nights is what makes the eventful one land. And they'd be willing to be ugly. Real jealousy over a spouse's affection is petty and specific — it's about who loads the dishwasher correctly, who remembers the in-joke, who is better in bed — not a clean arc labeled "jealousy curdles into self-loathing." Humans let narrators be mean, ashamed, funny by accident, and bored. An eight-thousand-word captivity narrative with no humor in it anywhere isn't scary; it's airless. # Telltale LLM Approaches — and Why They'd Hurt This Piece **Thesis-first writing.** The model writes to demonstrate a concept, so every scene illustrates the theme and the final chapter announces it. In this piece, the danger is that "three people in a two-person marriage" stays a *line about* the ending rather than an ending. Humans plan events and discover emotions; plans like this one plan emotions and schedule discoveries. **Visible architecture.** Palindromic structure, a hook per chapter, "motif discipline" — readers feel the scaffolding. Serialized stings at every chapter break give the rhythm of a TV pitch, not quiet horror, which wants chapters that end flat, or wrong, or on nothing. **Aphoristic dialogue.** "Soon." "You could rest. She did." "Small things sleep." These are quotable, which is the problem. Real intrusions are banal, repetitive, or slightly off. A whisper of "Soon" is a genre cliché even before the LLM tell. **The oracle character.** Iris delivering rules in chapter three is a tutorial in a horror story's clothing. And "rules" themselves — must sleep, feeds on love, cannot take what is freely given — are a magic system. Note that the last rule is a cheat code planted in chapter three to fire in chapter seven. Humans muddle mechanics or make them unreliable. **The empathy redemption.** Turning the entity into "a small, starved thing from a place where no one ever came" that is wounded by acknowledgment is the therapy resolution: *the real exorcism was attachment all along.* This is the plan's single most LLM-shaped idea. **Safety.** The plan keeps the entity's superiority to stories and laughter. Possession horror that won't touch the body — sex, appetite, handwriting, which side of the bed — is toothless, because bodily violation is the genre's core dread. **Emotion labeled, not dramatized.** Category detail instead of lived detail ("coffee, the crossword, reading glasses"). Monotone "restraint." No

# Intention **Core conceit.** Mara is the possessed one; "her" in the prompt line is the entity, which surfaces at night believing its host is dormant. Mara has learned to feign inner sleep and watch. I'm keeping the possession-as-grief conceit but committing to its real implication: the story must stay *unfalsifiable*. For most of its length, everything Mara reports — lost hours, the window behind her eyes, the thing in the mirror — must also be a textbook description of traumatic grief. Mara herself can't be sure. The reader shouldn't be either, until the story decides, and even then it should decide reluctantly, through evidence Mara can't explain away (a physical object she couldn't have known about, her own handwriting on a letter she never wrote) rather than through the entity performing for us. No mind-house with doors and corridors. The interior is rendered as felt sensation and uncertain perception — the behind-the-eyes image from *Get Out*, kept, but as Mara's private metaphor for her own dissociation, never confirmed as real estate. **The entity.** Unnamed, unexplained, and never pitiable. Its origin is not revealed; there is no gray nursery and no wounded inner child. What we get instead is behavior: it is *better at being Mara than Mara is*, and its superiority is specific and bodily. It makes love to Daniel with more ease than Mara has since the hospice. It keeps the house cleaner. It laughs at his jokes at the right speed. Its horror is competence and tenderness, and — increasingly — its appetite for the domestic trivia of her life. Bodily wrongness accumulates in small physical facts: Mara is left-handed and the handwriting on the grocery list isn't; her coffee order changed; a bruise she doesn't remember; her wedding ring worn on the wrong hand one morning. The entity speaks rarely, and when it does it is banal — it asks Daniel ordinary questions with faintly wrong phrasing — never aphoristic. **Daniel.** He is the story's second horror. He notices — a wrong pet name, a story told with the ending changed — and he tests her the way you test a failing appliance, hoping it passes. When he glimpses the truth he retreats from it, not because he's weak, but because he lost his mother-in-law too, because the thing in his bed is kind to him, and because grief already taught him to live with an absent person. His complicity is quiet and self-interested and entirely human. He is not a villain and not a dupe; he is someone choosing the better wife. **Plot spine, revised.** The entity came in during the six months Mara slept at her mother's hospice bedside — or that's Mara's construction after the fact; she can't locate the moment, which torments her. Ch. 1–2: the watching ritual and the history of lost time, with the first hard-to-dismiss evidence. Ch. 3–4: Mara's surveillance deepens; the entity's performance of her life exceeds her own; the marriage stakes turn physical and petty and specific (jealousy about sex, about her mother's stories retold wrong-and-better). No oracle figure — Mara learns any "rules" empirically and unreliably, mostly through the entity's own slips, and she's wrong at least once in ways that cost her. Ch. 5–6: Mara's offense — the dawn minutes, the signals, the gamble of a full confession — fails because the entity (or the world; the ambiguity holds) has pre-framed her: grief dissociation, a therapist's card, pills. Daniel chooses the diagnosis. This is the midpoint reversal: the horror is not that no one believes her, it's that belief was available and he declined it. Ch. 7: despair; the medication makes everything foggy and *also possibly genuinely helps*, so even Mara's resistance becomes ambiguous. What saves her is not empathy and not a magic rule — it is spite, love, and one small, cruel, human advantage she's noticed: the entity has never once gotten one thing right. It has her mother's stories slightly wrong — the endings are always a little too neat, a little too consoling — because the entity can mine memory but can't *know* what it's like to have been loved badly and well by a difficult woman. Mara weaponizes this: she makes herself harder to play. She becomes difficult, cold, unkind to Daniel during her stolen minutes — deliberately poisoning the performance — so that the entity must either play a bitch (losing Daniel's love, its food) or break character. It costs Mara the thing she wants most, Daniel's belief, and she does it anyway. Ch. 8: the truce. The entity sleeps more — or the medication works — and Mara holds the nights. She watches Daniel pretending to sleep, knowing she'll never ask and he'll never say. The final line mirrors the opening: *He caught her staring at him again. He thought she'd been sleeping.* No cure, no confession, no bow: two people and whatever else, all pretending to sleep. **Voice and style.** First person, present tense, close, dry, occasionally funny in a bitter register — Mara is allowed pettiness, boredom, shame, and gallows humor; monotone restraint is banned. Domestic detail must be *lived* (the specific crossword clue she was stuck on; Daniel's side of the bed always colder; her mother's habit of licking her thumb before turning pages) rather than set-dressing. Sentences: short and flat for surveillance; looser and more digressive when Mara drifts into memory. Endings of chapters: mostly flat, deflating, or on a wrong note — at most two chapter-break hooks across the whole piece, and neither may be a one-word whisper. The mirror stays as a recurring object but never becomes a portal or a literal membrane; it's where Mara checks whose eyes she has today. **Aims.** Unfalsifiable dread held as long as possible; a marriage rendered with real pettiness and real tenderness; an entity whose menace is precision; a middle-aged woman's fury at being outperformed at her own life; an ending that resolves the *situation* without resolving the *horror*. **Avoids.** No magic system, no oracle, no origin story, no redemption of the entity, no exorcism, no twist ending, no gore, no priests, no Latin, no aphoristic dialogue, no one-word chapter hooks, no mind-house geography, no scenes whose purpose is to illustrate the theme. No safety around the body: sex, appetite, handwriting, bruises are all in bounds. Above all: no moment where the story explains itself to the reader. # Chapter Planning **Ch. 1 — The Watching (~1000w).** Opens with the prompt line, verbatim, then immediately destabilizes it: Mara describes the staring, then admits she may be describing a dream, then admits she's been telling herself that for weeks. 3 a.m. ritual established through concrete detail. First small wrongness: her own hand on the quilt isn't hers. Daniel asleep, harmless. End flat: morning comes; nothing is resolved; the coffee tastes like someone else made it. **Ch. 2 — The Hospice (~1000w).** Mara's construction of the beginning: six months of sleeping in a vinyl recliner at her mother's bedside, the exhaustion, the first lost hour (nurse said she'd been talking all night; Mara has no memory). Post-death months: the dissociation of grief doing most of the entity's work for it. First evidence she can't dismiss — a grocery list in handwriting almost but not quite hers. End on doubt: she keeps the list in a drawer like a held breath. **Ch. 3 — The Better Wife (~1000w).** The performance survey. The entity laughs at Daniel's jokes with better timing; the house is cleaner; Mara watches her own hands make a meal she'd have ruined. The turn to the body: she and Daniel haven't been like this since before the hospice, and he's gentler with her than he's been in a year — and she is jealous of herself. She catalogs physical evidence: the bruise, the ring on the wrong hand, the changed coffee order. End flat and mean: she makes a note to hate it more efficiently. **Ch. 4 — Her Mother's Stories (~1000w).** The entity tells Daniel one of her mother's stories at dinner — and Mara, watching from behind her own eyes, hears the ending wrong. Cleaner. Consoling. Her mother never told it that way; her mother told it mean and funny. Daniel cries with happiness. Mara's realization that the thing mines memory but not *knowledge* — it doesn't know what it was like to be loved by that particular difficult woman. She doesn't yet see the weapon in this; it's just grief and fury. End: she tries to say the true ending out loud during a stolen dawn minute and can't reach her own mouth. **Ch. 5 — The Dawn Minutes (~1000w).** Mara's empirical research: the seam of grogginess at dawn, minutes only, unreliable. Her signals: a wrong pet name (Daniel's college nickname for her, never used in company), a crossword message, a bruise she gives herself on purpose. Daniel tests — asks a question only Mara can answer — and the entity, she fears, answered right. Or Daniel never understood the test. Her first costly mistake: she assumes a rule (dawn is safe) and it isn't; she surfaces mid-morning, in front of Daniel, mid-sentence, and the sentence was wrong. End on Daniel's face, not on a sting: he is not confused; he is *tired*. **Ch. 6 — The Confession (~1000w).** The gamble: she spends weeks hoarding strength for one full takeover and tells Daniel everything — the hospice, the watching, the handwriting. The speech is not eloquent; it's rushed, repetitive, half-apology. Daniel listens. And then — the reversal — he asks the questions a concerned husband asks a sick wife, and there's a therapist's card already in the junk drawer, and the pills are already in the cabinet, and Mara realizes she cannot tell whether the entity arranged this or the world simply has a better explanation. Daniel says the kindest possible thing: "Let me take care of you." End flat: she takes the pill. **Ch. 7 — The Poison (~1000w).** Medicated fog: the watching gets harder, the evidence softer — and her mood, infuriatingly, better. This is the lowest point: the pills might be working; she might be ill; the entity might be the medication talking. What pulls her out is small and spiteful: the entity tells her mother's story again, wrong again — and Mara decides that if she can't have her life back she can make the life *uninhabitable*. In her stolen minutes she's cold to Daniel, needlessly cruel about small things, so the entity must either play a wife no one loves or break character against the record. It costs her everything she still wanted from him. The chapter ends ugly, on a small domestic cruelty and Daniel quietly deciding to stop asking questions of her entirely. **Ch. 8 — The Nights (~1000w).** Time has passed. The entity sleeps more, or the dose was raised; Mara holds the night shift and no longer knows which of them won. The house is quieter, sadder, functional. The final scene: 3 a.m., Mara awake in the body, watching Daniel — who is awake too, eyes shut, breathing performed. She knows he saw the switch, months ago; she knows he chose the story that let him stay; she has decided this is a kind of love anyway, or the closest thing available to either of them now. Closing movement inverts the opening line: *He caught her staring at him again. He thought she'd been sleeping.* Neither of them moves. The house goes on pretending.

Twenty-two years as a liability claims adjuster at a mid-sized insurer — her whole working life has been listening to people describe the worst day of their lives and deciding what their grief is worth. She was good at it, and it's the only thing she's ever been smug about: she can find the seam in a false story by page three. This is both her gift and the story's central irony — the one false story she can't get anyone to adjudicate is her own. She's been on leave since Ruth died in March; the leave quietly expired into not going back. She grew up managing a difficult mother, which is where the vigilance comes from: she learned to read a room before she learned to read books. The possession picked a host who was already trained to watch — and that training is the only reason she notices. **Idiosyncrasies & flaws.** Does the crossword in pen and never finishes it (the entity finishes them; correct, in pen; she has to live with the fact that it could be done). Counts things when frightened — stairs, seconds. Timed the staring once: four minutes. Eats her toast burnt on purpose, a preference Ruth called a cry for help. Says "fine" when it isn't, a direct inheritance. Keeps a mental ledger of Daniel's small failures — the anniversary he was forty minutes late for in 2016, every "I'll handle the taxes" — and knows the ledger is unfair and keeps it anyway. She was already a hard wife before the hospice: the marriage had cooled into logistics, and there's a buried fault line — a pregnancy at thirty-nine that ended at eleven weeks, which they have never once discussed. Part of her shame is that the entity didn't steal a good marriage. It renovated a failing one, and she knows it. She irons pillowcases. She apologizes for things that aren't her fault to end conversations faster. **Physicality.** Medium build; put on vending-machine weight during the hospice months and has watched, secondhand, as the entity walked it off — her clothes fitting better is one of the evidences she hates most. Glasses she pushes up with her middle knuckle. A chin scar from a bicycle at nine. Left-handed. Dark hair going gray at the temples. Her tell, when thinking, is twisting her wedding ring — and the thing's hands are still, always still, which she notices the way you notice a clock that's stopped. **Motives & allegiances.** From inside her own head: she wants her life back, but the honest version is she wants *the theft acknowledged* — someone to say *this happened to you*. She loves Daniel with the exhausted specificity of long marriage and is furiously jealous of her own body's success with him. She is loyal to the dead — to Ruth's actual, mean, funny self — and that loyalty is ultimately the weapon: she'd rather poison her own marriage than let the thing keep improving the story. Her lowest motive is spite and her highest is grief and she can't always tell them apart, and shouldn't. **Voice.** > "The nurse said she went at 4:12 in the morning. I'd like to tell you I was holding her hand. I've known for twenty-five years and declined to honor it, and now I get to watch it honored every morning at 7:10." > "I spent two decades deciding which griefs were real for a living. Grew up with a father who drank quietly and a mother who asked no questions, and learned early that inquiry makes things worse — so his kindness, which is real, is also his armor. I caught her staring at me again. She thought I'd been sleeping. She stares out through my eyes at 3 a.m., mostly at Daniel, sometimes at the ceiling, once — this took some composure — at the smoke detector, long enough that I started counting seconds to keep from screaming. Four hundred and eleven. I count when I'm frightened. It's a habit from childhood, from standing in doorways reading my mother's moods, and it turns out four hundred and eleven seconds is seven minutes short of what a person can bear of watching her own eyes look at things. I want to be careful here, because I've told myself other stories about the staring. For a while I told myself it was a dream — that I dreamed the watching from inside the dream of sleeping, which is the kind of thing you can believe at 3 a.m. and cannot defend at noon. I told myself it was grief, which is the explanation my whole life has politely queued up for me, standing there like a relative at the door with a casserole. My mother died in March. I slept six months in a vinyl recliner at her bedside, and if you want to know what that does to a person's interior weather, I can tell you it doesn't leave a lot of rooms furnished. So yes. Fine. Grief. I know how this sounds. I've spent twenty-two years listening to people describe the worst day of their lives and deciding what their suffering is worth, and I know exactly what I'd write in the margin of a claim like mine. I know what I'd write in the margin of me. But then it's 3 a.m. again, and she surfaces, and I feel the surfacing — a settling, like a big house going quiet when the owners come home — and I go flat and still inside, the way I've learned, and I pretend. She thinks I sleep when she's out. That's the arrangement as she understands it: her shift is the night, mine is the day, and never the twain. Except I've learned to be absent the way I learned to be present for my mother — a stillness that looks like vacancy. It took weeks. The first time I tried it, she noticed something, cocked my head like a bird, and I felt her attention turn inward, and I folded myself down to almost nothing and thought burnt toast, burnt toast, burnt toast, and it passed. Now I can hold it for hours. It's the worst thing I do all day, every night, and I've gotten good at it, and I hate that I've gotten good at it. Here is what she does, in order. The body breathes three slow breaths, deeper than I breathe, breaths that use the whole chest — she has better posture than I do, which of all the indignities ranks surprisingly high. Then the eyes open. Mine open. Then she checks Daniel. Not anxiously. The way a nurse checks a monitor that has never once alarmed. Then she looks at whatever she looks at, and her looking has a weight to it, an appetite, and the nearest I can come to describing it is how my mother looked at a menu when she'd already decided but wanted to want something else. And then sometimes — this is the part I've only admitted to myself recently — she looks for me. In the mirror over the dresser, which I can see from where the body lies. She looks into the mirror and through it, the way you look at a dark window at dusk, testing whether the glass goes both ways. She has never found me. Or she has, and she's patient. My mother could sit on a grievance for a decade and call it patience, so I know the difference is invisible from the outside. Daniel sleeps on his left, back to the middle, a hill under the quilt. He snores on his back, a soft regular motor, and she has fixed that somehow — the body sleeps on its side now — and I know that's on the list titled Things It Fixed, right under the dishes and the bill paying and the coffee. Twenty-five years and I made his coffee the way I thought it should be made, which is to say correctly, which is to say not the way he likes it. He likes it bitter and over-extracted, likes it objectively wrong, and I declined to honor that for a quarter century on principle. At 7:10 every morning now I hear him come down and make pleased sounds about the smell, and it takes everything I have not to be sick inside my own skull. Tonight she looked at Daniel a long time. Then my right hand came out from under the quilt — and I want to be exact about this, because this is where the story either holds or doesn't — my right hand, the one I don't write with, came out and lay flat on the quilt, palm down, and she looked at it like it belonged to someone she was meeting. She turned it over. She looked at the wedding ring. She took the ring off, quietly, the way you'd remove a splinter from a sleeping child, and held it up to the streetlight coming through the blinds, and turned it, and put it back on the wrong hand. Then she slept. Or the body did. It's her sleeping I can't verify. Mine I can fake. In the morning Daniel gets up and showers and hums, and the body gets up too, and I go along the way you go along, and at breakfast he notices the ring, because he notices almost nothing and even he caught that, and the body laughs — my laugh, but landing cleaner, on the beat — and says, *slept funny, must have done it in my sleep.* And he says huh, and eats his toast, and the moment is over, and that's the thing about my life now: the moments are always over. They end before I can get my evidence out. She made the coffee before he came down. Wrong the way he likes it. I could taste it through her hands — you can't taste through someone's hands, I know that, I know the list of things I know — and I sat inside my own head this morning, in the clean kitchen, in the better marriage, drinking it secondhand, and thought: I have to write this down somewhere she'll never read. So. Here. Whoever you are. Page one.

The entity's line is banal in exactly the right way; Daniel's response captures his tendency to let moments close before they open. **Overall:** This is writing that trusts its reader, maintains its ambiguity without cheating, and renders a specific domestic horror with genuine literary craft. The plan is executed with intelligence and the voice is one of the stronger first-person horror voices in recent memory of this type of exercise.
